gottry. FIVE-AND-TWENTY YEARS AGO. Ah, good wife, have you forgotten, Days when you were young and fair? Time of rosy cheeks and dimples, • Time of sunny golden hair? t Not a thought of toil could vex us, Grief and care we did not know; You and I were young together, Five-and-twenty years ago. In the strength of hopeful nianhood, Lithe and straight and tall I stood: And you waited close beside me, Crowned with blooming womanhood; Now life's twilight shades are falling, While the years crowd on apace, L And on heart and form and feature, Care and grief have left their trace. We have hoard the church bell tolling, • . We have filled pale hands with flowers, . We have robed our precious darlings • For the grave's dark, lonely hours; k., We have seen the wee chairs vacant, Aged friends we've bid" Goodbye ;" O'er green graves we've wept together— Au! how often! you and L But the summer's bloom is foll Owed • By the " sere'and yellow leaf," • And the golden harvest comes not Till we break the burdened sheaf. Hearts may love in sunny weather, ; When youth's freshest roses glow, That can ill betide the waiting For the ripening years of snow. But the rapture of love's morning Brightens still our noontide ray, And hope paints a glorious sunset • For our last declining day: And or long or short the journey That our lagging feet may know, Love is ours, the love we plighted Five-and-twenty years ago.

IN EXILE. The sea at the crag's base brightens, And shivers in waves of gold; -And overhead, in its vastness, The fathomless blue is rolled. There comes no wind from the water, There shines no sail on the main, And not a cloudlet to shadow The earth with its fleecy grain. Oh! give in return for this glory, So passionate, warm, and still, The mist of a Highland valley— The breeze from a Scottish hill Day after day glides slowly, Ever and ever the same; Seas of intensest splendour, Airs which smite hot as flame. Birds of imperial plumage, Palms straight as columns of fire, Flutter and glitter around me ; But not so my soul's desire. I long for the song of the laverock, The cataract's leap and flash, The sweep of the red deer's antlers, The gleam of the mountain ash. Only when night is quiescent And peopled with alien stars, • Old faces come to the easement ' - And peer through the vine-leaved bars. No words! But I guess their fancies, Their dreamings are also mine— Of the land of the cloud and heather, The region of Auld Lang Syne. Again we are treading the mountains, Below us broadens the firth, And billows of light keep rolling Down leagues of empurpled earth. Speed swift through the glowing tropics, Stout ship which shall bear me home; Oh, pass, as a God-sent arrow, Through tempest, darkness, and foam; Bear up through the silent girdle 1 That circles the flying earth, Till there shall blaze on thy compass The lode star over the north, That the winds of the hills may greet us, That our footsteps again may be In the land of our heart's traditions, And close to the storied sea. —Chambers's Journal.

A precious carpet has been destroyed in San Francisco. It had covered the floor of one cf the rooms in the Mint, and had been used for five years. The dust of the pre- cious metals used in the coinage had during that period •" • --dilly' fallen up-on it; and when it was takea up the authorities had it cut its small pieces and burned in pans. The ashes were subjected to the process employed with mining dust, and they realised 2,500 dollars. ' Thus, the ; carpet, after years of wear, was more precious than when; it was new. THE Vattrz or OBSERVATICEs7.—I never saw anybody, do anything that I did not watch him and see how he did it, for there was no telling but that some time I might imam? have to do it myself. I was going across a prairie once; LW my horse began to limp. Luckily I came across a black- ; or smith's shop, but the smith was not at home. I asked the woman of the house if she would allow me to start a ! fire and make the shoe. She said I might if I knew how. j So I started a fire and.heated the shoe red-hot, and turned it tort my horse' T foot, and pared the hoof, and turned the points of the nails out cunningly, as I had seen the blacksmith do, so that, in driving into the hoof, ; they should not get into the quick, and I shod the horse.; At the next place I went to I went straight to a smith I and told him to. put the shoe on properly. He looked at ; the horse's foot, and paid me the greatest compliment I ever received in my life. He told me if I put on that shoe I had better follow blacksmithing all my life. Now I never should have known how. to do that if I had not loOked on and seen others do it—H. W. Beecher. CHINESE Viscriwo Ernanirrrs.—The Chinese visiting ; etiquette is that the rank of the caller is denoted by the I size of his card. Thus the visiting card of a high man- darin would be an immense roll of paper, nicely tied up. j Admiral Porter lately engaged a full-blooded Chinese , servant, and Mrs. Porter immediately thereafter held a I reception"—whether to commemorate the employment of the yellow boy" or not is not known. John China- man attended the door, and received with great disgust ; the smell pasteboards of the visitors, and, evidently with an opinion of his own of the low condition' of the Ad- miral's friends, pitched the cards into a basket, and, with scant ceremony, showed their owners into the drawing-room. But presently the gasman called with a bill on a big piece of cream-coloured paper. That "card" satisfied John—with deep reverence he received it. With low salaams he ushered the bearer not only into the drawing-room, but—with profound genuflections— to the dismay of the gasman and horror of Mrs. Porter—led him up to the centre of the room, where that lady was receiving her distinguished guests; and then John, with another humble reverence, meekly retired, doubtless sup- posing that the owner of that card could be no less than the President. Woitxx AN WORE,—We commend to girls who wish or expect to engage in any self-supporting occupation, especially where they may come into competition with men, the following extract from St. Nicholas :—" But girls, if you don't mean to make a thorough business of the occupation you have chosen, never, never, never begin to be occupied at all. Half-finished work will do for amateurs. It will. never do for professionals. The bracket you are sewing for a New Year's present can hang a little crooked on its screws, and you will be for- given ' for the love's sake found therein' by the dear heart to which you offer it; but the trinket carved for sale in the Sorrento Rooms must be cut as true as a rose leaf. You can be a little shaky as to your German de- clensions in the Schiller Club, which you join so enthu- siastically after leaving school, and no great harm ever come of it-; but teach Schiller for a living, and for every dative forgotten you are so much money out of pocket. People who pay for a. thing demand thorough workman- ' shiP,or none. To offer incomplete work for complete maratet Price is to be either a cheat or a beggar. The terrible grinding laws of supply and demand, pay and receive, give and get, give no quarter to shilly-shally labour.The excellence of your intentions is nothing to the point The stress of your poverty has not the slightest connection with the case. An editor will never . pay you for your poem because you wish to help ,your • mother. No customer will buy her best bonnet or her wheat flour of you because You are unable to pay your rent. When you nave entered the world of trade, you ; have entered a world where tenderness and charity, and perSonal interest are foreign relations. Not for friend- ship's sake.' nor for pity's sake,' nor for chivalry's mkes' runs the great rallying cry of this great world, but • only 'for vale received.' It is with sorrow and shame, but yet with hope and courage, that I write it--there is reason for the extensive complaint made by, men, that 7°lnen do not work thoroughly. I am afraid that, till tune and trouble shall have taught them better, they Will not. Is it because they have never been trained ? Is it because they expect to-be married? AN ENOINERR'S STORY.—" Yes, indeed, we have some queer little incidents happen to us," said the engineer, as he plied his oilcan about and under his machine. "A queer thing happened to me one day about a year ago. You'd think it queer for a rough man like me to cry for ten minutes, and nobody hurt either, wpuldn't you? Well, I did, and I can almost cry every tithe I think of it. I was running along one afternoon pretty lively, when I approached a little village where the track cuts through the streets. I slacked up a little, but was still making good speed, when suddenly, about twenty rods in front of me, a little girl, not mdre than three years old, toddled on to the track. You can't even imagine my feelings. There was no way to save her. It was im- 'sck

lessythan that cif selecting a Sire. Our typit... should be short in the legs; loçg, deep, and roomy in the barrel, combined with a general compactness of form and free from hereditary diseases of all kinds. The system of breeding from old, worn.out mares, still pre- vails; when unfit for work they are deemed by some still good enough to breed, but there cannot be a more unsound principle. Although an old mare may occasion- ally throw a good foal, exceptional cases only more clearly prove the rule. Throughout the whole range of Nature, the offspring of aged parents prematurely as- sume the characteristics of old age. . . . As a rule, suckling mares should not be worked, except it be for a day or two during the busy seasons of hay or harvest. We have repeatedly tried th( breeding of horses oh a tillage farm, and are thoroughly convinced of the im- practicability of such a course. Our experience runs thus—during the busy season of preparing the land and putting in the root crops; the suckling mares leave the stable at six o'clock every morning, whilst the foal is shut up in a loose box until the mare returns at mion. Although liberally fed, she is necessarily soft and weak; . .

In ten seconds it would have been all over; and, after re- versing and applying the brake, I shut my eyes. I didn't want to see any more. As we slowed down my fireman stuck his head out of the cab window to see what I'd stopped for, when he laughed and shouted to me, "Jim, look here !" I looked, and there was a big black New- foundland dog holding the little girl in his mouth, leisurely walking towards the house where she evidently belonged. She was kicking and crying so that I knew I she was not hurt, and the dog had saved her. My fire- man thought it funny, and kept on laughing, but I cried like a woman. I couldn't help it. I had a little girl of my own at home." A LAST CENTURY CRARACTER.—With what excitement , did we note any interchange of civility between mother I and Mrs. Clowes, the widow of a clergyman, and who I styled herself in conseqUence the Rev. Anne Clowes. I Although she was known by everybody, and was an i ! honoured if not an acceptable guest n the best houses I of the neighbourhood, she lived quite alone in a narrow withoot a bell or knocker to her house door, on which her friends were instructed to rap loudly with a stone. She occupied an upper room confusedly crowd 4 I with goods and chattels of every description picked u'D I at auctions, and piles of crockery and china, having the 1 casements filled with as many pieces of rag, pasteboard, ' and cobwebs as small panes of glass. She slept in a large salting trough with a switch at her side to keep off the rats. This mean and miserable abode she termed, in her grandiloquent language, "the hallowed spot into j which only were introduced the great in mind, in wealth, !or birth." And on one occasion spoke of 'a most de- lightful visit from two of Lord Waterpark's sons, when • the feast of reason and the flow of soul' had been so absorbing, that one, Mr. Cavendish, in descending the stairs had set his foot in her mutton pie, which was , ready for the oven." Each Whitsuntide we saw her marching at the head of the Oddfellows' Club, with a ' bouquet of lilacs and peonies blazing on her breast up to her chin, holding in one hand a long staff, her usual , outdoor companion. She was not insane, only a very original person, running wild amongst a number of I other eccentric worthies, all of whom left indelible im- pressions on our minds.—Mary Howitt, in Good Words. THE USE OF TEA.—Like alcohol, and all other poisons, tea (says a recent writer) is a stimulant for no other ,• reason than that it is a poison, at least its alkaloid theine and its tannic acid. It stimulates just to the ex- tent that it irritates, the nerves being the special ob- jects of its attacks. The chemical, poisonous stimulant acts only because it is in antagonism—at war with every function of the human body, like the whip and spur exciting increased activity, acting'on the offensive, never creating any real power, no real strength and en- durance. The nerves seem to have a perfect aversion to this tea alkaloid, manifested by a decided attempt to eject the invader whenever it comes in contact with them. This violent expulsive effort, this rousing of the powers of the system to eject a foe in the shortest pos- sible time, to avoid harm, is but another name for stimu- lation. Its well-known power to induce wakefulness while watching with, the sick is attributable to this irri- tating influence over tho nerves, this goading, rasping excitation to an extent to preclude the idea of rest, quiet, comfort, and sleep. The watcher is kept' awake as she would be by any other form of confusion, com- motion—any other form of discomfort and pain. lam at a loss to decide what can be said in favoilr of the use of tea and coffee as beverages, beyond the idea ofsen- sual gratification, whatever may be claimed for them as medicines, as stimulants, always to be followed by de- pression, a loss of power. No one will claim that they were used in the earlier ages of the world, when man was at his best, when he lived for centuries, when his body was agrand magazine of vital force. During the two centuries in which these artificial drinks have been to some extent known to the civilised world, the in- creased consumption of tea has been quite rapid, par- ticularly for the last half-century, previous to which our forefathers knew but little of its general use, being equally ignorant of neuralgia', ,phough there were rare cases of nervous attacks resembling it, generally con- fined to the nerves of the face and head, instead of as at present, attacking all parts of the body • the women, the more especial votaries of the heathen 14, being the special sufferers. It is now estimated that the annual consumption of tea is 3,000,000,000 pounds; of coffee, 1,000,000,000; cocoa and chocolate, 1,000.900 pounds; while similar drinks are used by less civilised nations and:tribes. It is the favourite drink of Russia., Holland, I and England, the last country annually importing 100,000,000 pounds, or several pounds to each man, wofnan, and child. Public Analysts have submitted rAnnmar's COCOA to Close tests and the result has always proved Its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— ..Met.

the separation and consequent irritation tcr the nervous system causes her to return' to the mid-day meal steeped in perspiration, with the bag distended, and the milk streaming from the teats at every step, into much suffering. In this state she is turned the box where the hungry foal sets heartily to work; after a short respite she returns again to work, and again the same contingency is repeated in the even- ing. The extra labour and exertion to which the mare is subjected entails a corresponding waste of animal tissue, hence the leading constituents of the food are expended in -restoring the waste. These facts go far to prove the extreme poverty of the milk, as clearly indicated by the stunted growth of the foal. We have never succeeded in rearing a really strong, healthy foal from a hard-worked mare; and more particularly in the case of young mares, we have, in many instances, permanently injured their constitutions by such a prac- tice. The foal may safely be weaned at the age of five months; the mare should then be taken up and put on dry food." • Beb UDDER.—" J. W." says I have lately had two cows taken with bad udders, more particularly in one hind-quarter. The milk in that quarter comes away clotted and poor, and it is very painful, and, in spite of all I have done, one has lost its milk in that quarter. Will you tell me the best remedy for such cases ?" "J. W." will find the following treatment successful in checking the disease in his cows' udders :—Give each animal a drench composed of of a pound of Epsom salts, oz. of ground ginger, 1 oz. of carraway seed powder, warm water 1* pints; then on the second day after this commence giving each cow 1 oz. of the bicar- bonate Of soda in a pint of water once each day as long as the case requires; also thoroughly bathe the udders with warm water for half an hour each time after milk- ing (which, we presume, is twice a day), then wipe them dry, and well rub in a little extract of belladonna dis- solved in glycerine. The teats from which the clotted milk comes should be frequently drawn so that the clots do not remain long in the udder, where they are a source of irritation and consequently increase the 'disease. Do not give the patients anv food calculated to force the flow of milk, as cake, &c:

Said a conscientious auctioneer: "Ladies and gentle- men, there is no sham about the carpets. They are genuine tapestry carpets. I bought them from old Tapestry hindself." "My dear," said Rattler at the tea table, looking up from his evening paper, "This French-China trouble looks serious." "Yes," answered Mrs. R., "Bridget broke the handle off the sugar-bowl to-day, but I didn't think you would notice it so soon." On seeing, "Milton, Livery Stable Keeper," written over a mews, Hook composed the following impromptu lines

"Two Miltons In separate ages were born, The clever Milton 'tis clear we have got; Though the other had talents, the world to adorn, This lives by his mews, which the other could not!" HOLIDAY PnovEnss.—He's a wise traveller that knows his time-table. A bag in the hand is better than a port- manteau in the van. The nearer the pier the greater the rush. A friend with a house at the seaside is a friend indeed. Too many Cockney tourists spoil the trip. A full house at night is the hotel Imeper's delight. div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING;! to think' tha- weeds pertain liaturaily to
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING;! to think' tha- weeds pertain liaturaily to

poor soils. ',But, as the Rod tells us, "Most subject is the fattest soil to weeds. Like other plants, they love best to grow in the richest soils. The pertinacity or hardiness of weeds is, however, superior to that of most cultivated plants, so that when the intruders,once get a ..place in the soil they. possess an advantage. Yet, whether we meet with them in rich or poor soil, their presence is indicative of slnggardliness and neglect on the part of the cultivatdr. The annual loss occasioned by this neglect, on a single farm, is often very great. It behoves every farmer, indeed, not only to wage inces- sant war with weeds that show themselves on his land, but to take very good care that he does not introduce a seeding of them by means of manures, and by means of farm seeds which have been badly ,cleaned. Weeds differ greatly in their nature. Some are annuals, others are perennials; some are only propagated by seeds,' others have creeping roots, and are propagated from these, whilst others, again, are propagated both by roots and from seeds. Annual weeds grow chiefly amongst corn and other arable crops; and as they every year spring up from seeds, it is a very difficult matter for the farmer to prevent their increase. The seeds of most of the annual weeds will lie in the ground for many years, if they happen to be placed deep; so that all land is more or less impregnated with them, and a fresh supply is produced every time the land s ploughed. The only effectual mode of getting rid of them is either by hoe- ing them up when young, or by cutting the plants over with any instrument when in bloom. Creeping-rooted weeds, of the perennial kind, are of the most trouble- some nature, and extremely difficult to get rid of. It unfortunately happens that, where the land is Most worked, and the roots the more broken thereby, the more the crop of weeds increases' on the land. Therefore, the only effectual mode of extirpating i plants of this nature s by picking out the roots after the plough or cultivator, and by forking them up at every opportunity. But, as prevention is better than cure, more care ought to be taken than generally is of an our hedges and waste pieces of land by, roadsides, &c. Many of these plants are found growing in such places, and their seeds are of that nature that they are calcu- lated to fly consiierable distances. Those perennial weeds which are not creeping-rooted, although they are very troublesome, are more easy of extirpation; for, as they do not spread underground, they are effectually removed by taking up the plants by their roots. And if weeds are to be destroyed at all, the time to attack them is when they are young. Old Tusser would have been at them ere this, for he says— In May get a weedhook, a crotch, and a glove, And weed out such weeds as the corn doth not love. All fields should be weeded several times in regular suc- cession earlier than this, in order to keep the land and the crops thoroughly clean. It is wonderful how little labour suffices to do this when it is judiciously applied at the right time. Never mind if the land looks clean, put the hoe over it; the land is never so clean as it looks, and even if there be no weeds to kill, the hoe will be pro- ductive of great good in freeing and aerating the surface of the soil, and thus promoting growth in the crops. Besides, when land is in this condition, the work is easier and better done; whereas if the weeds are allowed to grow till they rival the crop, process of cleaning is not only more expensive but less satisfactory in the end. This is the only way to defy the weeds, whether they are annual or perennial. If destroyed as soon as they show themselves above ground, they cannot develop and live. In the case of non-drilled crops, these should be regularly hand-weeded and picked over, say, once a fort- night in the season. Some weeds in pastures should also be hand-pulled, or carefully dug out with the spud; others may merely be mown down sufficiently often to prevent their seeding. EXIIIBMNO VEGETABLES.—The setting up of a collec- tion of vegetables on the exhibition table has something to do with awarding the prizes. It is customaryto pro- vide staging for vegetables, but at times no provision is made beyond the grass covered by the tent, and the ex- hibitors have laid out their exhibits on that. Others have acted more judiciously, and brought their products already arranged in round, shallow hampers. The baskets should be filled up with soft, dry grass, nearly to the edge, and slightly raised in the centre, so that when the vegetables are arranged they will assume a convex form. Each dish of vegetables in the basket should be arranged in a circle as, far as practicable, and space left all round, which might be filled with parsley or nice green moss. Where the stage methons adopted these baskets unless made purposely, are too cumber- some, neitheli is the shape suitable. Shallow trays are, however, well adapted, and the vegetables can. be arranged on them at home if the journey is a short one, -itherwise they are best packed in a hamper, and dealt _ .
We are

BLO . with in the exhibition. Too much care cannot be exer- cised in packing, or it will be found that they will have many rasures on them. Potatoes, Turnips, or Carrots rubbing against each other will alter their appearance by the time they are Staged. In order to avoid this plenty of parsley or soft grass must be used for packing. As vegetables intended for exhibition should not be handled too much, those that are inexperienced in arranging should practice with the same things of in- ferior kinds so that on the exhibition day haste and con- fusion will be avoided,'aa well as frequent handling of the vegetables. To have an idea of the size of tray re- quired the inferior collection of vegetables should be first arranged on a table, &the tray may be too small, which would spoil the whole affair if made haphazard and taken to the exhibition. After all are placed the tray should be raised at the back about Cin. with a block or two of wood, so that they may be readily seen by tho visitors. Judges should also allow a few points for effective arrangement. All vegetables are best collected together either early in the morning or in the evening. . .

If "gathered during sunshine they -soon become flabby, and no amount of coaxing will induce them to regain their crispness. All roots, such as Turnips and Carrots, should be washed, but there must be no severe rubbing to cause scratching, as the marks will all show when the roots dry. The contents of every dish should be as near alike as possible, and large coarse samples must be .e- -jected where there is a choice. Large Turnips, for in- stance, at this season of the year are usually "woolly," and devoid of sweetness and it is always best to cut one or two that are not likely to be required down the centre, so as to have some idea of their soundness. Peas are very deceptive; many that appear full when opened have the peas about half-grown, and not fit for exhibi- tion at that stage. Other pods that appear little naore than half-grown will have fair-sized peas and if left till the pods become what may be considered fully developed they would be too old, and their sweetness gone. Till the grower is thoroughly acquainted with the habit of the different varieties he will do well to examine a few pods, and when he has ascertained the stage at which' they are tender and sweet he will have no difficulty in selecting others similar. Much care should be exercised in gathering the Peas, or the bloom with which some of the pods are covered will be rubbed off, and instead of handling them in the usual way we prefer to use a pair of scissors. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The rain of the past few days has been highly beneficial to front gardens situated near public thoroughfares, inasmuch as it has washed the dust off the foliage. For some days previously it was Quite distressing to look at vegetation near the road sides, so thickly covered had everything become with dust. What the rain has now done to the occupants of our front garden many ecottager might have partially done by a little effort providing he had a few gallons of water at his command. To wash the foliage it is not necessary to be possessed of watering pots with various sizes of spreaders. A moderate-sized preserved meat tin or two with holes made in the bottom will form excel- lent substitutes if held over the plants and the water poured into them from another vessel. It will descend with sufficient force to wash the dust if the tin is held high enough. Tag Wumow.—Tropaeolum Tricolorum has been suc- cessfully grown in cottage windows. The plant flowers during April and May, but a few weeks earlier when grown in a greenhouse. A specimen was exhibited last March at the Preston and Fulwood Horticultural Society's Show, when its black orange, yellow balloon-shaped flowers attracted considerable attention. The plant has been totally neglected, and has become rather scarce. 'The tubers should be procured at once and potted in fresh rough turfy loam with about one-sixth of leaf mould and a •sprinkling of said, in which they cannot fail but grow. Beginners might succeed better if they could purchase them in the pots just as they are starting to grow.

TRAP ACCIDENT TO A BARONET—AS Sir Robert Con- life was driving through Chester from Aston Hall, Wrex- ham, on Tuesday, his carriage caught in the tramway metals, and the horses fell, overturning the vehicle and throwing Sir Robert and ,his coachman on the road. Beyond a severe shaking Sir Robert was not hurt, and was able to proceed on his journey to London. Some of BossVell's sayings were really worthy of pre- servation. Of these not the worst was his thrust at the stupid fellow who was declahning against the kind of raillery called "roasting," and who added, ",I am sure I have agreat deal of good nature—l never roast any." "Why, sir, said Boswell, "you are an exceedingly good- natured man, to be sure; but I can give you a better reason for never roasting any. Sir, you never roast any because you have got no fire." M. S. Pusisou..—Mr. Samuel Plimsoll has consented to become the Liberal candidate for the Central Division of Sheffield. He had received invitations to stand for Feveral constituencies, but he hesitated to accept any on account of his health. Now that it is greatly improved, he has been strongly pressed to become a candidate in the central divi- sion, in opposition to Mr. Howard Vincent. Mr. Plimsoll visited Sheffield on Tuesdiy, and after a long interview with the leaden of the Liberal Association for the division, he unreservedly placed himself in their hands. When completed the work will be included among the publications of the Cheatham Society. .The letters of Thackeray, which Messrs. Scribner are , about to publish, are reported to be of more than ordinary interest. It is stated that, "as was his wont, Thackeray enriched those letters with numberless little pen-and-ink sketches, all of which will be faithfully reproduced." Further, that "the letters are published with the full authorisation of the surviving tnembers of Thackeray's family. PHOTOGRAPHING THE LARYNX.—Dr. Steine, a French electrician, has devisecta,very handsome little apparatus for enabling surgeons to photagraph the larynx, and thus obtain a record of the progress of certain throat disorders from day to day. The apparatus consists of a very small electric incandescent lamp, which illuminates the throat, and is kept cool by circulating water, and s small camera with gelatine-bromide plates. The com- bined apparatus is neatly mounted in a portable form, and provided with a battery to supply the necessary current.

A RAILWAY Psnoitgrgii.—Herr Stork, the Director of Swedish Railway Telegraphs, has invented an electric apparatus which promises to become valuable for pre- venting railway collisions The apparatus indicates at stations the place of the train on the line. This is dope by a contact device set at intervals along the rails, and the train in passing it closes an electric circuit and works a needle indicator at the station which points out the locality of the train. The details of Herr Stork's invention are not yet made public; but it is being tried on the Liljeholman Railway, near Stockholm, and 'is found to work satisfactory. Pianoforte players have always complained of the diffi- culty of making the ring-finger work as freely as the others, and according to the British Medical Journal, Mr. Noble Smith, of Queen Anne-street, has by a delicate operation succeeded in enlarging the powers of the pian- ist. He says; "I have just succeeded in freeing the ring- " finger of the right hand of an accomplished lady pianist, I without causing her much more pain than is felt from the prick of a needle. Before operation she was able to raise the finger only five-eighths of an inch beyond the others. Directly after operation she could raise the finger easily to one and a half inches, 'without the least feeling of loss of control over its action. The division was, of course, made subcutaneously, so that only a minute wound was left in the skin, one-eighth of an inch in length." The excavations at Olympia are to be recommenced immediately under the auspices of the Greek Archieo- logical Society of Athens. On these excavations the German Government has expended so far a million marks, £20,000 more than is generally supposed, the sums voted by the Reichstag and granted by the Em- peror having been supplemented at a later date by tb large bequest from an unknown quarter in Berlin. It is declared by those best qualified to judge that two-thirds of the site of Olympia still remain to be excavated. The Germans themselves however, seem to be glad to have done With the work, as they have cleared out the prin- cipal parts where the richest harvest of trouvaille was expected, while nationally they have derived very little profit from the undertaking. They think they made a great mistake in stipulating only fer duplicates of what they found, as of course no important objects existed in duplicate. They fancy that nothing of any great artistic value can now be found in the vast area of the Stadium or in the other outlying structures; but the Greek so- ciety has determined to clear away the vast nriss of superineumbent earth, and to bring back the whole site to the original level, so that the lines of ancient Olympia may be clearly discerned. The local museum, the gift of a patriotic Greek gentleman is a large building now troofed over, and is being plastered. In a few months it will be ready for the reception of the Statues and bronzes already found. COMETS THAT MAY COMB IN VIEW THIS YEAR.— Several periodical comets may be expected to return to perihelion during the present year. Ericke's comet has already put in an appearance, having passed its peri- helion on the 7th of March. It was detected in 1884, but as comets techically belong to the year in which they pass perihelion, Encke's comet finds place on the records of 1885. This comet is our oldest friend among the class to which it belongs, for it was first seen in 1786, though its periodicity was not discovered until 1819. Since that time it has not failed to make us a visit at intervals of about three and one-third years. Olbers's comet is an- other celestial guest whose return is looked for during the present year. It was discovered by Olbers in 1815, and 'was found by Bessel to have a period of about 75 years. It will, therefore, probably appear either this year or the next. It will be as warmly welcomed, it it -deign to make us a second visit, as the comet of 1812, or the Pons- Brooks comet was last year, for it will rank as third on the list of comets of a long period that have made more than one record return. Halley's comet, with a period of about 75 years, stands first on the list. It has been traced back to the year 1456, and since that time has Made five record returns, the last being in 1835. It will be due in 1911. The comet of 1812, or the Pons-Brooks comet, made its first recorded return during the last year. If the comet of 1815, or Olbers's comet, visit us during the year or the succeeding one the solar system can rejoice in the possession of three comets of a long period, as they are called, to distinguish them from the larger family of comets of a short period. Tempel's comet of 1867 was expected to reach perihelion in April. It has a period of about six years, was first observed in 1867, was seen I again in 1873 and 1879, and was due in April, but has not yet made its appearance. On the 13th of March, Dr. Gautier, of Geneva discovered a suspicious celestial I that was thought to be the expected visitor. Diligent search was made for it at the principal observatories, but without success, for the object soon proved to be a far- away nebula. Either some unforeseen calamity has de- layed its advent, or OM of the giant planets has turned it into a new course by its resistless power of attraction. Tempel also discovered a second comet of a short period in 1889. It was discovered by Swift in 1880, when its periodicity was determined. It is consequently known as Swift's comet, and has a period of five and a half years. It is expected to return to perihelion at the end of the year. But it is likely to pass unseen at its pre- sent return, as it did in 1875, being, in like manner, in an unfavourable position for observation. One more comet closes the list of members of the cometic family that are expected to return to perihelion in 1885. It is Tuttle's comet, and seems to occupy a position of its own, having a period of 13i years, end therefore ranking neither with comets of a long period nor with those of a short period. It was first discovered by Mechain in 1790, and rediscovered by Tuttle in 1858, when its periodicity was recognised. It was observed in 1871, passing its perihelion in November. It was therefore due in July of the present year. • ,

BY THOMAS GIBBONS. Author of " Boxing the Compass," "Naval Songs and Song Writers,"" The Way to lehang," No. IX.—ITEMS OF JAPANESE FOLK-LORE Japan is a land of myth and legend, and the middle and lower classes, as a rule implicitly believe the quaint tale and traditions repeated in every Japanese household. The fears and fancies of our ancestors, as associated with animals, birds, insects, herbs, odd numbers, and the spilling of salt, have their parallel in the folk-lore of Japan to-day. Tales of the supernatural abound. A good story-teller is highly appreciated, and speedily be- comes a favourite with the women and children, espe- cially in the country districts. Salt is associated with . many Japanese supertitions. We find evidence of this during first walk in the country. At the entrance of native cemeteries, at the doors of Japanese houses, and before the shrines in the temples, we see little earthern pots of salt placed as offerings. The Japanese regard the 'presence of death as defiling, and salt is used for purifieatoryiourposes. It is sprinkled abont the house after a funeral, and people who attend the corpse to the grave use salt to free themselves from contamination. At special festival seasons, observed for purification, salt is scattered over the ground. Throwing salt in the fire averts evil. It prevents family quarrels I also. It is unlucky to buy salt in the day-time, unless a small portion is cast in the fire; but no one will buy salt at night. To accidentally upset newly-purchased salt is a sign of impending peril. If a person, trimming his finger nails, allows a clipping to fall into the fire, he receives it as a death warning. Salt, however, may be burned to ward off the danger. Japanese wrestlers eat salt before closing in the combat. Perhaps it is supposed practically to illustrate the Japanese proverb of "rubbing salt on a sore"—i.e. adding insult to injury. Rice being the staple food of the Japanese, we can , understand that it comes I in for a share of popular ' beliefs. All taxes were formerly paid in rice, and the wealth of a family was estimated at So many koku of rice. The wealth of one of the three illustrious families was assessed at 810,500 koku of rice. The Samurai (the great literary and military class) paid their retainers in a daily ration of rice; some of them above the coitimon rank, received additional rations. Sanctified rice can be bought in many Japanese temples. Stalls abound, laden with sanctified sweets and gram, and the bonzes (priests) make a: revenue out of the sales. Visitors buy the rice, as a religions observance to feed the pigeons and bantam fowls usually found about the temples. Buddhist law forbids the destroying of life; consequently many birds and soimali find a safe refuge within the precincts of the temples. Sickness awaits children who eat burned rice taken out of the pot after 'boiling. Young people who persistently eat the charred grains after a warning are sure to get pock-marked husbands and wives. Red rice is served on occasions of expected good fortune or great family rejoicings. Friends are asked to assemble at these gatherings. Beet roots or beans are boiled with the rice to colour it. If the red is not bright and clear, it foreshadows evil to the family and loss of fortune. On the fifth day of the fifth month the Japanese eat rice bound with an edible leaf and boiled. The custom is evidently of Chinese origin, and dates back twenty-three hundred years. A distinguished Chinese minister, named Chu Yuan, drowned himself on this day, vowing he could not survive the ruin of his country. He was greatly beloved by his people, who, failing to find his body, were accustomed to scatter rice on the water to nourish his spirit. But his shade appeared to many of them complaining that a dragon seized the rice from him, and he was unable to benefit by the compassionate act of the people he begged that the rice might be wrapped in the leaves of the di plant, a vegetable highly poisonous to the serpent family. It was done, and the spirit of the minister was appeased. The Japanese consider that May is a very unlucky month, and fraught with especial evil with those who chance to marry within its limits. Young people would just as soon wear purple-coloured garments at a wed- din, a colour typical of the speedy cooling of the affec- tions. It is a very unlucky circumstance for a birth to occur on the fifth day. If the offspring is a girl it will do harm to its mother; while a son born on that day will assuredly work harm to its father. We have heard many stories relating to the fifth day of the fifth month. One Goko was born on that unlucky date. The child Was placed by his father in a little boat of bulrushes, and left among the weeds near the river bank. A traveller discovered and adopted the child. The foundling be- came a distinguished man. In time Goko's parents ap- peared at Ns house and claimed irom him the perform- ance Of filial duties. The son, as a good citizen, would not violate the most important obligation of his nation, but t• leave his preserver would be an act of equal in-,' gratitude. But he quickly decided and replied, "I have no parents; my home is a boat of bulrushes," to which he retired, and therein spent the remaining years of his life. Although the day is marked as unlucky in the matter of birth, it still is the occasion of a peculiar ob- servance highly gratifying to Japanese boys. On the fifth of May the "Feast of Flags "is celebrated. Long previous to the day, which is anxiously looked for, the shops are lull of toys of a martial character swordsand helmets, drums and regalia, and effigies of soldiers and wrestlers. The lads are well pleased to obtain such articles. It is customary for parents, too, on this day, to hang a nobozi—a paper representation of a large fish On a high bamboo pole--outside the house, as a sign that there are sons in the family. The paper fish being hollow, with open mouth, the wind fills out the body, giving it a very natural appearance. Thousands of these Ashes are to be seen swapmg in the air on the occasion of the festival. Tradition well accounts for the martial character of the day. When Japan feared a foreign in- vasion the duty of protecting the country was intrusted to a commander who was unable to muster very many followers. He bethought himself of his idol, and for hours he prayed to it for supernatural aid. As the in- vaders approached, on the fifth day of the fifth month, a terrible typhoon (great wind) swept over the coast and destroyed the enemy. It is worth noting, in this connection, that Marco Polo mentioned an attempt made about 1281, by the Great Mongol (Kublai Khan), to invade Japan, and the destruction of his fleet by a fearful storm. Matsuri, or religious festivals, are observed all over the country. At such times the people dress in their gayest clothing, and mark the occasion by signs of great mirth and festivity. One of the most notable is the Feast of Lanterns at the paves of the dead. We have witnessed several ceremonies of the kind. The principal feature of the occasion is the illumination of the graves with lanterns, and viewed at a distance, around the hills over- looking Nagasaki harbour, the effect is very novel and striking. On this occasion, according to the Buddhist belief, the spirits of the dead return to their families, remaining with them until the evening of the third day; and the living relatives, for their entertainment, spread the tomb with sweetmeats, fruits, cakes, and saki (a ' native wine). It is no season of mourning. Thousands of people visit the cemeteries, and strangers are freely invited to share in the festivities. On the last night of the festival, small straw boats, laden with saki, rice and fruits, are launched on the water, ready for the passage of the spirits back to Hades. Before sending them adrift, the people set fire to the boats, to light the spirits of the dead to their resting place. Harts Kin, the act of self-disembowelling, was the recognised heroic death of vanished military commanders and others until very recently. It is still occasionally practised, but by a remnant only of the exclusive Japanese aristocracy, the Samurat. In order to preserve his honour, when defeated in battle, it was customary for a general to commit hara-kiri. Many of his relatives and vassals did likewige, out of respect for their master. Some centuries ago, especially during the military age in Japan, we learn of innumerable instances of immolation, and retainers offered themselves for burial alive. Perhaps that ancient manner of sacrifice led to the horrible custom of providing a "living prop" for the support of river banks and castle foundations. When the construction of new embankments was in progress in districts subject to inundations, purely patriotic men have submitted to be buried • alive in order that their spirits might protect and give strength to the founda- tion. It was necessary that the devotee should be of good repute among his neighbours. Four men were buried under the new forts at Tokio (Yeddo), and a man was buried alive, 1865, at Ishikawa, to support the em- barkment of the creek near Yokohama. Such occasions of sacrifice were observed as a religious ceremony, crowds of people assembling to witness the interment. Household beliefs and proverbs are numerous, and we hear them constantly quoted during conversation to "point a moral or adorn a tale." We select a few of the most popular. The Japanese lay their dead with head to the north and feet to the south, and the living are care- ful to avoid reclining in that position when going to sleep. It is counted unlucky to sweep a house imme- diately after the departure of one of its inmates on a journey; it sweeps out all good fortune. A person who eats first fruits of the season is supposed to have seventy-five days added tolis life. Should a sick per- son accidentally upset the cup of medicine it is a sign of recovery. Girls who pour hot water or tea into a bowl of red ice will have a rainy wedding night. Large ears in women indicate longefity of their husbands. Ugly women have no wish to use a looking-glass. The folklore of Japan is replete with traditions of the tender constance and quiet bravery of the daughters of the land. The idol Dal Butsu (Great Buddha), one of the wonders of Japan, is supposed to tell a tale of women's devotion. It is said that, in the thirteenth century, Its, one of the palace ladies of the Shogun (General) Yorito- mo, went on a pilgrimage through Japan, and succeeded in collecting a sum sufficient to pay for the erection of an enormous wooden idol, but a terrible typhoon swept it • away. Nothing daunted, the lady set out on a Second pilgrimage, and met with such eminent ' success that she was enabled to erect thq great bronze Buddha now at Kamakura. The legend of Boshayamad (mountain) is another tale of woman's tenderness. From the bank of the broad Chihumagawa (river), one of the most picturesque spots in Japan, rises the haunted mountain. In former times, during a war between two princes, the nurse of the infant son of the vanquished prince took refuge in the mountains with the child, and there kept it concealed from the conqueror. At length both nurse and child died; and now—so the country people thereabouts aver—the nurse's voice mayoftenfbe heard among the mountains during the night, calling or the lost child. A pretty thread for the minstrel's art,
and Miss Effin Isabella Tupper has turned the lege° into verse:— •
A JAPANESB

When the dogs of war were at large, And all the land at strife, A loving nurse took her infant charge And fled to save its life: Fled to the mountains away, With eager step and look, And there for many a day They dwelt in a laidden nook. Dwelt secure, till at length Both child and nurse must die! „ With dimming eye, and with failing strelpgio, Within the cave they lie. No trace they leave behind, For the outer world to tell Where their bodies to seek and to find, To give them burial. And years hay passed since then, Yet the moubtain's depths are stirr'al At the midnight hour' again and again, A wailing sound is heard: And the traveller listens with dread, 'Forkhe knows that murmur wild Is the voice of one who has long laid 0161'4 Calling her dear lost child.

I LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

On Satarday, the 79th half-yearly general meeting of the , proprietors in this compaey took place at the offices, Euston Station, Mr. R. Moon in the chair. The report of the , directors, an abstract of which has appeared, was taken as read. The CirlinatAN said they would have been pleased to see, with regard to the capital account, that the directors were now asking them for a vote for only £598,000, including the different items in the bill of last session ; and the arrange- ments they had made enabled them to cancel votes for about £630,000. In point of fact, therefore, the amount of capital for which they were now liable had been reduced to some- under £3,700,000. They proposed in the preeent half-year to spend only £550,000, and they did not intend to have a bill in Parliament in the next session. (Applause.) Taking the year altogether, from the 30th of June, 1884, they had earned the dieidends they had declared, and added £3,000 to the reserve. Perhaps the moat satisfactory item in the accounts was the small amount for compensation. During the last two and a half years they had carried 135,000,000 passengers, and had had no fatal injuries owing to any fault of the company or their servants. There had been some minor injuries, but they had not been much, and the whole amount paid for personal injuries in the half-year had been only £3,150. On the other side, looking at the revenue account again, the most unsatisfactory feature was the large loss on the working of the Birmingham Canal. They guaranteed a Small dividend to that canal, but such was the state of the trade of the country that, even in the heart of England, they had to put by a large amount to pro- vide for the contingent loss. Besides that, for the first time the number of their third-class passengers hsd fallen off in the half-year. If they wanted anything to show the depressed state of the trade of the country, these two items spoke volumes. Ile concluded by moving the adoption of the report and the half-yearly statement of ac- counts.—Mr. W. CAW/SWELL seconded the motion.—Mr. T. Anems thought if next session they could get the passenger duty brought down to ld per mile all round, it would save immense trouble and litigation.—The Commute, in reply, said that as to the question about the North Union Railway and the other companies, the circumstances altegether dif- fered. The North-Western Company were practically owners of a certain portion of what had been the North Union Railway. It went from Preston to Bolton on the one side, and from Preston to Parkside on the other. The North-Western Company owned the piece from Parkside to Euxton, the Lancashire and Yorkshire Company owned the piece from Bolton to Euxton, and the intermediate piece from Euxten to Preston was joint. From Preston to Park- ride the North-Western Company worked toll free, and they gave no account whatever of the transaction to the North Union Company. The company worked harder now than ever, they had more trains to run, and the competition Was fiercer than ever, because the companies struggled keenly for what little traffic there was. With respect to terminals, he had never had any doubt that they were entitled to charge. They would try and keep up the dividend of the company, but they would endeavour in every way to meet the traders as fairly as they could. He then put the motion, which was carried unanimously.—The following dividends were next declared for the half-year ended June 30th last :—.£2 upon each .£lOO of 4 per cent. consolidated guaranteed stock and consolidated preference stock, and £3 upon each £lOO of consolidated stock, and so in proportion for any less amount.—On the motion of the Commute, resolutions were next passed sanctioning the addition to the capital of the company of the sums of £385,933 and £204,403 for the execution of works. A special meeting was afterwards held, at which the Luis. ing of various sums was sanctioned.

div.head: SHALL WE REPUDIATE FREE TRADE? BY H. Warrant.
div.p: SHALL WE REPUDIATE FREE TRADE? BY H. Warrant.

Fair Traders need not be surprised because Free Traders refuse to accept appointments on the Royal Commission to inquire into trade depression. There are a thousand and one reasons why any attempt to tamper with the principles of Free Trade should not have the support of eminent political economists. The experience of • business men, and it is to these we must look, is that to the greater freedom of trade and to the still wider spread of Free Trade we must look for the possibilities of holding our own in the world's markets. A pamphlet, headed "The Revival of British Industries," is now being vigorously circulated amongst the people, written by "A Can- didate." It sets forth the kind of legislation we are likely to have should the people be so far misgnided as to support Fair Traders. We are asked to put so , Der cent, on manufactured goods. The object evi- dently is to keep these goods out of our markets, but the writer goes on to say that we should gain the •1 amount of £7,500,000, entirely losing sight of the ' prohibitive tax. With this £7,500,000 that is to be i raised from goods that we should not import, the Fair I Trade candidate proposes 'that a subsidy of one ! pound per acre should be paid each year on all the , land in the United Kingdom which is sown with wheat." This is the kind of nonsense that is placed , before the people in order to induce them to support 1 Fair Trade. It should not take an extraordinary sharp man to say into whose pocket this one pound per acre would ultimately fall, nor out of whose pocket it must first come. It is but ' another trick to secure the lasdlord his rent. I think I have proveel, in previous letters, that we are to a great extent using a wrong term when we speak of elepressed trade; small profits would be a more accurate phrase. It must be understood that , the competitive system that now rules the whole of the manufacturing world is but the growth of the last twenty years. During the last ten years we have s. felt its effect, and we are now in this position, each manufacturer is bound to produce as much as possible from his machinery; he is also bound to have the , best machinery. He hopes 'by attending to these matters to reduce his expenses to the least possible point. The manufacturers of England, the Continent, America, Russia, and India, ell attending to these points, finally produce a glut in the market, that is, in the words of the President of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, "If all manufacturers throughout the world would agree to reduce pro- duction, there might he some ,hopes of an improve- ment in trade." .As this is simply impossible, we must look to other sources for help. In the speech already referred to are these words, " It was perfectly clear that in point of trade the supremacy of Great Britain had really passed away, owing to the in- creased facilities of communisation atid the increased out-turn of the industries of other countries." I sug- gest that these are pregnant words, coming as they do from the President of the most important Chamber of Commerce in the kingdom. We speak of depressed trade, and yet the same speaker goes on to say that " In Oldham the spinners were really contending for a reduction in production," which anyone may see is simply suicide to the trade. It is clear from these arguments that to repudiate Free Trade would be to turn our back en our best friend, It must also be clear that with constantly improving machinery, followed by a constantly increasing output, we must pay greater attention to new markets It is mere childishness to look to our colonies; until it suits them to change their fiscal policy we must do the best we can. Evidence is not wanting that wherever Protection exists individuals become rich at the expense of the community. Can anyone look a,t Ire- land and say that all that was possible has been done to encourage her trade? We have no need to go back to times when barbarous and most inhuman laws were passed for the sole purpoae of stamping out her trade. Things almost as bad are done now. For instance, the freight for coal from Belfast to Omagh (sixty- nine miles) is 7s od, or more than double that from Wigan to Stafford (66 miles, 34 8d per ton). Coals can be carried from Ayrshire to Ireland at 25 per ton, while the rate of freight from the landing place in Ireland by rail for io miles is 25 411 per ton. The flax, woollen, and other industries may well suffer when it is cheaper to send certain classes of goods from Ireland to England and re-ship them to ports in Ireland. And yet the Tories sided with the railway interest in its opposition to Mr. Chamberlain's railway reforms, and expect working-men to give them their support. Mr. Parnell owns a granite quarry at Bellynaelnsh, and brings over Welsh quarrymen to teach Wicklow men how to square the stones, yet ever since Dublin streets were paved they have been laid with Welsh setts, and Dublin Custom House was built of Portland stone. In conclusion, I say, as one entirely dependent upon labour, that if working-men , support the Fair Traders they will be supporting what cannot possibly give them relief. No Royal Com- mission can tell manufacturers more than they know es to remedies and what can it tell working-men? Nothing. Wi:at I tell them is this ;at home, aiding a ruinous competition which must simply end in mak- ing their yoke mcre galling, they are competing with their fellow working-men abroad, which must con- tinue this system. As workmen, their remedy is to unite in sinh a fashion that the Trades' Congress shall be truly representative of British skilled and unskilled labour. When this is done thoroughly they will then hemn a position to take steps for form- ing one grand International Parliament of capital creators, and may possibly see then that it is better to manufacture for use than for profit. As it is we have factories and shops full of goods, and the poor are starving in our streats.

Everything known to the medical faculty was tried in vain. I became 13 At times could not lift my hands to my he in bed, was in constant pain, and looked upon lire as a curse.
