Mr. STELFOR supported this opinion. Mr. Bea Low said the question of tithes was a somewhat complicated' one, but he did not wish to convey by his answer that he particularly wished the landlord to be saddled with the tithes but rather that he wished the tenant should not be saddled with them. It was only fair that he as the descendant of an old Quaker family, and whose ancestor had often been distrained upon for tithes,should say that he had got no particular affection for tithes. (Applaese ) Mr. BROADBENT moved "That this meeting considers Mr. W. E. Barlow to be a fit and proper person to represent the Knutsford Division of the county of Chester in Parliament, and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his return at the next election." The Knutsford division, he said, was a strange and funny arrangement; it stretched and straggled half over the county of Chester. However, it had been done by the wisdom of the Commissioners, assisted by Lord Egerton of Tatton. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It Was certainly not the most convenient !or the inhabitants of Cheshire, but it had had the good effect of bringing them in some very good men formerly belonging to east Cheshire, and amongst the rest it had brought in Mr. Barlow. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the great measure of reform which Mr. Gladstone and his Government had passed, he said they must remember that the constituents of the Knutsford Division did not consist entirely of farmers, but he could assure those other electors that Mr. Barlow would understand their posi- tion as well as he did that of the farmers. In fact he (Mr. Broadbent) took the view that when properly understood the interest of one class was the interest of all. (Rear, hear.) That constituency and other constituencies would be wooed net alone by Liberals and Conservatives but also by Tory democrats, who did one thing in opposition and quite a different thing in power, but he thought the elector. would be able to distinguish between those people who were in favour of Liberal measures merely as a matter of expedi- eocy, and those who advecate them on principle. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. BRADFORD seconded the resolution. Mr. Jenne CROSFIELD, who was received with loud ap- plause, said he had not meddled with the politics of the county of Cheshire heretofore. He had weight enough on his shoulders in Warrington without going anywhere else. They knew Warrington was a very hot place when they started a political battle, and they should have some warm work there during the next two months. (Hear, hear.) His friend and neighbour, Sir Gilbert, was coming out as a Tory candidate, and he intended to win, if he could— (laughter)—and they intended that he shouldn't. (Ap- plause and laughter.) He was very glad to be there that night, and very pleased to listen to the speech from Mr. Bar- low, which was sound and Liberal, and he thought it was a good deal in Mr. Barlow'', favour that he came from a Quaker stock. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) There had been one question asked that night which he was interested in a good deal, and that was the question of tithes. He said, abolish them altogether. (Applause.) It grieved him every time he had to pays tithe, and he thought it was an infam- ous thing that he had to contribute money which was sent, as he understood, to Oxford to maintain a church there, and moreover he was told that there was a wealthy land- lord in Cheshire who made £2,000 a year in farming these tithes. (Hear, hear.) It was high time they did away with them. He did not went to put the tithe on the landlord ; he did not want eitheelandlord or tenant to pay, but he said abolish them. (Applause.) If Mr. Barlow went into the House of Commons he hoped he would vote for a total abolition of these tithes. It was true that the members of the Society of Friends had borne distraint and even im- prisonment in days gone by rather than ply these tithes, and it was a monstrous thing that such tithes should be levied on the people of this country to support one denomi- nation. (Hear, hear.) If the tithe was spread equally all over every denomination he should not care so much about it, but it was an injustice that they should pay tithe to go to one denomination. Therefore he would vote for abolish- ing them altogether. (Applause.) There was one thing he wanted them to remember which was that those who were going to have votes now and never had them before owed them to the Liberal party ; they owed them more to Glad- stone and Bright than to any other two living men. (Ap- plause.) Let them not be gulled or have the dust thrown In their eyes by the Conservatives, who would try to argue that they were the party who had given them the votes. Their trick had been ever since he could remember to steal the Liberals' clothes whilst they were bathing—to pick up Liberal measures when they got into office. (Hear, hear.) These last two months the Tories had passed a few measures just on purpose to get the credit when they went before the people at the time of the election, and they would not have had the power to pass these measures had not the Liberals behaved to them like gentlemen and allowed them to pass them, whereas when the Liberal party was in office, as they knew, the Conservatives by their obstruction stopped many a measure passing which would have done so otherwise. (Hear, hear.) There had been a paper circulated a goad deal ; one bad been sent to him, and he expected one had been sent to Mr. Barlow and every candidate throughout the country. It was celled "The Revival of British Inter- ests," and was a rather cleverly written little pamphlet, and apt to take the head of a good many people. In this pamphlet the anonymous writer suggests that manu- factures imported into this country should be taxed and that the farmers should be given L 1 an acre for every acre of wheat that was grown in the country. He had no doubt the farmers would think that was a very good thing. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) It was very pleasant for him to have Ll an acre to put into his pocket, but let them listen for a minute to a speech made by Mr. Morgan, M.P., in which be referred to the subject, and he would like to read to them just a few lines. Mr. Morgan said "be had recently travelled On the continent and stayed in the South of France, and he would tell them what protection had done for that country. He could speak from experience 1 and not from hearsay, and he would tell them how protec- tion affected the working classes in Fraece. It would be for them then to say whether workingmen would like to return to such a state of things in this country. The loaf which cast 44 in this country cost 94 in France, and sugar which could be bought for 2liel per pound here was 7d there. Salt Was three times as dear as it was in England. Tea was so dear that working men. could not afford to drink it, and a nair of workmen's shoes which could be purchased here for 81 cost 25e in France." That was the result of proteotion in France, and if the same thing was done in this courftry every consumer would have to pay more money for every article on which duty was paid. It would make him that much poorer, and ,then he would have to contribute his proportion to pay the LI. , per acre to the farmer, which would go into the landlord's pocket, because he would instantly increase the rent. (Hear, hear.) That was the length and breadth and height of that scheme. From a political point of view, he should very much like to see a Tory Goeernment bring in a measure for putting a duty on corn, as they would not exist for another twenty-four hours. (Hear, hear.) It was all moonshine attempting to do that. (Applause.) What the farmer wanted in this country was proper protection for the improvements that he made upon the land, and he wanted perfect freedom to cultivate the land in whatever way he chose. Another thing which he thought the farmer wanted was a proper leneth of lease. In Scotland they had 19 years leases, and he did not see why they should not have them in England, as the farmer§ would then be able to receive the results of all the improvements he made in the land. (Applause.) Mr. WILLILDI DARBYSTURE, in supporting the motion, said the more he heard Mr. Barlow the better he liked him. (Applause.) Alluding to the agricultural questions he said he thought there was a revolution springing up amongst the tenant farmers of the Knutsford division. As Mr. Bar- low had said the Warrington Farmers' Club was of a non- political character, and he believed that if any great national act was being brought forward the members of the club would sink politics and vote for whoever supported that measure. (Applause). The resolntion was then carried unanimously. Mr. BARLOW briefly responded and moved a vote of thanks to the chairman. • Mr. Z. ARMITAGE seconded this proposal. The answers, he said, which Mr. Barlow had given to the questions ad- dressed to him were of a reverse kind to those which might be expected from many Tory candidates. They had been characterised by great thoughtfulness and by his going into the questions deeply, and showing what had been the action of Liberal and Conservative Governments on the various questions, and, he thought. had proved successfully that in those matters that interested tenant farmers and the agri- cultural population the Liberal Governments had been the friends of the people, and that they had brought forward the measures which had produced the best results. (Ap- plause.) With regard to the question of tithes he believed the newly enfranchised voters would have something to say on this subject, and that the man who WAS able to say that he would abolish tithes and disestablish the church would be the man who would carry the sympathies of the newly-enfranchised people of the counties. (Hear, hear, and applause). The vote of thanks was then carried, and the chairman having briefly responded the meeting ended.
Mr. Gladstone arrived at Bergen in the Sunbeam on Wed- nesday, and la reported to be in excellent spirits.
GENERAI NEWS.
A supposed tramp was found dead in a barn nom glom Leicestershire,im Tuesday morning. The police are mak-
! log inquiries In the garden of the Rev. F. Collier, 18, Richmond- place, Dublin, the gardener has discovered a human skull and some bones, which have been apparently there a long, time.

FATAL STABISTNG Ctsr..—On Tuesday morning, George Turlington, who was stabbed while going home at Lough- borough, Leicestershire, on Saturday evening, died at his residence, at Quorn, from his injuries, which had affected his brain. Andrews, his alleged assailant, will be charged with murder.
THE NATIONAL DEBT.—.A return relating to the National

Debt issued on Tuesday, show that the tota amount of debt In 1883.84 was £754,455,270, and that the total debt paid off during that year was £8,031,306, leaving the total amount of debt funded and unfunded at the end of the year £746,423,964. TITHE RENT CHARGE —7Twe incumbents in the neigh- . . _

bourhood of Canterbury, the Bev. J. Cr. Brine and the Ile;. F. Metcalf, of Lower Hardres, have announced their inten- tion of foregoing the extraordinary tithe rent charge on hops this year, owing to the bad times and the depression in agri- cultural districts.

REWARD FOR BRAVERY.—The Queen has been pleased to confer the Albert Medal of the second class upon Ed- mund Charles Thompson, surgeon, of Tyrone County In- firmary, for the conspicuous heroism be displayed in endeavouring, on April 4th, to save the life of a child, named Herbert Mitchell, who was suffering from diph- theria.

ASSAULT ON SALVATIONISTS.—At Derby, on Tuesday, Pevera I Salvationists were fined for creating a disturbance in the Market-place. There was an angry mob outside the court, and the Salvationists were pelted with rotten fruit. The windows of their stores were broken on Monday night,
the Army was assailed, its standard captured, and its musi- cal instruments were destroyed._

THE PROTECTION OF YOUNG GlRLS.—General Booth has propounded a " nstionai " scheme under which a central office of help and inquiry is to be established in London, together with Homes of Refuge in different pas of London and the provinces, to contain at least 1,000 girls. Tne cost is estimated at £20,000, towards which the following con- tributions, amongst others, have already been promised : Mr. S. Morley, M.P., £2,000; Messrs Francis Peek, T. A. Denny, and Cory Brothers, £l,OOO each; an anonymous Manchester friend, £3OO ; Mr. S. Smith, M.P., £lOO. The sums already promised exceed £7,000.

ROYAL GIFT TO THE NATIONAL LIFE-BOAT INSTITUTION. —The Queen, in view of the intention of the late Mr. Samuel Fletcher, of Great Ancoate-street, Manchester, pawn- broker, to build and endow a life-boot, has been graciously pleased to direct that a portion of his property, which ow- ing to his intestacy has devolved on her Majesty in right of her Duchy of Lancaster, shall ba appropriated to the building and maintaining in perpetuity by the Royal National Life-boat Institutivin of a life-boat, to be named the " Samuel Fletcher, of Manchester." The new life-boat is shortly to be stationed at Blackpool, Lancashire. A FATHER ATTIMPTING TO MURDER HIS SON.—A. des- perate attempt to murder a son has taken place at 94, Brewery-road, Caledonian-road, London, and the victim, a boy, aged 12 years, now lies in the Great Northern Hos- pital, Caledonian-road, suffering from such injuries that it is feared be will not recover. On Saturday evening neigh- bours were alarmed by hearing Walter Burchett screaming very loudly, and when some of them went up to the room they found the boy lying on the floor bleeding. His father, William Burchett had in his hand a Portion of a poker, which had marks of blood upon it, the other portion of the poker lying on the floor. The father was arrested. THE Tatum' CONFERENCE. —The Amalgamated Tailors' Congress, formally commenced on Monday at Glasgow, was resumed on Tuesday with an address from the president. Mr. Bailey, of Preston. He congratulated them on the progress made since the conference was instituted, and spoke of the changes which had occurred. Of sixty-seven delegates assembled at Manchester twenty years ago when the society was formed, only six were now with them. Various trade questions were afterwards discussed. The confer- ence lasts a week. The triennial statement showed that the funds amount to e 0,165, an increase of £3,631. £30,000 had been paid in sick benefit and funeral dona- tions. . . _

Fault PERSONS BURNED. —On Saturday afternoon a fire broke out at an oilshop in Grange-road, Bermondsey, Lon- don. Owing to the inflammable nature of the contents of the building the flaws made rapid progress. The outbreak originated in a room usad es a store, and was caused by the vapour of spirit coming in contact with flame. The in- mates of the house in their eff )rts to put out the fire were much burned. Chas. Sampson, the proprietor of the estab- lishment, his wife, and infant child, were so severely burnt that they had to be removed to Guy's Hospital; and Emma Clements, a young woman who was in the house, was also slightly burnt. Mr. Sampson died, and his wife and child are in a critical condition.

A Tato or SENSATIONAL INCIDENTS.—The American papers record a series of sensational incidents which marred the pleasures of a recent trip for the pissengers in the Atlkntic express in their journey from the West. A hand- some, distinguished-looking Frenchman, whilst the train was at a standstill, suddenly left his hat and stick on the seat of the car, and struck off bareheaded at a quick run for the lofty hills, which, rising almost pe.pendicularly from the city, are crowned by rocky summits. Some railway employes went after him, but are they overtook the poor fellow he threw his mane wildly above his head, and, leap- ing from a crag, disappeared. Later on, an Irishman travel- ling with his eieter, left his place beside her, saving he WU going to see a friend in the rear of the train. He never returned, and, it is conjectured, committed suicide. Lastly, on the same journey, a young American gentleman, suffer- ing from consumption, grew worse, and breathed his last, in the presence of his compassionate fellow-traveller& THE TOUR OF THE LORD-LIEUTENANT.—The Lord-Lieu- tenant and the Countess of Carnarvon arrived at Galway on Monday afternoon, and met with an enthusiastic reception. Addresses of welcome were presented, and his Excellency, in reply, said it w ts the wish of the present Government to do all that could be poesibly done for the people of Ireland. It gave him pleasure to see that the energies of the people of Galway were concentrated in the attempt to develop the resonrces at the port. He pointed out that railway commu- nication and steam power had made Galway nearer to America by two hours' travel than any other important town on the coast ; and he hoped to see, during his own time, Galway raised to the distinction which she boasted of in former days. Referring to the labouring classes, he re- gretted to see that there was a universal depreseion caused by many reasons, but chiefly by foreign competition. He impressed upon the labouring classes the necessity of looking to the interests of their employers, and said he hoped to see Irish fisheries and other interests developed. Sin Cumarats DILEE.—The Times is requested to and flounce that a marriage is arranged between Sir Charles Dilke, M.P., and Mrs. Mark Pattison, widow of the late Rector of Lincoln College, Oxford —A specially summoned meeting of the members of the Eleusis Club has passed a unanimous vote of entire confidence in Sir Charles Diike, and pledged itself to give him its support at the coming election.—On Tuesday night, a crowded meeting of the Council of the Borough of Chelaea Liberal Association was held at the Chelsea Baths for the purpose of considering Sir Charles fluke's letter to the president of the associa- tion. Mr. G. W. Osborn (president) occupied the chair. The meeting was most enthusiastic, and only lasted half-an- hour. The following resolution, moved by Mr. W. Xneas Smith, and seconded by Mr, H. J. Statiesby, was unanim- ously carried amid loud cheers :—" Chat this borough council, having duly considered the letter from Sir Charles Dilke, resolves to accept fully and completely, and without reservation, the statement there made that the charge brought against him is untrue; that, bearing in mind the long and valuable services rendered by our member to his , country and party, his high integrity and stainless character, this meeting does not attach much importance whatever to a vague, unproven charge. This meeting, therefore, decline* to consider the advisability of a temporary severance be- tween the constituency and one who has served it so faith- frilly and well, and hereby pledges itself to exert every i effort to return him triumphantly at the next election." It was then resolved that the following telegram should be sent to Sir Charles Dilke, who is now staying with the Right Hon. J. Chamberlain, M.P., at Birmingham : "Crowded and enthueiastic council meeting decided unani- mously to unreservedly accept your denial of vague charges made against you. They pledge themselves to use every effort to return you triumphantly." A vote of thanks to ' the chairman and three cheers for Sir Charles Dilke brought the meeting to a close. Tea TRADES UNION CONORRSS, 1885. The "final notice of the Congress," to be held in the Cambridge Hall, Southport, on Monday, Septemher 7th, and five following days, woe issued on Saturday. The notice states :—" The Parliamentary Committee and the Reception Committee ap- pointed by the Southport Trades Council have great plea- sure in giving a most cordial invitation to the trade societies and the trades councils of the United Kingdom to send re- presentatives to Congress. As the next Congress will be ' held on the eve of one of the most important general elec- tions that has taken place in Great Britain, and the first in which the workinvinen will have the power to largely in- fluence, if not to determine, the future policy of the legisla- tion of this country, it is of the highest importance that the desires of the organised trades on domestic questions should be authoritatively expressed and widely known. For these and other reasons, it is hoped that the Congresa will be the largest on record. The Parliamentary Committee have reason to believe that the representatives of the trades will meet with a reception in Southport which will equal that given at any previous Congress. We do not mention this as an inducement to send delegates, but as a sign of the growing respect in which the Congress is held by other classes of society." The amended list, although still not final, of the questions to be discussed on the proposed Par- liamentary programme for the session 1885, is as foliows (1) Employers' Liability Act (1880) Amendment Bill ; t 2) certificates for competency for mea in charge of steam en- gines and boilers ; (3) the desirability of increasing the number of factory and workshop inspectors ; (4) the I right of relatives of deceased minors to be represented at coroners' inquests •, (51 co-operation and its relation Sol trade unionism ; (6) representation of labour in Parlia- ment ; (7) codification of the criminal law ; (8) codifica- tion of the laws summarily administered in petty sessihns; (9) reform of the land laws; (10) public inquiry into sud- den and accidental deaths in Scotland. ALLEN'S WORLD'S HAIR RESTORER ts pre- fection for its wonderful life-giving properties to faded or falling hair, quickly changing gray or white hair to its youthful colour, gloss, and beauty.—Advt.

ILord Coleridge was married at Kensington last week by special license. The bride was Miss Amy Lawford, an American lady. An official denial is given to a rumour which Isis got abroad that the Post-office intends to withdraw "reply post- cards from use. The recent strike in the South Staffordshire coal trade . caused a loss to employers and employed (asr stated at the Sandwell Park Company's meeting) of about £150,000. • Dean Reichel was on Wednesday elected by' the Bishops of the Irish Uhurch to fill the See of Meath, which was some time ago vacated by Lord Plunket on his translation to the Archbishopric of Dublin. ROBBERY OF £6oo.—An American gentleman staying at the Adelphi Hotel, Liverpool, has been robbed of money and valuables left in his bedroom worth from £6OO to £7OO. No clue to the thief has been obtained. CHILD MURDER AND SUICIDE.—A wOOl2ll living at Bal- barn, earned Merritt, murdered her infant, and subsequently fatally cut her own throat with a razor, on Saturday night. No cause is assigned for the tragic occurrence. GREAT FIRE IN LONDON.—A great fire occurred is Bucknell-street, Bloomsbury, on Tuesday morning. The premises of Messrs. Thonet Bros. were burned out, and ' serious damage was done to several other buildings. The anual horse show at Buxton was held on Wednesday, and the entries are reported to be quite equal to the average. I Lord E. Cavendish, M.P., presided at the luncheon, aid congratulated the members on the success of the show.

Three large fields of barley centiguous to the branch line of the Great northern Railway at fleckington, were on Tuesday completely consumed by fire. It appeared to have originated from the sparks from the engine of a passenger train.

On Sunday, a man named Dory, escaped from the Criminal Lunatic Asylum, Dundrum, near Dublin, where he was confined for having murdered his wife and child. He was captured on Tuesday in a tree about a mile from the Asylum. nak.—£ls,ooo DAMAGES.-A fire broke out on S ttur- day night on the premises of Messrs. Tudor and Sons, lead manuftcturers, Hull, and destroyed !pad), the en- tire plant and stock. The damage is estimated at about £15,000.

The Commissioners of Woods and Forests have decided to replace and restore the Buckstone, the celebrated rocking stone in We Valley, near Monmouth, which was overturned by a party of excursionists a few months ago. A local con- trector has undertaken the work. Messrs. Hibbert and Stanley. the members for Oldham, addressed a meeting of their constituents on Wednesday evening at Shaw. A resolution thakking the hon. gentle- men for their consistent support of Mr. Gladstone and as- suring them of their continued confidence was passed. Two boys named Murray and Connelly, of Derrvdonnelly, county Galway, quarrelled while playing at marbles a few days ago, and Murray ran home for his father's gun and shot his companion in the face. Connelly died the same day. Murray has locen committed for trial on the charge of murder.

The statue of the Duke of Wellington, which was re- moved from Hyde Park Corner to Aldershot some months ago, was on Wednesday formally " dedicated " by the Prince of Wales, who, is the short speech he made, said he entrusted the statue of the greatest British General of his day into the custody of the British army in per- petuity,

THE Corrorx TRADE —Notices were issued on Wednesday by the Bolton master cotton .pinners .of a reduction of 5 per cent in the wages of the operatiies. The employers have informed their workpeople that the state of the cotton trade justifies and demands this reduction, and the opt,ra- tives have as yet given no indication that they are opposed touch a step.

_ ENTERPRISE IN BIRMINGH&3I.—A company has been formed to purchase all the cabs in Birmingham, about 500 in number, and replace them with 600 new and improved vehicles. The old rate of fares is to be abolished, and a uni- form rat 4of 6d per mile substituted. The drivers will all wear smart uniforms, and a new A.nerican system of check- ing is tu be introduced. The total number of divisions taken in the House of Com- mons during the session ended last Friday was 281. The first was on the Address to the Crown, in reply to the Queen's Speech, and the last was on the Lords' amendments to the Land Purchase (Ireland) Bill. Sixteen divisions were taken on the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, and 66 on Ike Redistribution of Seats Bill.

THE HUDDERSFIELD ACCIDENT. —The coroner's inquiry into the fall of a railway station roof at Huddersfield, where- by four men were killed, was resumed on Wednesday. A witness named Morten, who saw the accident, thought the fastenings of the roof gave way first, and that the conse- quent pressure upon the columns caused them to soar/. One of the workmen stated that be had mistrusted the stability of the roof. The inquest was adjourned until the Ist of October.; THE ELECronAL DUTY OF TEMPERANCE REFORMERS.— Mr. T. H. Barker. Consulting Secretary to the United King- dom Alliance, read a paper on "Our electoral duty as tem- perance reformers" at a meeting of temperance advocates in Manchester on Monday night. Every Parliamentary candidate should be asked, he said, whether he would vote for the direct popular veto; and temperance reformers would be recreant to the highest and best interests of humanity if they voted for any man, whatever his politics, who replied in the negative. MINE ACCIDENT : Two MEN KILLED.—An accident, resulting in the death of two men and serious injury to a third, occurred on Wednesday in the Minerva Lead Mines, a few miles from Wrexham. The men were exploring a part of the mine which had not been worked for some time. when a portion cf the roof gave way and buried them. Several hours elapsed before the rescuing party could get to them, and it was then found that an aged man named Robert Ellis and Edward Hughes, aged 25, were dead. The third, a son of the deceased miner Ellis, was rescued alive, but badly hurt. Mu. GLADSTONE'S MIDLOTHIAN CONSTITI7ENCY.—By the extension of the franchise, Mr. Gladstone's constituency in Midlothian is increased from 4,295 to 13 315. The effect of this large addition to .the electorate will be to rank what has always been a doubtful seat among the safest for the Liberals in Scotland. At the last election Mr. Gladstone's majority was limited to hundreds, but it is confidently believed that in November next, if the right hon. gentle- man contests the seat, his majority will be counted by thousands It is in those districts of the county in which Liberalism is strongest that the increases to the electorate are greates'. • ALARMING FIRE AT ROCHDALE.—Fire broke out early on Wednesday morning in a hosiery chop in Rochdale, oo- cupied by Mrs. Baker. Several persons were sleeping in bedrooms over the shop, and were prevented from escaping by the stairs catching fire. Mrs. Baker's diughter and a young lady companion, Miss Greaves, jumped from a three- storey wiadow into blankets held by neighbours, but both were seriously injured. A fireman, at great personal risk, ascended to the third floor and brou ,ht down two boys, eons of Mrs. Baker, who were slightly burned and half auffoca- , ted by the smoke. Two other occuo in's of the house es- caped unhurt. The cause of the fire is not known. Con- siderable damage was done to the premises and stock.

• THE SHOEBITaYNESS COMPETITION —The winners of the Queen's Prize and Badges at Shoeburyness were announced on Wedneslay. The coveted honour fall to the 4th de- tachment 3rd Middlesex, with a total of 105. The Ist Shropshire and Stafford, with P 6, were second; the 2nd Lancashire, with 93, third; and the 2nd Durham, with 90, fourth—all taking aggregate prizes. The Queen's prize winners also secured the prize for the highest score in the 40-pounder competition. The let Eqiex won the Harcourt Challenge Cup for shooting and drill combined and general good behaviour. In the competition on Wednesday with the 40-pounder at 2,000 yards. the prizes were awarded as follows a—The first to the 7th detachment let Gloster ; iecond te 2nd detachment Ist Shropshire and Stafford; third te 6th detachment 2nd Middlesex ; and the fourth to 7th detachment 3rd Kent ; whilst the 4th detachment of the 3rd Middlesex received a certiicate. AN OFFER OF MATRIMONY OR MunnEn.—At Carlisle, on Saturday, Thomas Routleige was charged with having, on or about the 18th of June, delivered to his neice, Jane Dalston, knowing the contours of the same, a letter threatening to kill and murder her. The prosecutrix, who ' is about 22 years of age, at one time resided in prisoner.'" house, occupying the position of servant or housekeeper. While there the prisoner made overtures of marriage to his niece, and this coming to the ears of Wilson's mother, she removed her daughter home to D aston. The prisoner wrote several letters to the prosecutrix on the subject of the. marriage, including in the one in question a threat to mur- der her unless she fulfilled her promise to him—Superin- tendent Semphill stated that when the prisoner was appre- hended he admitted that the letter was his. Upon it were representations of coffins.—The Bench kept the letter in their own hands, the contents being ef a disgusting nature. —The prisoner was remanded for a week, Dreesreons FLOODS.—THREE VILLAGES DESTROYED.—* The latest advices from the East give details of the most disastrous floods that have occurred at Canton for the last thirty years. For eighty miles round Canton the country is under water, and mine of the straets in Canton itself have been under water for a whole week. In some of the rivers the water rose to upwards of forty feet above the normal level, and the strength of the current was so strong that it was impossible for boats to get alongside the steam- ers lying off Canton to load or discharge cargo. Large numbers of sampans and cargo boats were overturned and swamped, and the bodies of men, women, and children, car- cases of pigs, furniture, rafts, k.c., were seen everywhere floating down the troubled waters. The greatest damage done appears to be between Canton an% Catsham. A large portion of the embankment of the river was carried away and three villages entirely submerged, most of the inhabi- tants being drowned. At another place the water broke through the city wall, and it is stated that several thousands of people were drowned. The distress was very great. Many families lost all they possessed. To make matters worse, the crops were destroyed, the second and third silk crops were seriously injured, and the rice crops were dam- aged to such an extent as to raise the price of grain by about 18 per cent. It was suggeeted that in face of the dis- tress the war tax should be remitted, at any rate for a year or two, but to this appeal the Chinese Government did not lisfen, although the people are very heavily taxed. The Oy Yuk Sin Tong hospital and the Tung Wan hospital at Hong , Kong took all the measures they could for the relief of the sufferers. div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT LA.TCHFORD.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT LA.TCHFORD.

On Tuesday.eiening a meeting of Liberals was held in the Temperance Hall, Latchford, in support of the candidature of Mr. J. E. Barlow for the Knute- ford division of Cheshire. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Long, and amongst those present were Messrs. E Barlow, J. Crosfiold, Z. Armitage, C. Broadbent, F. Thornely, W. Derbyshire, J. P. Hud- son, A. Kenworthy, W. Pierpoint, W. Bradford, Stel- fox, &A There was a good attendance. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said that in coming before the electors of the Knutsford division that night to introduce the candidate that they as Liberals hoped to return, he thought that perhaps his first word should be one of explanation as to why that meeting was held outside their own county, or rather he should say within the municipal borough of Warrington. It was caused by the fact that in the village of Grapoenhall they had not many rooms suitable for their purposes, and he was sorry to say that some of their Conservative friends would perhaps rather not hear tiler side of the question. (Hear, hear,) For that reason they had been thrown back upon ,the hospitality of their good friends in Latchford. He thought that apology was necessary to those who might ; have to come farther owing to the fixing of that meeting place. They were all aware of the great increase in the number of voters who would record their votes at the next general election. There were now eight divisions in the ceenty of Chester, where formerly there were only three, the Mid-Cheshire division numbering, if he remembered rightly, some 7,000 or 8,000 voters. Now the Knutsford division, which was the eight part of Cheshire, numerically he believed as well as in the apportionment, numbered some 2,000 or 3,000 more than the old Mid-Cheshire division of the county. That would give them some idea of the large increase in voting power. (Hear, hear.) They, as Litnarals, had the feeling that the great majority of the newly enfranchised would seriously consider the questions that were put before them, aad, as they hoped, their sympathies would be on the Liberal side, it was naturally hoped that in the coming contest the decision of previous contests would be reversed. (Ap- plause.) They hoped that Cheshire would do its pert in forwarding the legislation of the country according to Liberal ideas. (Hear, bear.) The candidate who had pluckily come forward to tight the divieion was a gentleman of whom he would at that time say little, because he hoped that the various constiteents would' have ample opportunities of knowing him themselves. But he the chairman) con- sidered it was a very plucky thing to come forward to fight that well known name of Egerton, a name which bad ruled. the county pretty well in the past. and had left a good ,1 maev of them unrepresented in the British House of Corn- i mod. From that day forward they hoped to have a larger voice, and they looked to both the electors and non-elec- tors, if they were satisfied with the Liberal choice of can- didate, to do all that lay in their power to forward his return. One part of Mr. Barlow's speech that night would , be directed to the answering of certain questions emanating , from their friends, the farmers of the district, and if they would allow him (the chairman) he should like to congratu- late those gentlemen upon their spirit in forming their club in Warrington for the discutsion of subjects interesting to themselves. He was glad they were taking bold of the right method of ventilating these questions a,nongst them- , selves, questions which had a special bearing on their in- I dietary, and in framing questions to put as a united body to the various candidates throughout the county. He only hoped they would scrutinise closely tee answers which the ' candidates gave to the questions, and that they would net be content to support any man at the poll who did not I satisfy them with his answers, feeling as he did that the best legislation ,in their interest had been promoted and I would be promoted in the future by the Liberal party. (Applause.) The chairman also re:erred to the action of the Tories since they accepted office, and to the evolutions which Lord Randolph Churchill had been lately practising, and said one could not help feeling that a party must be In a most pitiable condition that would submit to be led by a man of that calibre. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. .1. E. Raertow, who was received with loud applause, said that he had to deal with a list of questions which he understood had been or were to be submitted to the candis dates for Parliamentary honours in the county of Chester. The list had been leaned by the Warrington Farmers' Club, and he ought to say he was pleased to receive such a list. (Applause.) It showed that the farmers in Cheshire were waking up and looking after their own affairs in Parlia- mentary matters, and meant to have what they believed to be right. (Hear, hear.) In fact they were beginning to wake up to the fact which, he might tell them without dis- respect, some other classes had been aware of for some time, that " Union is strength," and that if they wanted to further their own interests they must have some definite programme, and must agree amongst themselves what it was ta be. (Applause.) The Warrington Farmers' Club was not a political association, but an association to promote the interests of farmers; it was an association of practical men who had in times past got their living by farming, and who would, he confidently believed, in times to come, get it in a like manner. Therefore they had no theorist questions I to dead with. They had to deal with the practical wants of men who had come together, not as politicians, but who, without bias, had agree I amongst themselves what they wanted, and they might assume their expression of opinion was a moderate and not an extreme one. At any rate it was certainly entitled to respect when they bore in mind the importance of the farmers as a body. (Hear. hear.) There I were, he believed, over half a million tenant farmers in Eng- land, and they owned in produce and live and dead stock I capital to the value of one-fifth the capital value of the land, and by their industry and intelligence they had brought the English soil into such a satisfactory state of cultivation—though he thought more remained to be done in certain directions—that it was from being one of the most barren soils in Europe one of the most productive. (Applause.) An English acre yielded on an average about 29 bushels; in France the out-tarn was 161 bush-Is; in Austria, 12k; in theCuitedS tates, 12; and in Russia, g; other things being very much the same in proportion. I here- , fore some credit was due to the farmers for what they did, and they could only say thst men who trie 1 to help them- j selves in that way were deserving of respect and confi- dence. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The list of questions ' which had been submitted to him divided itself into two heeds. One were questions which dealt with matters of administration, and the other portion dealt with questions of landlord and tenant. The first administrative question was " Will you vote for the main roads of the county being maintained out of the imperial fund im lie was aware that it was a very great grievance in some districts that main roads, which were used for carting produce and other things from outside districts into towns, were supported by the only district which obtained no benefit, but rather the reverse. He thought the request was a very fair and reasonable one, and he promised to support it. (Applatre.) The second question was "Will you vote for the election of county government boards?" He was of opinion that they very much wanted elected county government boards, and he believed in their being electiVe and representative. (Ap- plause.) The next question was "Will you vote for a bill to compel railway companies to carry farm produce at rates not exceeding the rates charged by. them for the carriage of the goods of other industries?" That was a subject of great importance. He was in the same boat as the farmers on that question, as he suffered from some of the rates of the railway companies. He had to do very often with the shipping of manufactured produce to other countries, and he found that if they sent goods from Manchester to Bombay there would be a total freight of 24s 9d per ton. How was that 24s 93 divided amongst the different people who had to dc with the carriage et the goods ? Seven shillings and ninepence went to pay the Suez Canal dues, 2s went to pay dock and town dues and load- ing in Liverpool, leaving 15s to pay for the actual carriage of the goods. Out of that 151 about 103 was token to convey them from Manchester to Liverpool, and 5s from Liverpool to Bombay. (Laughter.) Therefore be thought he was in the same boat as the farmers, though he did not think these charges affected him so much as it affected the working- men who made the goods. (Hear, hear.) He was asked, " Will you support the regulations as to the exclusion of live stock coming from all countries infected with disease ?" They must remember, he said, that the home supply was eight-ninths of the whole live meat censumed in the country, and, therefore, he thought Mr. Gladstone was right when he stated that in protecting the sources of eight-ninths of the whole supply they were protecting the interests not only of the producer, but of the consumer also. (Applause.) He need hardly say that he app-owed cf the present regula- tions. In answer to other questions, he said he would vote for ,an amendment of the Agricultural Holdings Act, 1883, to secure to farmers freedom of cultivation and absolute cer- tainty of adequate compensation for unexhausted improve- ments ; and also in favour of local rates being equally borne by owner and occupier. With respect to the ques- tion "Will you vote for the abolition of tithes? "he bad since been informed that the question was meant to read " Will you vote for the responsibility for the payment of tithes being shifted from the tenant to the landlord so that the tenant will not be liable to be distrained upon for the payment of tithes? " He thought that that request was not at all an unreasonable one (Applause.) Another question was "Will you vote for the above programme whether brought forward by your own party or otherwise? " (Laughter.) His experience was that the LEierals brought forward most of these measures, but occasionally they got the Coneervatives in office, though not always in power, and they took to passing Llberel measures. (Laughter and applause.) If the Conservatives took to passing Liberal measures, and he termed those referred to Liberal measures, he should he very glad indeed to support them. (Ap- plause.) In conclusion Mr. Barlow argued that the Liberal foreign policy had been more successful than that of the Conservatives, for the simple reason that they had followed one of the mottoes which he saw on their walls "Do right and fear not." (Loud applause). Questions having been invited, Mr. WILLIAM DARBY.. SHIRR said that Mr. Barlow seemed to have been dealing more particularly with preferential rates connected with foreign goods ; but what farmers desired was that their goods should be be carried at the same rate as those of manufacturers. Mr. BeuLow said he meant to include those latter rates in the remarks he had made. Mr. STRLFOX asked would Mr. Barlow if returned to Par- liament use his influence to further the interest of farmers in that matter. Mr..Beneow : I will answer that question shortly with the one word "yes." (Applause). Mr. W. DARBTSHIRE said with regard to tithes that he underslood the Warrington karmers' tilub to mean that they be abolished altogether, and not merely taken off the tenant and put upon the landlord.

In the United Kinrdoin the births of 285,612 children, and the deaths of 176 256 persons. were registered in the three months ending 30th June, 1885. The natural Increase of population was, therefore, 109,356. The registered num- ber of persons married in the quarter ending 31st March, 1885, was 105,464. The birth-rate was 31.5, the death-rate 195, and the marriage-rate 118 per 1.000. During the three months ending with March last, the marriages of 78,126 persons were regis:ered in England and Wales, corresponding to an annual rate of 11.5 per 1,000 of the estimated population in the middle of the year. In 1879 the proportion was equally low, but with this single exception the marriage-rate in the winter qtrarter of 1885 was the lowest since civil registration began, and showed a further considerable decline from the rates that prevailed in the two preceding corresponding quarters, which were 134 and 123. The births regist-red in England and Wales during the qnarter were 222,280, corresponding to an annual rate of 32-4 per 1,000 of the estimated population. This birth-rats was 3-1 below the mean rate in the ten preceding corres- pending quartas. So low a rate has not been recorded in the second quarter of any year since 1813. In London the rate did not exceed 314, whereas in the 27 provincial towns it was 342. and ranged from 256 in Brighton, 27'9 in Huddersfield, 292 in Halifax, and 294 in Bradford, to 390 in Newcastle,, 398 in Preston, 40-1 in Sunderland, and 411 in Cardiff.

During the quarter 132.202 deaths were registered in England and Wales, corresponding to an annual rate of 19-3 per 1.000 of the estimated populati m. This death rate WAS -9 below the mean rate in the corresponding quarters of the ten years 1875-84. The lowest county rates were 14-8 in Sussex, 15-7 in the exit-a -metropolitan portion of Middlesex, 15-8 in Worcestershire, 16-1 in Northamptonshire, and 165 in Hantingdonshire, while the highest were 206 in Cheshire and Monmouthshire, 20-9 in Durham, 212 in South Wales, 21-8 in Lancashire, and 231 in Northumberland. The 132.202 deaths last quarter included 68,749 ef males, and 63,453 of females. The annual death-rate among males was 20-6, and among females 18-0 per 1,000 estimated to be liv- ing of each sex. In equal numbers living the deaths of males were 114 to 100 deaths of females. The urban rate was 20.2 per 1,000, while the rural rate was 17-9. For equal numbers living, the deaths were 113 in the urban to 100 in the rural population, against an average proportion of 112 in the second quarters cf the ten years 1875.84. In 28 great towns the registered deaths correspond to a rate of 206 per 1,000, being -4 above the general urban rate. In London the death-rate did not exceed 19 3, whereas it was 21-8 in the 27 provincial towns, among which it ranged from 15-7 in Derby, 153 in Brighton. 18-1 in Portsmoute and in Leicester, and 18.2 in Hull, to 25-5 in Cardiff, 27-0 in Pres- ton, 295 in Manchester, and 31-8 in Newcastle. In fifty other large town districts the rate was 19-5 per 1,000, being 1•1 below the rate in the 28 larger towns. The deaths included 29.467 uodsr one year of age, 66,977 between one and 60 veers, and 35.758 60 years and upwards. Infant mortality was 133 per 1.000;in tsn preceding corres- ponding quarters it averaged 127 per 1,000, and ranged from 121 in 1881 and 1884. to 139 in 1875. In 28 great towns the proportion was 147 to 1,000 births, and ranging from 94 in Derby, 101 in Brighton, 114 in Portsmouth, and 133 in Bolton and in Halifax, to 182 in Manchester, 198 in New. castle, 203 in Blackburn, and 215 in Preston.

EXTRAORDINA RY SUICIDE ON THE RAILWAY. On Thursday morning, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Railway Ilbtel, St. Helens Junction, touching the death of Joseph Webster, a labourer, residing at 2, Rolling Mill-lane, Sutton, who met with his death on the railway on Monday night. Mr. Ferrand was present on behalf of the railway company.—Agnes Woodcock said deceased, was her brother, and was a labourer at Rolling Mill copper works, Sutton. Ile was 57 years of age.— James Lucas said: I am stationmaster at St. Helens Junction. I knew the deceased by sight before Monday night. I saw him on Monday night about 20 minutes past seven. He was on the "up" plat- form (to Manchester) when the express from Liver- pool was signalled, and he got up from a form and. walked towards the edge of the platform. He seemed to be stumbling forward as he was very drunk, and I called out to him to stand back. A. passenger pulled him back on the platform while the express passed. I afterwards attended to the " down " express and then saw the deceased walk- ing down the -sidings towards the cabin. He had no right to be there and I called to porter Taylor to fetch him back. He was removed into the station road. He was removed from the station about 7-27, and at 4ht o'clock breaksman Renton came and. told me that they had knocked a man down. I sent for the doctor and a "stretcher," and I went to the man. He was lying clear of the line, on the "slope,". about 250 yards from the station. Breaksman Ren- ton was in charge of a goods train from St. Helens Junction to WinsforcL—Robert Grice, a lad, residing at Grape's Cottages, said: I saw him get over the sleepers of the line, and he fell down from the sleepers. When he got down he ran and "popped" ' his head on the rails. I was on the sleepers and I - then fainted and fell off the sleepers. I afterwards I ran and told several women.—William Handles, 1 engine driver, said: At live minutes to eight o'clock on Monday night I started with a goods train from St. Helens Junction to Winsford. I saw the de- ceased about 50 yards ahead. He ran to the rails and got down, after which he turned over on his back and deliberately nestled his neck on toe rail, stretching out his arms. I then whistled and reversed the engine, but the " life guard " of the engine struck him and dragged him about 50 yards. All his clothes were stripped from him. I got down from the engine, and found he was quite dead. We were going from 18 to 20 miles an hour.—P.S. Sheriff and Thomas Ingleby, with whom the deceased. lodged, gave evidence to the effect that a neigh- bour named Price on Monday morning lodged corn- , it had d indecently withther di police the effect that ts to p grandchildi a girl about four years of age. It was said a warrant was to be issued for his apprehen- sion. Mr. Swift, solicitor, was consulted about the ' matter. Up to Monday he always seemed to be in his 'right mind.—The Coroner, in summing up, said he thought there was no criminal negligence attaching to anyone, and there was little doubt the deceasel took his own life. That was shown by the evidence. and if the witnesses were to be believed he h good reason for it. He was charged with a very serious offence, and after rambling about the dis- trict he got intoxicated and then deliberately placed his head on the line. The question for the jury to consider was had the deceased a sufficient degree of reason to know that he was doing wrong, and if they believed he had that they must say that he feloniously killed himself, or a verdict of felo tie se' If they believed the deceased did not • know what he was doing, then the jury must return a verdict of suicide whilst temporarily in- sane. 'But they had no evidence that the deceased had been insane.—The Foreman observed that it lookedexcit great ._tAhe djeurocearluweasseesuffmeoierintgo be 01 his "chump" all morning.—The Coroner: There is no emasenitf evidence of that.—The jury subsequently considered their verdict in private for two minutes. They then called the Coroner and the reporters into the room, and the Foreman said: We are agreed that he deliberately put himself on the line for the purpose of taking away his life.—The Coroner said that that that was a verdict of file de se. or that the deceased did feloniously kill himself.—The jury said that was so.

!danger I It is in danger, if at all, from men who would use it for political purposes, and who attend it not from any regard for its , teachings or its polity, but to serve personal ends and as a means of social aggrandise- ment. Dr. MACKIE comp tred those. who sought to disestablish the Church to tigers, and his illustration was hooted. He said he did not want to see 1,500 ministers disappear as they disappeared after the disestablishment of the Irish Church. But what a reflection on the ministers who " disappeared " after they had got all they could get in the way of loaves and fishes! The spiritual good. of the flock is nothing; the great thing is the material good of the shepherd. Dr. MACKIE did suggest, as something we suppose almost as terrible as the "tiger," that "the Roman Catholic College of Maynooth got some- thing like £600,000 or £700,000 out of the fund which belonged to the Irish Church ;" and he spoke of Mr. FORSTER as "beloved by all sensible men in England and Scot- land." These are points to, which Irishmen and Roman Catholics should give their atten- tion. It is not the sort of stuff that is talked to them now by Tory candidates in English constituencies; but it is thought safe to reveal the Old Adam in Scotland. They may be quite sure, if they will reflect, that they have nothing to gain by an alliance with the Tories; what is bred in the bone cannot be got out of the flesh. Dr. MACKIE, amongst other fables, went on to tell the electors of Montiose that credit must be given to the Conservatives for such Agricul- tural Holdings Acts as were worth anything at all. No wonder the audience laughed at this as a good joke, remembering as they would that the Agricultural Holdings Act of Lord BEACONSFIELD'S Government was de- nounced even by such Tories as Mr C. S. READ as a miserable sham, and that it had to be "reformed altogether" when Mr. GLAD- STONE came into office. Such a statement was quite in keeping, however, with Dr. MACKIE'S assertion that the Tories repealed the Corn Laws, as if Sir ROBERT PEEL him- self had not acknowledged that "whatever merit might attach to the measures he had introduced" measures introduced amid Tory opposition of the fiercest kind—that merit did not belong to him, "but ought to be attached to the name of a man whose pure motives, indefatigable energy, unpretending and unadorned eloquence had forced them all to listen to him—the name of RICHARD COB- DEN." Another piece of base coin which Dr. MACKIE threw down to find it instantly challenged was composed of the statement that the Reform Bill of 1867 was carried by the Tories. It is notorious that the Bill which Mr. DISRAELI brought in was a paltry subterfuge which would not have added more than r iB,OOO electors to the voters' lists: and that the Bill which was carried was modelled by the Liberals and carried by the Liberals with Mr. GLADSTONE at their head. Lord SALISBURY (then Lord CRANBORNE) 'knew who had framed the Bill,; he hated it as the outcome of what he called "a policy of legerdemain," and this is his testimony : "The real parent of the Bill as we are about to pass it," he said, "is not the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER .(Mr. DISRAELI), but the Member for south Lancashire (Mr. GLAD- STONE)." Will Dr. MACKIE give history and Lord SALISBURY the lie when, as in this case, they happen to be in accord? With such instances before us of the patent facts turned topsy-turvey, we need not be surprised that the Monstrose journal from which we have quoted should say that Dr. MACKlE'Sqpeeches to the electors are "full of absurdities and glaring inaccuracies." It is severe criticism, but it is not undeserved.

THE Marriage Law Reform Association has been making a useful experiment with a view to testing public opinion on the question of the prohibition of marriage with a deceased wife's sister. Woodstock is known not only as a Tory borough, but as one in which the local clergy have shown themselves decidedly hostile to the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, which has been again and again .brought before Parliament with the object of break- ing down an absurd barrier. The Association has not, however, hesitated to take the opinion of Woodstock on this question. By means of the past the electors have been asked to sign a petition in favour of the Bill, and the result is that "considerably more than two-thirds of the entire constituency have §igned the petition." This is a striking testimony to popular feeling on the matter; and it can hardly be doubted that the Bill will pass in the next Parliament. The House of Commons hasiong been convinced of the necessity of legalising marriage with a deceased wife's sister; and the House of Lords would ere this have followed suit, if it had not been for the votes of the Bishops. A great wrong is being done to a consider- able section of her Majesty's subjects through the stupidity of a body of .men who ought to be removed from the House of Lords. We say stupidity, because they stand by the canon law when they have neither Scripture -nor common sense on their aide. The text in Leviticus,which is often referred to as sup- porting the prohibition runs—" Neither shall thou take a wife to her sister to vex her, to uncover her nakedness, beside the other in Iher lifetime." When it is remembered that, this law was laid down to a people who practiced polygamy, it will be seen that what is meant is that a man was not permitted' to marry his wife's sister whilst ,his wife was alive—or as the text has it, "beside the ,other in her life time." This is far different from saying that a man should not be per- mitted to marry his wife's sister after the death of his wife. The canon law is, there- lore,based on a misconception, and as it is opposed to reason and morality it ought to be :Jolished. The law as laid down in Dee- ,teronomy gives a widow who is childless the light to espouse her deceased husband's ,brother. Surely if -it was right to marry a deceased rhusband's brother there can be no wrong in marrying a deceased wife's sister. We are not urging that the people of this generation -should abide by the Levitical law; but when the Levitical law is erroneoudy quoted it is as well to point out the blunder. The fact is the Bishops are conscious that power is slipping from their grasp; but they are struggling against the inevitable. The House of Lords will be compelled to pass the bill, and the Bishops will be compelled to leave the House of Lords. It is all a matter of time.

WE regret to see that Mr. joior CROSS, late Miners' agent for St. Helens. is playing into the hands of the Tory party by coming forward as a labour candidate for the borough. It may not be his intention to strive for the success of the Tory candidate, but that will be the result of his efforts if he persist in his candidature. If he and his friends wanted a voice in the representation of St. Helens, why did they not attend the Liberal Caucus,

and make themselves heard! It does not look well, this putting himself forward at the eleventh hour; and we warn Liberal working- men not to be led astray by false hopes. We would ask Mr. CROSS, tOO, to reflect upon what he is doing. Does he really think that he has the ghost of a chance of being at the head of the poll, if there are three candidates in the field? If he does, he is more easily deluded than we take him to be, and in that case he belies his assumed fitness to be- come a legislator. Perhaps he thinks he may induce Mr. SETON KARR to retire in his behalf. Well, let him try his powers in this direction, and, if he is successful, we will admit that he is justified in pushing himself to the front. At present he is acting most unwisely; he is risking a grave injury to the class he professes to be anxious to benefit; for what could be more injurious to working-class prospects than the return of a Tory for St. Helens consequent upon a divi- sion amongst the Liberals ? Colonel GAMBLE is the selected candidate of the Liberals of St. Helens; he has been nominated at a pro- perly constituted representative meeting of the party, and his nomination has been pub- licly and unanimously confirmed. His pro- gramme does not embrace all that everybody wants—that would be impossible ; but it is Liberal in the fullest sense of the term ; and if Mr. CROSS is .at heart a true Reformer, he will withdraw his address, and work for the candidate who least divides the Liberal party, and who is therefore most likely to in the election.
