THE REVS. J. Causwen, (superintendent) and W. Lagar , have entered upon their ministerial duties in the Preston Brook circuit. the former is stationed at Runcorn and the latter at Frodsham. MERSEY 01mm:e5 TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN. The anni- versary sermons will take place in the Public Hall, to-mor- row (Sunday),,aad on Monday the annual excursion will be ba made to Liverpool. DEPARTURE OF THE REV. S. MBES FROM RUNCORN.—On Sunday evening the Rev. Sidney Mees preached his farewell sermon to a large congregation at St. Paul's Chapel. On Tuesday he departed for his new circuit. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—The Ray. J. Cawland has entered upon his duties as superintendent of the Preston Brook Circuit. His residence is at Runcorn. The Rev. W. L igar, his colleague, is stationed at Frod- sham. SHOOTING MATCH AT WIDNES.—The warrant officers and sergeants of the Warrington Military Depot bad a shooting match against ten members of the Widnes Volunteer Corps on Saturday at the Widnes Range. The Widnes Company were the victors by 24 points. Subsequently the teams bad a good tea at the Alexandra Hotel. NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING AT WIDNES.—On Sunday, the daughter of Mr. W. H. Parsons. who is the caretaker of the gas works property at Ditton,Yell into the water surrounding the gas tank. Her father was in the vicinity, and rescued her in an unconscious condition. Dr. McDonnell was sent for, and prescribed the necessary reme- dies, and the girl quickly recovered. TRINITY CLITJRCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.—The children attending these schools bad their annual treat on Friday, wheillethey were conveyed up the canal to Daresbury in boats belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, and Mr. Jonathan Horsefield. A fidd was placed at their disposal by Mr. Churchwarden Lowe. On Saturday the in- tuits enjoyed themselves in a field kindly lent by Mr. Chas. Hazlehurst. NELSON-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The Rev. Lloyd Jones, of Rhyl, preached two sermons in Camden Chapel on Sunday on the . occasion of the Sunday school anniversary. In the afternoon Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst delivered an address to parents and children. The scholars, assisted by the choir, rendered specially selected music, under the leadership of Mr. S. Bayley. The collections amounted to £2l ss. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH DAY SCHOOLS.—At St. Paul's and St. Mary's Churches, on Sunday, sermons in aid of these schools were preached by the Revs. J. Stowell, A. P. Hamilton Wilson, and C. Ruinfett. The Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson in the afternoon conducted a children's service at St. Paul's. The collections amounted to .£l4. It may be stated that there are between 760 and 800 children on the rolls of the day school, and the staff has been recen- tly increased at an extra cost of 4100 per annum. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The treat to the scholars of this school, which took place on Thursday, was a very successful and enjoyable re-union. Tt.e saholars, to the number of 550, left Runcorn by special train in the afternoon for Frodsham. Here they formed into procession, and accompanied by the ministers of the circuit and the superintendents and officials of the school, proceeded to the Mersey View Pleasure Grounds, Overton Hills. A variety of games lent swiftness to the hours, and prizes were given to the children for running contests and ' other sports. Tea was provided for the whole of the scholars at the expense of Mr. J. Simpson, senior superin- tendent, whose generosity was li:tingly acknowledged. The scholars left Frodsham by train at eight o'clock, reaching Runcorn in good time. SAMARITAN LODGE, 1.0.G.T., WIDNES.—The members held their usual weekly meeting on Monday night, under the presidency of Bro Machin, W.C.T. There was a large attendance, and one member was initiated into the order, and one received the associate card. The programme for the ensuing quarter was submitted by the committee and accepted. After the usual routine business an. entertain- ment took place, and the following programme was gone through :—Bra. Machin, reading from " Mrs. Candle's Cur- tain Lectures ;" Sister Smith, song, " The anchor's weighed ;" temperance reading, Bro. Bullivant ; sone, " Thinking of home," Bro. Wright ; duet, " I will arise," Bro. and Sister Wright ; song, " The farmer's boy," Bro. R. Widders ; recitation, " The servant maid," Sister Belli- vant ; recitations, Sister Buckley and Bro. Webb. TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT PARNWORTH. The Farnworth branch of the C.E.T.S. held a demonstration on Saturday afternoon. The members of the adult and juven- ile society, strengthened by several members of the Widnes branches, paraded the principal thoroughfares headed by the Widnes C.E.T.S. Brass sand and the large banner. Subsequently service was held in the parish church, and the Rev. Webster Hall, of St. Alban's Liverpool preached a sermon. In the evening a tea party was held, followed by an entertainment over which the Rev. George Bond presi- ded. There was a good attendance. Addresses upon tem- perance topics were given by Mr. Thomas Storey, president of the Liverpool Carters' Christian Associatien, and Mr. R. Comyn, of Liverpool. The Rev. R. Hold's, of Salford, formerly of Farnworth, was presented with a gold badge, and an illuminated address by the members of the society, as a mark of the appreciation in which they regarded his services to the society as vice-president- Mr. Heiden ac- knowledged the gift in a few choice words.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—Lieut.-Colonel Ash- ton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present—The Revs. J, W. N. Tan- ner, J. J. Bryant; Messrs. Weir, Hadfield, R. Ashton, War- burton, Knowles Wallington, Davies, Fisher. Lewis, High-, field, Norman, H. Linaker (clerk) and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—Mr. Dansey, the distric^ auditor, submitted a state- ment of the pauperism and expenditure in the Runcorn Union, exclusive of common charges. lunatics in asylum. and vagrants. The acreage of the union was 40,593, and the p3pulstioo 33,960, with a rateable value of £211,754. For the year ending January, 1885, there were 211 indoor, and 693 outdoor paupers; total, 904. The expendituref or in- door relief during the half year ended Lady Day last was £576; outdoor, £1,063; total, £2,239. During the same period £9 Its 21 was paid in school fees for non-pauper children. There was a decrease in the expenditure as com- pared with the corresponding half year in 1684 of £97. The cost per head Of the population was is 311.

ATTEMPT TO ROM A. WIDNES PUBLIC-ROUSE.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Craskell, jan.; at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Christopher J. Farrell, a young man, was charged on remand with being on the premises of Owen Tansey, the Commercial Inn, Lugsdale-road, for an unlaw- ful purpose. On Sunday night the doors of the Inn were secured as usual at ten O'clock, and the family retired to rest. About eleven o'clock Miss Tansey heard noises in the bar, and shouted to her father, who descended the stairs and discovered the prisoner standing near the money drawer in the bar. The door leading into Ann-street was open, and it was supposed that the prisoner had pmvioits to clos- ing time secreted himself ha one of the rooms where there was no light. P.C. Davy found 2s 4d in thu pockets of the prisoner.—The prisoner accounted for the money by the statement that he had received a letter from his sister in which 51 in postage stamps was enclosed. 'there was a letter of that description in his pecker, but no mention of monev.—The prisoner, who had been twice convicted of felony, was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

PRE'S= BOARD OF GDARDILNS.—The fortnightly meet- ing of this board was held on Thursday, at the Workhouse, Whistbn. Mr. Leatherbarrow presided.—The Master re- D orted that there were 405 inmates this week, against 412 last week and 480 in the corresponding period of last year. —At a meeting of the Visiting Committee a vote of thanks bad been tendered to the Rev. J. Johnson. Congregational minister, Prescot, for presents of flowers to the inmates.— The following gentlemen were appointed a deputation to visit the Kirkdale Schools, Pantasaph Orphanage, and asy- lums in which pees ,ns chargeable to the Preecot Union are now confined :—Revs. Thomas Chambers and Thomas Fine- gan, Messrs. Lowe, Fisher, Birchall, Matthews, Newsome, Jackson, Hall. Kenwright, and Tyrer.—Ls a deputation to attend the Poor-law Conference at Blackpool in September, Messrs. Leatherbarrow (chairman), Lowe, and Newsome were appointed.—The Assistant Clerk stated that the various townships in the union were in arrears to the extent of £8,316. No action was taken by the guardians—Mr. New- some called attention to the fact that on the next board day the Faruworth Agricultural Show would be held. He should like to suggest to the board the propriety of begin- ning the business at eleven o'clock, in order to give the members an opportunity of attending the show. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Longton was of the same opinion.—Mr. Tyrer remarked that the last time they were detained by Dr. O'Hara.—Mr. Newsome : Yes.; but he won't do it again. (Laughter.)—The suggestion was agreed to. GOOD TEMPLAR DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES.—The Good Ternplars of Widnes on Saturday celebrated the 14th anniversary of the establishment of 1.0.G.T.in the town by a demonstration and gala. The members met at their respective lodges, and marched to the Promenade, where they were marshalled into processional order. In front was the band of the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions, and following was a handsome banner bearing on one side the words "Sunbeam Temple, 1878," and on the other "Star of Widnes Lodge, 1871." The juveniles, 500 in number, formed the first part of the procession, the adult, number- ing 200, and preceded by the Soap Works Brass Band, bringing up the rear. The procession filed up Mersey, Waterlco-road, Victoria-road, Widnes-road, and Albert-road, to a field off Millfield-lane. The sun was shining brightly, and the demonstration gay with flags and music, and the regalia of the members, presented a pleasing sight to the hundreds of spectators that lined the route. The lodges represented were (juvenile). Star of Widnes, Sunbeam, Lily, and Onward; (adult) Star of Widnes, Samaritan, Haste to the Rescue, and Hope of Appleton. The gala was an- nounced to be opened by Mr. B. A. Naylor, of Thelwall, near Warrington. but that gentleman was late in arriving, and proceedings had commenced. A seriee of athletic sports had been arranged by Brothers John Thompson and Turton, and Sister liewson. superintendents of the respec- tive juvenile temples, the Onward, the Sunbeam, and the Lily. The results were as under :-150 yards flat race: 1 Arthur Emery, 2 Thomas Prescott. 100 yards flat race : 1 Isaac Taylor, 2 J. W. Mellor. Three-legged race (80 yards) ; 1 Andrew 111`Kay, 2 Peter Ince. Backward race (60 yards): 1 Rich. Parson, 2 Isaac Taylor. Blindfold race (60 yards): 1 Isaac Taylor, 2 Richard ham A tog of war was won by six members of the Sunbeam Temple. Girls' sports: —lOO yards race: 1 Elizabeth Platt, 2 Elizabeth E. Jones. Skipping rope race (80 yards): 1 Elizabeth Platt, 2 Eliza- beth Hollins. A great attraction was the rounders match between Derby (Liverpool) and Widnes 1.0.G.T. Even- tually Derby won by 24 runs. The children were regaled with milk and coffee and buns, and a public tea was pro- vided at a small charge. In the evening there were baloon ascents, and the bands played selections of music until dusk. It was computed that there were upwarda of 2,000 persons upon the field during tbe aftercoon.

MR. J. E. BARLOW, the Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, gave an excel- lent address on Tuesday evening in the Temperance Hall, Latchford. If the far- mers of this Dart of the county do not rally round Mr. BARLOW, it will not be because they have not found in him a stout cham- pion of their order. He answered the ques- tions put to him by representatives of the Farmers' Club in a straightforward manner, and showed that he was thoroughly familiar with the agricultural problem. As a corn-1 mercial man, he looks at the question from a commercial point of view, and he is anxious in the interest not alone of the farmers but of the whole cpmmunity that the land should be free of the present heavy burdenS" of bad customs and bad laws. The new electors will find Mr. BARLOW in sympathy with their wants, and that, if sent to Parliament, he will be diligent in promoting meas- ures for their welfare. The good things of legislation will not require to be wrung out of him ; he is ready with hand , and heart for the work. Mr. C. BaoADBENT, in moving a resolution in Mr. 13AaLow's favour, aptly observed that he thought the electors would be able to dis- tinguish between those who yielded Liberal measures as a matter of expediency, and those who promoted them as a matter of principle; and Mr. JoHN CaosFrEvo, in seconding the motion, introduced a few facts by way cif exposing the evil and absurdity of a system of Protection. The meeting was well calculated to promote the Liberal cause, for, as Mr. DARBYSHIR.E remarked, the more the electors saw of Mr. BARLOW and the better they liked him.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH Cllont.—At the generous in- vitation of the churchwardens (Mr. W. Whittaker and Mr. F. A. Lake) the adult members of this choir had a trip to Buxton by the Cheshire Lines Railway on Saturday last. Favoured with fine weather, the party spent a pleasant day amongat the hills and dales of Derbyshire. Every arrange- ment had been made for creature comforts by the church- wardens, who were present, and were hbartily thanked for thqr kindness. On Monday the boys of the choir were taken to Southport, where a pleasant day was spent. FAREWELL SERMON LT WIDNES.—The Rev. R. Harper, superintendent of the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit, preached his valedictory sermon in Victoria-road Chapel. He had tried, be said, to preach the truth plainly that everyone might understand it. His term with them had been a very happy and a very pleasant one, and Inc was sorry to leave them, but the separation was inevitable. He should leave the town and circuit without a single hard thought of any- body, for there was on his part nothing but affection for them, and he hoped the Divine Spirit would go with him, and that it would abide with them, bless them, and make them happy and united. PRIXTTIVE METHODIST CAMP MEETINGS AT WIDNES.— The Primitive Methodists of Widnes held their annual camp meetings on Sunday. In the morning an open-air meeting was h.ld in West-street, the proceedings beina con- ducted by the Rev. J. Calvert. Addresses were delivered by Mr. J. .Jones, of Warrington, Mr. I. Whitley, of Stockton Heath, and Miss Mitchell, who is in command of the local branch of the Blue Ribbon Army. In the afternoon a meeting was held round the large lamp at Bimma Cross, and the congregation then walked in procession through a number of streets, halting in a field near the chapel in Princess-street. Addresses were delivered here to a very large assemblage of persons of both sexes. Love feast ear. vices were held in the Hutchinson-street and Sim= Cross chapels is the evening. The whole of the meetings were very successful.

IiIINCORN WATERWORKS COMPANT.—At the half-yearly meeting of eharebolders on Monday next the directors will submit the following report:—" The revenue account shows a balance of £523 Bs. including £2 17s 10d brought from the previous half year, out of which the direptors recom- mend a dividend to be declared of £.3 101 per centum per annum' free from income tax, payable on and after the lst day of September; this will absorb £505 131, leaving a bal- ance of £1:0 '5B to be carried forward. The arrangements made last year for supplying our district with water by means of the iron tank, bye-pass, and relief valve, while the reserveir on Runcorn Hill was tested and examined, have been found to fulfil our expectations, and to answer all the purposes for which they were erected and placed ; by these means the reservoir has been tested twice, for a week each time, during the present summer, and the result has regards leakage,.4;c., is very satisfactory. All the plant and machinery are in good working order,and the well continues to give an abundant quantity of first-elass water, and the supply to all the three townships has been continuous." THE IRISH NATIONALISTS OF WIDNEE.—The second of a series of lectures under the auspices of the Widnes 'Branch .of the Irish Nationalist League was held in the large room lat St. Paul's Chambers on Sunday afternoon. There was a good attendance. 'Dr. O'Keeffe occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. Quinn, O'Connor, Oak- .den, Ford, Horan, Mansdale, Green WElroy, Doyle, Osborne, and Gallagher. Mr. Fox delivered a lbcture en- titled "The rise of the Irish nation and its fall." He described the Irish Parliament of 1760. and the unjust manner in which it was formed and carried on. Out of 300 members only 72 were really elected by the people, and its proceedings were fettered and thwarted in every possible way. iie referred to the labours of Dean Swift, Grattan, and Flood, in their attempts -to obtain emancipation for the people. Speaking of the Irish Volunteers, he said that if Ireland had kept up her military powers she would-have been free that day. When -she parted with her power to fight all bar power went from her. The Irish people pro- tested when their Parliament was taken away, and they woald continue to protest until they had twain a legislature on College Green. (Applause.) The Chairman moved a vote of -thanks to the lecturer. Mr. Ford seconded, and ; impressnlapon those present the need for organisation. It • appeared strange that out of the great number of Irish peo- ple in Widnes they could only get 40 at 50 persons to join the League. Mr. APElroy supported the motion, which was carried with acclamation. A similar compliment was paid to the Chairman, who, in reply, remarked with gratification upon the crowded meeting, and said he should like to see Orangemen present as well as Roma* Catholics. He was not by any means a bigoted individual, and it would give him pleasure to see an Oraneeman shaking hands with a Roman Catholic, and to see him also taking up arms in de- fence of their common country for the purpose of establish- ing her freedom. (Applause.) That branch of the League was established.uot so mach for electioneering purposes as to bring the yoane raen of Widnes—Feniane, Home Rulers, Irish National Foresters, &c.—together for the purpose primarily of constituting themselves into a debating society for mutual improvement, because he thought there was an immense amount of latent talent and intellect among their people which ought to be developed. He believed this branch would bring their people together, and cause them to develops their talents in such a manner as would make them highly respectable citizens. (Applause.) A collection was made in aid of the fund for carrying on a reading room and debating society in the Chambers.

PIC-NIC FROM WIDNES.—On Thursday about 40 teachers and friends of the Hutchinson-street Primitive Methodist Sunday School were driven to Lymm in conveyances pro. bided by Mr. Lea, and an enjoyable day was spent at the pretty spat. TRACHERS' PIC-NIC FROM RUNCORN. In connection , with the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, about 50 teachers and friends had their annual pic-ric on Tuesday. Driven in waggonettes they visited Cuddington and Dela- mere Forest, and thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Messrs. W. Euxworth and Jabez Stubbs carried out the arrange- ments. SMITH'S ILLUSTRATED ALMANAC, ISM, AND DIREC- TORY OF RUNCORN, WESTON, AND HALTON —The atten- tion of the public is invited to this useful publication, which will be issued early in December next. It comprises the most extensive and complete local postal directory ever published. Early applications for advertisements to be made to the agent, Mr. W. Brookes. 7, Waterloo-road, Run- corn —Advt. - .

FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE AT HELSEY.—The "London Gazette " of Tuesday night contains a Privy Council Order declaring areas at Mickle Tr.tfferd and lieleby, Cheshire, to be infect.d with foot-aud-mouth disease, after the county had had a clean bill of health for some months. On Tues- day thirty-seven fresh cases were reported on five farms in the two adjoining townehios of fieleby and Mickle Trafford, near Chester.

SALVATION ARMY EXCURSION FROM Rtmcants.—The Runcorn branch of the Salvation Army had their animal excursion en Wednesday, when they journeyed in boats along the canal to Marbury Hall, the residence of Mr. A. J. Smith Barry. A steamer and two large boats were kindly Placed at the disposal of the p‘rty by Mr. Z. B. Wells, at Northwich, and Mr. R. Clark, of Weston point The ar- rangements were under the direction of " Captain " Tyler, and a pleasant day was spent. Dirrox PARISII Cntruca. The success of the recent bazaar at Hough Green has enabled the committee to give an order for an organ for that church, for which object tile hazier was undertaken. An instrument to cost £350 has bean ordered from Mr. C. H. Whiteley, of Chester, a well- known builder, and who supplied the Cathedral organ of the city. The committee have engaged Mr. R. B. Woodward, of St. Helens, to select the organ and superintend its erec- tion.

ELECTION OF RONCORN COMMISSIONERS —Particulars as to the forthcoming election will be found in our an- nouncement columns. Of the six retiring members, Mr. Briscoe, in consequence of declining health, will not again seek the suffrages of the ratepayers, but the remaining five intend to do so. There has been a vac incy on the Board for several meaths past owing to the disqualification of Mr. W. Handley, but there is a doubt as to whether it will be filled up at the present election. The Ratepayers' Associa- tion has, as yet, taken no action, but we understand that they will bring forward three or four strong candidates. ENGLISH CHOLERA AT WIDNES —A fatal case of English cholera, or "choleraic diarrhoea," occurred at Widnes on IVednesday. Mary Ann Fallon, eight years of age, who lived with her parents at 19, Lagsdale-road, was taken sud- denly ill on Wednesday morning after having eaten soar apples on the previous evening. She died the same even- ing, and Dr. Cooper gave a certificate that death was the result of " choleraic diarrhcea." Mr. Dickson, the nuisance inspector, has thoroughly disinfected the house and des- troyed the bedding, and no fear of the disease spreading is to be entertained. It may be stated that several cases of acute diarrhcea have occurred at Runcorn.

DEATH OF L LAY BROTHER AT Dryrota death of Mr. Heron!anus Weltering took place on Wednes- day evening at Ditton Hall, Widnes. The deceased, who was 74 years of age, was a native of Westphalia. Germany, and came over to England with the first exiled Jesuits from that c6untry. He was by trade a shoemaker, and the breth- ren of the college speak in the highest terms of his skill. The deceased had an innate gift for natural science, and though not a learned man, was able to impart much valuable information on a variety of scientific sul+cts. The deceased had been ailing for some time with a cancer in his throat, and was attended by Dr. McDonnell no to the time of his death, which occurred at half-past six on Wednesday even- ing. A WIDNES PUBLICAN FINED.—Mr. Arthur Parkes, land- lord of the Central Hotel, appeared before Mr. F. H. Go- cage and Mr. H. Gasket), jun., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of having in his poses- pion unjust measures.—Saperintendent Barker said on the Bth inst. he visited the defendant's hotel, and found four half-pint glasses were short measure, and were unmarked. A quarter gill pewter measure was knocked down on one side, and would not hold the proper quantity of liquor. Mr. Parkes informed him that he had boucht the glasses in a lot, and had neglected to test them.—Mr. Parkes said he was not aware that there was anything Wrong with the glasses, and he was exceedingly sorry that this had oc- curred. It would be a warning to him in future.—Superin• tendeat Barker said this was the first time Mr. Parkes hal appeared before their worships, and a fine of 10s and costs, 12s, was imposed.

A FEMALE FIGHT IN SURREY-STILEET.—Ou Mon d tV, At Runcorn Petty Sessions, Owen Robert; a powerful-looking man, was charged with using threats to Elizabeth Sefton, of Surrey-street, on Saturday night the Bth inst. After hear- ing the evidence, the Bench dismissed the catte.—Eliz theth Sefton and Martha Woodward were then charged with as• saulting Elizabeth Jones. Mrs Jones appeared in court with a black eve, and a countenance very much bruised. She said that on the night in question Sefton was "carrying on" for about an hour, and then she quietly asked her if she could prove her a thief. Sefton instead of replying knocked her down into an entry, and then dragged her by the hair into the street, and battered her about the face. Woodward then came up and struck her on the head and face.—lt was contended for the defence that the complainant was the agressor and knocked Set ton's baby out of her arms. :Numer- ous witnesses were called, and the Bench fined Set Lou 20; including costs, and dismissed the case against Wood- ward. C tptain liazlehurst characterised the affair as most disgraceful all round. A FIGHT BETWEEN WOMEN AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessi ms on Wednesday, Thomas Beard and Mary Beard, his wife, living in Charlotte - street were charged with assaulting Mary Keating, a neigo- bonr. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. The complainant, who appeared to be very ill, and almost fainted in the wit- ness box, produced a quantity of hair, which she alleged Mrs. Beard had pulled from her head, and showed a wound upon the top of her forehead. The CABO for the complain- ant was that on the 10th August the boys of the parties had a small fight. The complainant went to fetch her bov, when Mrs. Beard selz:Ni her by the hair, and struck her with great violence on the bead and ribs. The husband then interfered by putting his arm round complainant's waist, and threw her to the ground. She had suffered great pain,and was under the care of Dr. O'Keeffe. For the defence it WAS contended that the complainant was continually annoying the defendants, and gave them great provocation on the day in quiestims. Mrs. Beard certainly commenced actual hostili- ties, but it was afterwards a proper fight between the women. Beard, it was given in evidence only separated the women. The Bench fined Mrs. Beard 10t and costs 10., and Mr. Beard 5s and costs I.oa, and dismissed a cross-summons issued against Mrs. Keating,.

A DEPRAVED OLD WOMAN AT RUNCORN.—Yesterdav, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. W. Bashes and Mr. James Handley, Bridget Brown, an old woman, who lives at Prod- sham, was charged with stealing two jugs and a cloth, value le, from the Queen' a Head beerhouse, High-street.—Hannah Heyes, servant to Mies Sagaley, the prosecutrix, sail on the previous night whilst in the kitchen she heard a noise in the bar, and on going there saw the prisoner, who asked for half a glass of porter. She refused to serve her as she had had enough, and then Mies Baguley found the articles men- tioned in the charge secreted about the prisoner's clothing. --The prisoner was then charged with stealing two petti- coats and a table cloth, worth ss, the property of Thomas Lowe, of 21, Ueion-street. On the previous day the pro- secutor's girl, Annie, went with the articles to Messrs. Marsh and Smith, pawnbrokers, and placed the articles on the counter. She went to the door awaiting the arrival of Mr. Smith. and during her absence the prisoner took the cloth- ing and secreted it about her person. The clothing after- wards fell to the grotand.—P.S. Walley deposed to arresting the prisoner. The prisoner pleaded guilty to both the chargea—Superintenelent Leah said there might have been several ether charges brought against the woman. She was in the habit, when in the town, of getting drunk and then stealing from every shop she came near. She had been twice previously convicted of felony—Mr. Bankes said the prisoner was a perfect nuisance. She would not work and for years had been going round begging, and he had several times relieved her. Now she had commenced stealing, and she would be sentenced to 14 days' hard labour on each charge. ROBBERY OF ZINC AT WIDNES.—SERIOUS CRARG E9.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Catherine Hines (15), Martin Cannon (14), and Stephen Power (14) were brought up on remand charged with having, about the Bth inst., stolen a quantity of zinc worth 101 from the works of Messrs. Hutchinson and Company, Widnes. Alice Kerley, marine store dealer, Nelson-street, and her son Peter, aged 14, were charged with receiving the zinc knowing it to have been stolen.—Mr. J. W. Knowles de- fended the prisoner Kerley.—lt appeared that on the , Bth inet James Latchford, of 96, Deacon-road, weigher at the works, saw Hines leaving the works with a basket upon her head. He followed her to Mrs. Kerley's marine store, which she entered, but when he got inside he was unable to find her, and Mrs. Kerley 4enied that she had been there. Subsequently she was anprehended.-To P.C. Holbrook she ad- mitttd her guilt, and made a statement incriminating Cannon and Power. After a close search at Mrs. Kerley's house a block of the missing zinc was discovered buried under a heap of cinders, and three blocks were found in an unoccn. pied house in the locality. Mrs Kerley, when apprehend-d, said she had "never seen the piece of zinc before if she were going to die," and the son denied that there was any zinc in the house.—The cas-s were taken separately, and Hines was called on behalf of Kerley. She said the state- ment made to the constable that he most look under some beards at the marine store was false. She had never sold zinc to Mrs. Kerley, and she was not in her house on the Bth inst. She alleged that the canstable dictated her state- ments, and gave her tobacco on the way to gaol in order to get information.—Power also denied that he had taken zinc to Mrs. Kerley's store —P.C. Laing deposed that there was no ground for the assertion that P.C. Holbrook placed the zinc in Mrs. Kerlev's house. He was present when the search was made, and held the light. About two or three cwt had to be removed isefcre tbe zinc was revealed.—The Bench fined Hines 10s, and ordered Power and Cannon to each receive 12 strokes with the birch rod. They did sot consider there was sufficient evidence to convict Mrs. Ker- ley and her.son, and they were discharged.

THE PRIZE FIGHT AT WlDNES.—YvterdaT, Patrick Mc- Cabe, a soldier, arrested when on his way to join his regi- ment In Ireland, was brought up charged under a warrant with being concerned in the Crow Wood "prize fight" on the 19th June He was also charged with assaulting Michael Mutptiv.a labourer.—His worship granted a remand until Monday on the application of Inspector Wood. PLUCKING CORN AT Rneroouer.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- eions, on Monday, William Price, a younp, man, was charged with stealing or damaging wheat in a field belong- ing to Mr. William Baker, farmer, Clifton. On Sunday morning the 9th inst., P.O Cooper saw the defendant pluck corn off the plaintiff's field. Tnere had been a great deal of damage derne.—The Bench said this practice most be stopped, and fined the defendant 2s 6d, and costs 9e 61. DESERTION OF FAMILY By A WOMAN—Before Mr. Brock, at Widnes Police Court, yesterday, Elizabeth Connor, 34 years of age, was charged with deserting her four children, aged respectively 11, 7,4, and 2. On the 12th Mat the womaa departed from the town in the eorn erne, of a man, and left her family in a balf.naked and stet ving condition in an empty house in Pear•street. Mr. Scannorll had them removed to the workhouse, where they have been maintaineti at a cost of £4 Bs. The woman was apprehended yester- day at St. Helens, and was now remanded until Monday. FAILURE OF A WIDNES GROCER.—At the Liverpool Bank- ruptcy Court, on Wednesday, befo,e Mr. Registrar Cooper, a petition was filed by Messrs. Pemberton, Sampson, and James, on behalf of Jos-ph Pollirr, grocer and provision dealer, carrying on business at Lugsdele-road, Waterloo- road, and Mersey-toed. Sim'e Cross, Widnes, and also at Church-street and in toe Market Hall at Runcorn, and re- siding in lodgings at 36, Treuthem-street. Runcorn. On the application of Mr. Sampson a receiving order was made, and the public examination was fixed for the 3rd Sept., at eleven o'clock. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John ,rodband, a sailor, from Goole, was charged with assaulting P.C. Breeze. About half-past eleven on Saturday night there were a number of sailors and boatmen fighting together at Top Locke. Up n seeing the constable they ran away. He followed and seized the prisoner, who struck him four or five times. The con- stable was in nniform.—The prisoner alleged that he thought the officer was one of the mea who had been knocking him about. A fine of £l, including costs was Imposed. „ SHOCKING ASSAULT ON A GIRL. Before Mr. William Bankes and Mr. Henry Reynolds, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Henry Green, a boatman, 18 years of age, was charged with assaulting Rosannah Watkin, aged six years. On the previous niizht the boat of the girl's father and he boat upon which the prisoner was engaged were anchored near to each other at Top Locks. About eight o'clock Mrs Watkin beard screams of " murder " issuine from the prisoner's boat, and she ran there and found the prisoner acting in such a brutal fashion that it had been at one time decided to bring a more serious charge against bits. P.S. Walley apprehended the prisoner who was sentence 4 to a month's hard labour without the option of a. fine. THE PEST OF RAGGARS AT RUNCORN. —At Rancorn Police Court, on Wednesday, William Gardner and Arthur Chambers, trarnpe, were charged with begging. On the pre. vious evening the prisoners went into the shop of Mr. Roberts, draper, High-rstre,t, and demanded- monetary as- siatanc.. Gardner was drunk, and M. Roberts ordered then to leave, but they refused and became very abusive. Police- clerk Wallace came upon the scene and took the prisoners into custody. The sum of 90 was found upon Gardner. It transpired that is various parts of the town the prisoeers had shown a ird issued by the spinners' ass,tciation to the effect that they were entitled to oymeathy and support. Superintendent Leah said the town had recently been al- most beseiged with beggars, and the residents at Higher Runcorn bad been particularly annoyed. The prisoners were sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. SUSPECTED INCENDLA.RISM.— At an Occasional Court, held at Warrington on Saturday, before Mr. Z. Armitage, a county magistrate, Thomas Mason and Thomas Charles Clemo were charged, on sus- picion, with setting. fire to two haystacks at Dares- bury on the 15th inst.—They were remanded to Daresbury Petty Sessions, bsil being allowed. Tan HARVEST IN CIIESIIIRE.—In consequence of the fine weather of the past week large quantities of oats have been secured in splendid condition. Corn-cutting is now proceeding rapidly. The crops are exceptionally good everywhere, and in the ab- sence of heavy winds are in a favourable condition for machine cutting, which is a great advantage. The straw is long and healthy, and the ears are full of grain. Such an abundant harvest has not been ex- perienced for many years. HAYSTACKS ON FIRE AT PRESTON BROOK.—At 11-50 on Saturday, two haystacks on the term of Catherine Hood, a widow, Newton-by-Daresbury, were discovered to be on fire by Thomas Hood. He observed a light, and on going to see the cause of it found the two haystacks on fire. He gave an alarm, and the fire engine from Preston Brook came, and succeeded in putting ,out the flames at about six o'clock the following morning. The damage done is estimated at about £l2O, and fortunately both stacks are fully insured. A man named Thomas Clemo was arrested on suspicion of firing the stacks. He was met by P.C. Wynne coming from the direc- tion of the fire; and as he could not give any satis- factory account of himself as to where he had been since ten o'clock the previous night, when he was in the Grimditch Mill beerhouse, and 1-30 the fol- lowing morning, he was taken into custody. BRUNNER, MOND AND CO., LIMITED, NORTHWICIL —The ninth half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of Brunner, Mond and Co., Limited, alkali manufaC- turers, Winnington,Northwich, was held at the Law Association-rooms, Liverpool, on Tuesday. Mr. John Crosfield, the chairman of the company, presided. The report of the directors showed a balance to the credit of the profit and loss account on the working of the half-year ended 30th June last of £82,107 Os 10d, which, with the amount of £26,282 15s Bd, brought forward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £108,380 16s 6d. With this balance the directors proposed to deal as follows :—Dividend on the preference capital, at 7 per cent, per annum, £8,511 Is 3d; dividend on the ordinary capital, at 20 per cent, per annum, £49,750; amount to be written off patents account, £7,500; amount to be placed to the reserve fund, £15,000; balance to be carried forward, £27,628 Gs 3d. The directors added that they had resolved that interim dividends be , paid in future in May and November.—The Chair- man moved that the report be adopted, and that dividends at the rates of 7 per cent. and 20 per cent. per annum be paid on the preference and ordinary shares respectively.—Mr. T. Irvine (Liverpool) sec- onded the resolution, which was unanimously car- ried.—Mr. T. W. Read, accountant; Castle-street, Liverpool, was, on the motion of Mr. F. F. Law, seconded by Mr. W. Simpson, re-appointed auditor. A vote of thanks to the directors closed the meet-

ing. A WARRINGTON MAN'S SUCCESS IN NEW ZEA.- LAND.—The following paragraph from the "Otago i Daily Times," will be of interest to many persons n Warrington, Mr. Oakden beingthe son of an old War- ringtoman :—" A piano, one of the few that have been up to the present manufactured in the colony, has just been finished by Messrs. Oakden and Howell, of Princess-street. It is a tricord instru- ment, with a case of unveneered red pine, designed to match well with the modern style of furniture. The rest-plank is of beech, with a cross-veneer of oak and another veneer of walnut; and the back is also well constructed, with bracings of extra strength. Most of the action has been made by Messrs. Oakden and Howell, also the bass strings, and the instrument is thus genuinely one of local manu- facture. It is one, too, which reflects great credit upon them. The tone is full and of good quality, and some improvements in the sounding board are probably the means of a particularly good treble having been obtained. The soft pedal .is also re- markably sweet in tone, and is in marked contrast with the ordinary one. This particular instrument is to be shown la the forthcoming exhibition at Wel- lington. It found a purchaser immediately nupo completion, and the manufacturers state that they can produce similar pianos at a selling cost of about £5O, whilst they cannot offer imported ones of a like quality under £65. At the present time about £165,000 worth of musical instruments is imported annually, the greater part of which, of course, re- presents pianos."

ST. BEDES YOUNG MEN'S SOCIETY. The anneal re-union of the members of St. Bedes Catho.- lie Young Men's Society took place on Tuesday night an the large hall of the new school. The proceedines com- menced with a capital dinner, to which about 140 persons sat down, thlir wants briog attended to by Miss Foster, Miss Wright, Miss Flannery, Miss Nolan. Miss Colquitt, and Mesdames Edward Swift, Caldwell, William Dennett, John Swift, and Thomas Dennett. These ladies .had also per- formed the task of cooking the victulls. After dinner the Rev. Farber Fmeian, Mr. Joseph Morrison (president of the society), Mr. Alcoin &owley, and Mr. John Dennett (hon. vcretary) ascended the platform and addresses were delivered—the Hon. Secretary lead the third annual re- port as follows:—' During the past year our total receipts were Vio 13s 3d, and oor expenditure £42 198 91. leaving a balance in hand of LT 13s 61. The past vear'a expenditure includes £24 53 21 for new forms, £4 173 6d for a bookcase, and A donaiien of .£5 to the new school fend. Au excur- sion under the auspices of the society was organised for Whit Tuesday, to Southport, and Droved in every way A complete success. liierrly 1,400 persons travelled by this excursion, and one and all exprefsed satisfaction at the arrangements made by the managing committee. Our society has now comple'ed its third year. It commenced in August, 1882, and looking back at the time that has elapsed 'in" flies all must admit that it has been of great service t) the young men of the parish. The members have labourel with greit zeal and de'erreination in every work I they have undertaken, and if we continue our labours in the same spirit we shall achieve every object for which the 1 society was established."—•Mr. Morrison, in moving the

r adoption of the report, said they ought now reasonably hope that the society was established on a sound and permanent basis. During the past three years the society had done good work, and the members meant to do good work in the future. (Applause.) Father Finegan seconded the adoption of the report, and congratulated the members upon the position of the society, and the admirable work it had accomplished during the three years of its existence, and expressed the sincere hope that they would do still more in the future. (Applause.) Catholics had had a great deal to do in these times. They were in a progressive age and could not stop. They had to act up to the requirements of education and many require. ments which a large parish like that • always bad. They had to build schools, and continue to support them in the future ; aud no matter how adverse the legislators or the Legislature of the country might be to Catholic and den. minational education, they as Catholics must always pat Catholic education in the first and foremost place Although politics were forbidden as a rule in young men's societies, it was not forbidden them to look to Catholic interests. (Hear, hear.) And amongst Catholic interests at the present day there was nene that was more pressing, none that was at -present in greater danger then was the Catholic elites- tion of the country. They would have to consider this in the future, and what they had dme in the past showed what they could do in the future. (Applause.) They bad now a power given them which was unknown to their fathers, and he hoped the working-men would use it prudently, con- scientiously, and well. (Hear, bear.) They should not give their votes to any candidate unless he was .prepared to sanction denominational education, and give education a fair field, a fair fight, and no favour, which they never asked for. (Applause.)— Mr. A. Cowley supported the motion, and in his own happy fashion related a few fac s regarding the early history of Catholicism in Appleton. Forts' years ago there was no i church or schools at Appleton, but a mission had been n existeuce since 1760, and probably earlier. He attended that mission as a boy, and he was glad to say that the Cow. Icy family and their relations had been of tbe fain) for two centuries. Previous to 1760 tho 113 V. Marmaduka Wilson conducted a mission in Lower House, which then belonged to a branch of the Cowley family. Father Wilson, be bad heard, WAS a very clever man, and a very nice old gentle- man. People attended the services from far and near, per- forming the journey in carts. Mr. Pennington WAS the next priest, and then followed Mr. Rigby and Mr. Fisher. That mission progressed, and now they had a handsome church and schools, and a priest whom they loved and revered. (Applause.)—The report was adopted.—Mr. Mor- rison moved, end the Rev. Father Finegan seconded a cm, dial vote of thinks in very flattering terms, and it was carried by acclamation.—A musical programme Was tben gone tbrothr,h, songs beiog contributed by the President and Mesers. Hunt, Finn, Crompton, and Rafferty. The rest of the evening was spent in a social way.

The fortnightly meeting waS held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Lieut -Colonel Ashton presiding. Present— the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, J. J. Bryant, Messrs. Highfield, Lewis, Knowles, Weir, Wallington, Warburton, R. Ashton, Hadfield, Davies el. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy cleek), Dr. Adorns (medical officer). The minutes of the Frodsham Parochial Cammittee con- tained a letter.—A letter was read from the Local Govern- ment Board, suggesting that public notice should again be given of intentiou to construct service reservoir in Fluira- lane, as the present proposal was to construct a reservoir to hold 696,000 r ellen& of water, and in the previous scheme it was only for 371,000 gallons of water.—The Clerk reported that an advertisement had been forwarded to the local news- papers in accordance with the above suggestion. The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Bancroft, informing the committee that the extra cost of laying two iron pipes for the water scheme in Frodsharn main street would be for two pipes and extra valves £207 4s 2d, less for single main as shown on plan £99 73 11d, extra £lO7 16s 3d, whilst the saving to the property-owners if a double main be adopted would be cost of lead piping for single main £l2O 16s 6d, for two mains £139 33 63, or a saving of £Bl 138.—The committee, decided to recoram ml the Authority to instruct Mr. Ban- croft to provide for two water mains in Frodsham main street—Letters were read from the Rev. F. F. Edmonds and Mr. Thomas lligby objecting to the ventilating lamp pillar of the Overton drainage scheme in consequence of its contiguity to their respective properties, and the probable nuisance which would be caused by the discharge of sower gas frbm each pillar when connected with the main sewer. —After some discussion, it WAS resolved that the Clerk in. term the Bev. F. F. Edmonds and Mr. Rigby that the committee were anxious not to cause even an imaginary nuisance, and they were quite prepared to recommend the Authority to put a ventilating pipe up the house now occu- pied by Mr. Carpenter, as first proposed, instead of the ven- tilating lamp pillar, and would enter into the usual agree- ment for the proposed easemene—ln accordance with notice given at a previous meeting, it was moved by Mr. 'Thomas liadfield, and seconded by Mr. Robert Holland, that the I Authority be recommended to appoint a surveyor for Prod- sham and Frodsham Lordship to superintend the erection of new buildings and to see that the sewerage system was main- tained in an efficient manner. In the discussion which fol. I lowed, it was stated that the appointment by the Authority would have to include the whole Union, and the salary charged upon the general hind. The motion was negatived by four votes to two.—The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. Lewis. In answer to a question, it was stated that the total cost of the water scheme for Fredsham, &c., would be upwards of £7,000. IMPORTANT POINT TO BUILDERS.—In the minutes of the Frodsham Parochial Committee it was recemmended that the plans for a coach house,:stable, and rooms above in the rear of Mr. Kidd's shop in Church-street.—Mr. Hadfield moved that the minute be referred back, because the plans had not been deposited with the clerk seven days before the time of meeting of the Authority, accerding to a resolution passed to May. He also said that the plans, at the meeting of the committee, were not understood, and there were toe cifications. It was absurd to pass such a resolution, and not adhere to it.—Mr. R. Ashton seconded the motion.—Mr. Lewis said Mr. Bethel was not aware of the resold ion, and the Deputy Clerk read a letter to that effect, and saying that he would conform to all the Authority might wish.— Mr. Warburton contended that it was absolutely essential that the rules and forms of the Board should be complied with.—Tbe Chairman pointed out that Mr. Bethel had com- plied with the bye laws drawn up by the Authority and ap- proved by the Local Government Board and published. This resulatioa had not gone through that formula, and had not been made public, and be therefore contended that it would be very bard upon them to say that on that account the plans should not be passed.—The Law Clerk said the ques- tion was whether seven days was an unreasonable time for the proper discharge of the duties of the Authority.—Mr. Hadfi,-;:d said independently of that the plans did not com- ply with the bye-laws.—The Clerk concurred.—Mr. Had- field: To pass these plans will make the passing of plans a farce in the future.—Tho Chairman said with regard to the plans not being quite correct, a concession was made to the gasworks, a public company, and a private individuel ought not to be dealt with harshly.—Mr. Hadfield stated he was fighting for a principle.—For the amendment there voted—Messrs. Hadfield, R. Ashton, Wallington, Bryant, and Warburton-5. For the passing of the minutes—The Chairman, Messrs. Weir, Knowles, Lewis, and Davies-5. The Chairman gave his casting vote in favour of the minutes.—Mr. Midfield gave notice that at the next meet- inc be would move that the resolntion requiring seven days' notice be rescinded., CHOLERA PRECAUTIONS AT WESTON POlNT.—Captain H. Clarke, harbour master at Weston Point, wrote that the same precautions with regard to cholera were being taken as heretofore. The servants in command of the Weston tugs had strict orders to bring no vessel away from Liverpool, arriving there from foreign ports until inspected by the port authorities, but in case of steamers tradino et tare on Point there were no means of ascertaining whether there was any sickness on board until they arrived at the deck.. He had, however, given orders to his deputy and assistants to InAe every inquiry as to whether there was any sickness on board or not before admitting them into dock. THE NUISANCE Isseecron.—Mr. Wallington gave notice that at the next meeting he would move the re-appointment of Mr. Farrington. . .

THE IRISH Lanonnans'Acr.-31r. Sexton has applied to the Treasury that advances under the Labourers' Act to Irish Boards 'of Guardians for building labourers' cottages may be made on the same terms as advances under the Land Purchase Act, thereby becoming eatinguishab'e by payment of 4 per cent for 49 years, instesd of, as now, 4a for 45. In support of the application, 46 Irish members ot Parliament have 8i :Tied a declaration of their opinlon. RIOTING AT HOUGHTON GREEN.—The particulars of what appears to have been something near akin to a riot, were disclosed on Wednesday, at the County Petty Sessions, when charges of disorderly cenduct were brought against Isaac Eaves, James saves, Naylor, William purseow,lam,meischSaewiin xrdleeps,onWaladl,t John Griffiths, John Griffin, George Horton, Seth Woods, and John Mahoney. It appeared from a statement made by P.C. Whittingham, that on the 3rd instant a club dinner and procession was celebrated at Houghton Green. Defendants were there, and were very dis- orderly. They almost took possession of the club room in the Plough Inn, whence they had to be twice ejected. About 10-40 in the evening the gang assembled outside the house, and began hoot— ing and abusing the police, one of them threatening to murder Whittingham. The defendants then pro- ceeded on a lane in the direction of Warrington, where they armed themselves with bricks and stones, which they commended throwing at the police. They also pulled some pailings from the from the front of the infant school at Houghton Green. They were with difficulty dispersed by the police, who had to draw their staffs and charge them. Witnesses were then called to speak to what had occurred. They were all ordered to find sureties to be of good behaviour, or suffer various terms of imprisonment.

div.head: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held at the surveyor's office in Sankey-street on Wednesday afternoon, when the chair was occupied by Mr. R. Houghton. There wee also pre- sent Messrs John Fairclough (Burtonwood), W. B. Kerfoot (Great Sankey), Edward Marsh (Lowton), William Roy- ston (Poulton), R. Owen, jun. (Croft), John Grounds (Orford), Henry Woolf (Rixton). J. Hartley, and T. E. Witbington (ex-ofticins), H. B. White (clerk), and Thomp- son (surveyor).—The Clerk read the reports submitted by the surveyor of the work done in various townships in the Board's district. —The committee appoieted to inquire into the matter of the alleged obstruction at Glazebfook, at , the new chapel, reported that they were of opinion that a , footpath three feet in width would be sufficient, instead of , the present width of five feet. They recommended that , the trustees be required to mike an alteration accordingly. —The Surveyor said that the trustees simp'y desired per- mission to put a few flags in front of the wall for their own convenience, but they did not claim the legal right.—The recommendation was adopted on the motion of Mr. Owen, and it was resolved that the clerk inform the trustees of the decision of the Board,—The Finance Committee held a meeting on the 17th June, when the treasurer's book was laid before the committee, and it appeared that the balance of £4,0 7s 3cl was due from him. It was resolved that the contract with tbe Warrington Waterworks Company be entered into for one year for the supply of water for road watering purposes on Liverpool-road and Winwiek-road, at the rate of £4 a year for each road. Ten- ders for the supply of materials for the current year were read and considered. The minutes were adopted without discussion.—The CLERK stated that according to direction of the Board, he had forwarded a notice to the parties re- ported as having encroached at Lowton, asking them b re- store the highway to its original width—Tire consideration of the matter was adjourned for the surveyor to see the Parties who are alleged to have caused the obstructions—lt was resolved, on the provsition of Mr. OWE', that in futere the surveyor sanction no alteration in the line of boundary to the highways without bringing it before a meeting of the Board and a minute beipg made of it—The affixing of the seal of the Board to the tenders concluded the business.

THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, AUGUST 22, 1885. CRICKET.

A TRIP TO Mk WET WITH THE 1 RECHABITES. Having been invited by the Rechabites in this neighbourhood to visit. their conference in Exeter, and feeling some curiosity to see the beautiful scenery of the West of England, I gladly availed myself of the opportunity, and after some ten hours riding found myself on Saturday, the let inst., in the "ever faithful 'S city. Never having been beyond Worcester, I was greatly pleased with the variety of scenery through which we passed. Having two hours to spare at Bristol, I took the opportunity of visiting the Clifton Suspension Bridge and the other objects of interest in that ancient seaport, all of which gave me infinite enjoyment. As arrangements had been made by the local committee for the reception and enter- tainment of those; 4ttending the conference, I made my. way at once to the address piovidecl, but on arrival found myself in a dfficulty. The lady of the house informed me that I had come that morning, and that I was in bed. Fancy my astonishment on being informed that I was in bed; but after some explanation I learned there were two of us bearing the same name to be entertained at the house in question, but that only one name had been given, and that my colleague had reached there early in the day and secured the vacant chamber. There was I, at 11 p.m. on the Saturday before Bank Holi- day, the place crowded with visitors, and nowhere to go; but after some trouble I eventually got into comfortable rooms. 1 Rising betimes, I rambled out on Sunday morning and commenced an exploration of the "ever faith- ful." My first impressions were not very favourable, for the place seemed to me to be dirty, the streets very narrow, end everybody appeared to have built his house according, to his own idea and with the intention of having it as unlike his neighbour's as possible. I was struck with the number of churches and chapels. The churches did not appear to be able to seat more than 40 to 50 persons each. I could not get' to know, but I wondered if the endowments were of the same proportions. As the Lord Bishop of London was advertised to preach a special sermon for the Rechabites in the Cathedral that evening, it was arranged by the authorities that those people should have the first places in the tabernacle, so I joined the procession, which was headed by the Mayor in his official robes, preceded by the mace bearers (two veritable giants), the sword bearer, an ancient piece of cut- lery presented to the city by King Edward the 4th, and the cup of maintenance presented by Xing Henry the 7th. After these came the members of the body corporate, and then the great following of the Sons of Rechab. When all were comfortably seate,l the public were admitted, and judging from the great numbers who crowded into the sacred edifice the ex-Bishop of Exeter must have been very popular. The service was very indifferent—the singing not equal to our own Parish Church—but the sermon was a splendid essay on Charity, the Bishop very cleverly introducing friendly societies as charitable institutions whose benefits all ought to accept without feeling any degradation, seeing all contributed equally and took equally. He gave 'the palm to the Rechabite Society, and endeavoured Ito show that it was founded upon the highest and noblest principles. As a sermon, however, it was disappointing, and the conclusion I drew was 'quit if it was a trial sermon before a body of local preachers the preacher would only just get through. The Cathedral is without doubt. a most charming structure. It stands well, and its two towers are visible from all parts of the city. No one can gaze without admiration upon the unbroken range of roof vaulting and the general symmetry and beauty of the interior. There ate wonderful clustered pil- lars of marble and rich decorations, but the most beautiful piece of work I noticed was the bishop's ' throne, a piece of fifteenth century wood carving, with canopy ring some fifty feet in the form of a graceful pyramid. The present building is said to have been commenced in 1288, and, cer- tainly it looks very like as if the statement were true.

On the Monday morning, along with several friends I had become acquainted with, I visited Exmouth, taking advantage of a special train that I some of our Northern Railway Companies might imitate. Exeter is about twelve miles from the sea, and the Railway Companies have put on a train at seven in the morning called the bathing train, and return tickets are issued for the double journey at 6d. each. A proof of the value of the train was afforded by the number of passengers who went. There were something like 100 all off to enjoy the luxury of a swim, and a most enjoyable time we had. The quaint little town looked just half awake. It is situated on the extreme angle of the arm of sea, and is surrounded by tree-covered hills and verdant valleys, and forms as pleasant a picture as the eye could wish to see. The tide was rolling in when we reached the shore, and with a good num- ber of others we Lancashire lads enjoyed the plea- sure of a dip into the briny. It was pleasant for the air of the coast was unusually warm, and the salt water was very invigorating. We returned to Exeter early in the forenoon to. take part in a grand Temperance Fete to be held in the afternoon. There were some 7,000 processionists, but every- thing passed off in the most comfortable manner. The way in which all the people fell in and the quiet Of the crowd was a pattern to those of us who were accustomed to see the noisy crush and bustle of a crowd in Lancashire. The business of the Conference was preceded by a breakfast to all the delegates given by the Mayor in the Guildhall. This was one of the great features in the programme, seeing that it was no small honour to be invited to breakfast with a "Right Worshipful" Mayor, a sheriff, two real live Bishops, a Dean, and sundry other noble and notable person- ages. The • Guildhall, with an ancient projecting front, is an interesting feature in the street, and dates from the year 1466, and it is certainly worthy of the high commendation bestowed upon it. At the north end there is a fine armorial window, and the walls are hung with portraits, amongst which were noticed the Princess Henrietta and the Duke of Abermarle, painted by Lely. The breakfast was ex- cellent and quite in accord with the place of meet- ing, and the speeches of the Bishops, the Mayor, the Town Clerk, and others made up a memorable event. One could not help, however, wishing that it was possible to 'remind the .residents that Exeter was not the only faithful city in the kingdom, for really the way in which they kept repeating the ever faithful made the words jar upon the ear. The next two days were devoted to business, but the following morning the members of the conference were invited to visit the Castle, and whilst there a photograph of the company was taken. This castle, called the Rougemont, supposed to be so called from the colour of the soil, is a splendid ruin to this day. It was built by the Normans, and standing as it does on the highest ground within the city, with the beautiful walks that surround it, it forms one of the sights of the place. Amongst other ancient and remarkable places we noticed were the Mu- seum, built at a cost of £15,000, in honour of Prince ' Albert; the College Hall in South-street, which Icontains several portraits by Reynolds, and was built in the 14th century. The city is undoubtedly one of the most interesting cities in the kingdom; it is situated in the midst of the most delightful scenery, and well worthy of a visit. In the lower portions of Westgate are shown parts of the old walls, said to have been erected by Athelstan, and in various parts evidences of Roman occupation are to be seen.

The temperance question has clearly got hold of the public mind in the west, for there was no diffi- culty in getting public men to take Nat in the meetings, And the attendance at the evening meet- ings was very considerable. Though the Rechabites disclaim the use of intoxicants they by no means despise the good things of this life. The first day of their Conference was a day of feasting, for in ad- dition to the breakfast given by the mayor a grand banquet was provided for evening, and had one not known the popping of corks during that repast, would have given Colour to the suspicion that champagne was very much in request. The Hon. James Monro, a gnember of the Executive Council of Victoria, and`b, member of the House of Repre- sentatives of that colony, who was one of the dele- gates to the Conference, very generously invited the members to lunch on the second day, and it is needless to say, though no spirituals were present, the materials suffered considerably, for the chair- man. or High Chief Ruler as he is called, kept the Conference hard at work until two o'clock, by which time appetites had become considerably whetted. S. G.. (To be concluded in our next)
