MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. MEETING OF SUBSCRIBERS.—ENTHUSIAS- TIC PROCEEDINGS. A meeting of subscribers to the Parliamentary fund for the promotion of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was held on Wednesday afternoon in the Manchester Town Hall. There was a crowded attendance, and the proceedings were of an enthusiastic nature. Mr. " Daniel Adamson took the chair. Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., Mr. John Slagg, M.P., and Mr. W. H. Houlds- worth, M.P., who were not able to be present, wrote explaining their absence. Similar letters were sent by the Mayors of Manchester, Salford, and Warring- ton. The following gentlemen were amongst those present :—Mr. William Agnew, M.P., Mr. Benjamin Armitage, M.P, the Mayors of Stockport and Ashton, Mr. C. E. Schwann, Mr. H. P. Holt, Mr. Thomas Bradford, Mr. Thomas Mitchell, Mr. J. Fildes, Mr, Edward Mucklow, gr. Alderman Husband, Mr. Reu- ben Spencer, Mr. J. C. Fielden, Mr. Henry Bodding- ton, jun.. Mr. C. L. Samson, D. Lund, Mr. G. W. Groves, Mr. Alderman Bailey. Mr. William Fletcher, Mr. William Brown, Mr. B. T. Leech. Mr. Henry Whitworth, Mr. W. T. Windsor, Mr. W. H. John- son, Mr. Henry M'Niel, Mr. James Kershaw; Mr. W. J. Saxon, Mr. E. Leader Williams, Mr. Marshall Stevens (provisional manager), Mr. A. H. Whitworth (secretary), Mr. James W. Harvey, Alderman Batty, Chevalier Froehlioh, Dr. Mackie (Warrington), Mr. Frank Hollins, Mr. M. J. Riley, Mr. H. C. Ping. stone, and Mr. H. Birch.

The CHAIRMAN, who was received with loud cheering, said he wished to express his thanks for the generous sup- port they had given in the past to the committee over which he had the honour to preside and for their presence and reception that afternoon. (Applause.) What they had done with their subscriptions he trusted that they were there to establish with their support as shareholders and sub- scribers to the great fund. (Applause.) To them, then, the thanks of the committee were due; but he thought they ought not to forget the great corporations 4who had sup- ported them 'during the tight of 1885. (Applause.) The city of Manchester with all her power and authority, the I support of Salford, and the further aid of Warrington' no doubt had influenced the committee before whom they had to argue their case, and he had had the evidencg broughtl there so that they might be able to see they had had no trifling task to perform. He was sure the whole of the gentlemen were influenced by the support of these three great corporate bodies, and when they went a third time the greet northern port was bound to acknowledge that, by their pluck and endurance, they at least deserved the bill if they had no right to have it. (Cheers.) He hoped now that the contention and the fight were over they would have amongst their friends many of those who at one time were looked upon as their opponents and their enemies. (Hear, hear.) He thought that if Sir William Forwood was present that afternoon, he would be led by the influence of that meeting to hold his tongue and to talk reasonable talk. (Laughter and cheers.) He had no doubt they would be interested to know some- thing •of the progress through the committee-rooms in 1885. Through the Lords he thought they made a good fight. Very early in giving evidence it was manifest they took the view of the Duke of Richmond's Committee, the preceding Lords' Comrnitee of 1884, as regarded the great commercial interests that affected this question. They said they could not lightly look upon that decision, and, without evidence, would be certainly predisposed to give them the bill, because they had established a substantial, solid case. Therefore, they were encouraged in theireptrength, and he believed their opponents were discouraged in their opposi- tion before that first committee. A lot of the anxiety that fell on the committee took place about this period. They had to settle with landowners, with traders, with occupiers, and others whose property they interfered with, and he be- lieved it was the first time in the history of any great con- tention that the promoters never paid a sixpence towards the expenses of those to be dealt with in settlement, either as landowners, traders, or occupiers. (Applause.) But their anxiety did not finish when the work of the committee was done at four o'clock, for they had not only to work through the day, but they had to plod on at night with their best judgment, and all their power concentrated on every clause and condition that their friends put before them. What contributed largely to the settlement before i the House of Lords' Committee was the agreement to pur- chase the Bridgewater Canal and the Mersey and Dwell Navigation Company, and he was quite ready to confess to them that it gave him more anxiety than all the rest of the things put together except the continuous fighting. They interfered greatly with their property ; they would have been competitors in their carrying power ; their ; evidence would have sorely prolonged the sittings, and he had no hesitation in saying that they i would have let the bill through want of time.l He stood out as long as be could'against giving £1,710,000, for that joint property, but he had it impressed upon him, I time after time, by calmed, that they knew what they had to pay, but that if they went to arbitration they never knew—it might be far more, and it was not likely to be I much less. (Hear, hear.) That was a subject which affected their capital and earniog power. They had certainly got an income in the Bridgewater Canal of from £60,000 to £75,000 per annum. Then they had got the Water-street warehouses, tbey had get the waterway, a great deal of land, aed a variety of privileges—they had got it "lock, I stock, and barrel.'" (Laughter and cheers.) After they got the bill the committee resolved that they would nut leave London until the very last touch was put to it, so as to put it beyond the power of their opponents. They sent out a whip whtn the standing orders had to be suspended on Tuesday night; on.the Wednesday they sent another, and he was glad to say that their friends from Lancashire and Yorkshire, irrespective of politica—(cheers)—were in force when the third reading was announced by the Speaker, and before be could take his seat in the Strangers' Gallery a great cheer announced that the bill had passed. (Loud applause.) Such was the end of their anxious labours, and so well was the matter arranged by those in charge of the bills that the Royal assent was given and announced on Thursday afternoon at four o'clock, and then he considered be might come home. (Laughter and cheers.) So much , then for what had been done. and, he hoped they would be- lieVe, dens on their behalf. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had spent his own money freely ; he had contributed as I largely as he could ; be had not spared one moment of his time, and he had never been out of the committee rooms during the time the bill was being heard, ' except for two hours and a quarter through sickness. (Cheers.) Then, he had the support of those who never ceas,d to work if required, and their opponents were utterly con- founded when, having put something before them the night before, they found themselves confronted the next morning with new solid facts. (Cheers.) He thought they might ' say they were now on the way for fair, plain sailing, though this would greatly depend upon their future help. The shares, which were to be taken for the £8,000,000 wanted, had, by Act of Parliament, to be £lO each, though there was a disposition to make them £5 each. (Hear, and ap- plause.) The standing orders of the House would not allow of the amount being lower, but he would recommend a person, if he smoked liberally sod drank moderately— (laughter)—to save Is per week for these expenditures, which would give him £2 12s per annum, and this, in four Years, would be more than what was wanted for shares. (Hear, hear.) If he did nothing else than to encourage thrift, endurlance, and sobriety by this saving, that in itself Would be a blessing to Lancashire and to the whole of the country. (Applause.) He was astonished at the quantity of shares that had been spoken for without any solicitation, and amongst one lot he saw there was an application for 1,000—E10,000 in one offer. (Cheers.) If he was a con- tractor and had nine millions of money, he did not know that he would ask one of them So be a shareholder in this great undertaking, except for association sake, and so as to keep the thing in their own bands, and prevent any monopoly in the world taking it from them. (Cheers.) He thought the reiteration of one or two things connected with the canal would not be amiss. By the canal the millowner would save Zll2 in carriage on every 3.000 ton ship that came to Manchester. The amount of their saving could hardly be put into language, and he would advise them not to believe their opponents if they told them that it was too good to be true. Every word of the promoters' evidence in the House of Commons could be substantiated. Mr. Stevens had given them some big figures, and had told them that there was a prospect of the Canal getting 0,000,000 tons ef traffic per annum, and when that came it would be the moat serious thing for the direc- tors to keep the dividend under 20 per cent. (Cheers and laughter.) They had net found this an extravagant de- velopment, for it was founded on the traffic and dues of Liverpool. Each year 16,000,000 tons of naerchandize went in and out of that port, and it Manchester only got about one fifth of that they would be able to pay a handsome dividend. It would be a saving to him (Mr. Adamson) of £4,550 per annum. (Cheers.) Sir William Forweod bad talked largely about what would be done by liners—so much so be had said that the canal would be no use. (Laughter.) Did any man in Manchester think that Manchester had lost its understanding? It could have liners of its own—steamers 450 feet long—carrying passengers as well as goods, and with all the improvements that Manchester could give. There had net been suah a commercial enterprise as the Manchester t: hip Canal since the railway contruction in 1830. Railway shareholders were getting moomo in divi- dends, and £600,000 odd was paid for wear and tear. The same work, if done by the canal, would give £BOO,OOO in dividends, and only £20,000 for wear and tear. Let them unitedly combine to make this great waterway, as it would lead to the development of commerce and new trades, and, if nothing else, he felt persuaded they would have the thanks and prayers of thousands of their successors for the good work they had 'done in their day and generatkm. (Cheers.)

Mr. Adamson then vacated the chair, which was taken by Mr. E. Armitage, M.P., whilst Mr. WILLIAM AEINEW, M.P., moved a resolution thanking Mr. Adamson and his coadjutors, and expressing high appreciation •of their labours in connection with the scheme. Mr. Agnew thought It was a scandal upon our political institutions% and a re- flection upon the common sense of the age, that a measure of such importance as the Ship Canal Bill should have bad to pass six Committees of the Houses of Parliament. He believed that bill would set in motion a movement to enable measures of large public interest to be dealt with in a 11102 C business-like way. (Applause). M. E. C. SCHWANN, in seconding the resolution sad Mr. Adamson was worthy to stand by the side of M. De ',w- eeps. (Applause. After a few words from Mr. Armitage, the resolution was submitted and received with enthusiastic cheers.

Mr. ADAMSON, in responding, said if it were not for the four counties of Lancashire, Cheshire, Yorkshire, and Derby- shire where would be the trade of Liverpool? There would be none and Liverpool would go to the dogs. Mr. REUBEN SPENCER moved a resolution expressing con- fidence in the Ship Canal undertaking. He saw no reason, now that the scheme was adopted, and would be carried out, why the sawn of Liverpool should not join with those of Manchester to make the schemes till more successful. It was, at any rate, high time Sir William Forwood ceased whining about the poor Manchester men going to lose all their money. (Laughter.) They were capable of taking care of themselves. Liverpool never showed any sympathy for Manchester until the Shin Canal scheme was floated, then they generously made a reduction of 6LI per ton in her dues, the railway comoanies following suite with a reduc- tion of Is per ton. (Applause.) Mr. MITCHELL, manager of the Wholesale Co-operative Society, spoke to the resolution, as did Mr. Alderman HUS- BAND and Mr. J. C. FEILDEN. The latter gentleman accused Sir William Forwood of having gone before the Parliament- ary Committees of the Houses of Parliament and made widely different statements each time. In 1883 Sir William said Liverpool was not a manufacturing town: but in 1885 he stated that it was an important manufacturing place. Such statements as those were the result of having deviated from the path of strict consistency in a long inquiry. (Ap- plause.)

Mr. W. H. Bemnr,.in supporting the resolution, said so much had been said about the Liverpool Nebuchadnezzar— Sir William Forwood—that they might be benevolently in- clined towards him, even though he had refused to worship at the shrine of their prophet Daniel. (Laughter and ap- plause.)
• The 'resolution baying been carried with unanimity, the usual votes of thanks terminated the proceedings.
LIBERAL DENIONSTRATION.

IMPORTANT SPEECH BY COLONEL —GAMBLE. The'first of a series of ward meetings in support of Col. Gamble, J.P.' as the adopted Liberal candidate for the borough was held in the Volunteer Hall, St. Helene, on Thursday evening. Tho electors of Parr and Hardshaw wards were specially invited, but other electors of the borough were asked to attend. As on the occasion of Col. Gamble's first public appearance in seeking the suffrages of the electors, a week ago, there was a crowded attendance, and the proceedings were of a roost enthusiastic character. Shortly before the proceedings commenced Mr. H. Hough- ton, a member of the Liberal Council, sang "The Pilot of the State" amid cheers. The chair was occupied by Major Richard Pilkington, J.P., who was supported by Colonel Gamble, J.P., Alderman E. Johnson, Councillor J. Forster, Dr. E. P. 1 wvflrd, J.P., Dr. Jamison, Mr. C. M. Percy, Liberal labour candidate for the Inca division of South- West Lancashire, Mr. Samuel Woods, miners agent, Wigan, Messrs. James Birchall, B. A. Drotngoole, W. Wogan, John Cotton, H. L. Riley, and other gentlemen.

The Chairman, who was cheered on rising, said that that was a ward meeting called in support of the candidature of Colonel Gamble—(applause)—as the Liberal canditate for the new borough of St Helens. (Renewed applause.) He had no doubt many of them were at the meeting held last week, and helped to endorse the position of the Liberal As- sociation in the selection of Colonel Gamble as a candidate (Hear, hear.) They had heard that endorsement given with an enthusiasm and intenseness, and with a unanimity for which the Liberals of St. Helens might well congratulate themselves. They were in the presence of a great crisis. On the decieion that would take place in a few months the well-beieg of the country in a great measure depended. They knew well that they had a new reform bill, and that the welfare of the country depended upon which party was returned to power. It was pretty much the kind of crisis that happened in 1832, the last great and real reform bill that was named in this coup- try, and they knew also that when that bill had been passed, and when the opinion of the country had been asked, an immense Liberal majority was returned to power at 'se estminster. They might, he thought, congratulate themselves on the wonderful benefits that had accrued from that decision to which the country came. They knew well that increased happiness had come to the people of this country, that there had been an immense and rapid ad- vancement in trade from that time, that great reforms of law had been passed, whereby the freedom of the individual of various religious bodies, and of trade had been secured. They knew, toe, that 'through that great intelligence had spread over the country, over all the meaeures that had been passed, and over the wise direction of affairs; and they knew that there was far greater good feeling between class and class than ever tbere was before. Be would refer to one or two points that would fully prove the case that he had just put. It was sometimes said that England was declining as a nation in strength and prosperity, but he thought that when they had heard the few points he would take they would feel that that was not so. A. few years ago, when the population of this country was little more than half what it was now, after the passing of the Reform Bill of 1832, in actual numbers the paupers of the country was 20 per cent, more than was the case now. This was because the measures that hid been passed had cheapened the necessaries ef life and conduced greatly to the well- being of all classes. Thirty or forty years ago education amongst the masses was hardly known. In 1855 there were Only 230,000 children in attendance at school, and irt 1883 there were 4,000,000. (Applause.) Then freedom of trade had been secured also, which was a thilme that all the rank and file of the Liberal party, all the men and women of England could fully realise. In 1840 there were 1,200 articles of common use that were taxed, and now there were only twelve. The result was that there had been increased comfort and happiness throughout the land. There had been a diffusion of happiness, comfort, and plenty that was not known 40 years ago. There bad been such an increase in trade that whereas in 1810 only tire millions of goods were exported front the United Kingdom, in 1883 no less ,than 239 millions were exported. He could give them in- stance after instance of the triumphs and achievements gained by the Libefal party were he permitted to state them. But the point they had now before them WAS the great importance of returning a large Liberal majority to Parliament to. adminis- trate the affairs of the country (applause) and should anything short of that happen, he thought it would be A great national disaster. Having eulogised the leader of the Liberal party, the Chairman remarked that it was for them to see that Colonel Gamble wee returned to Parlia- ment—(cheers)—and to close their ranks as one man in front of the enemy. He exhorted them to put forth every effort to return the man whom they had chosen to do battle for them. (Appleuse.) Colonel Gamble, who was received with loud applause, said there had been iSilled a aries of twelve questions by the miners associttion upon subjects which they thought of the utmost importance, and answers to which they had asked. These were momentous questions So far as South- West Lancashire was concerned, and he propesed to give them answers to those questions as well as he was able. (Applause.) He knew that the opinions of their friend Mr. Percy on these questions were such as they would approve of, and if he should not be able to agree with all his opinions be hoped that their opinions were so nearly alike that they should be able te go on almost all oceasionsinto the same lobby of the House of Commons if the electors gave them the right to go there. (Applause) He hoped that at any rats they would find that he entered on those questions with a wish to do all that he could for the good of the COM- inunity at large. (Applause.) The first question was Will you vote for a bill to amend the Employers' Litbility /keg as Introduced by Mr. Burt, M.P.? 'i`he o present retsheentkiAncgtd lotamd, been a great boon to the working ' classes and if it had not been .all that it was intended to be or should have been it was one of the first measures that were brought in by the Government of Mr. Gladstone when they took office in 1880. But some employers had thought pro- per to induce their workmen to contract themselves out of the benefits of that Act, and it happened that the same thing occurred with the Agricultural Holding's Act which was passed by Mr. Disraeli's Government for the purpose of protecting farmers improvements to their holdings. That Act contained in so many words, he believed, a clause per- mitting landlords to contract the tenants and themselves .out of the Act altogethereand almost all the landlords of the country did so contract themselves out of the Act. It was not until Mr. Gladstone'll Act of 1883, which provided that so agreement to contract the landlord and tenant out of the Act should be legal, was passed that the benefits of the Act were felt. (Hear, hear), He thought that what Mr. Burt proposed to do with the Employers' Liability Act was simply what was done by Mr. Gladstone with the Agricul- keltural Holdings Act, that was to prevent masters and work- -1 men contracting themuselves oat of the Act. (Applause.) It would really be insisting upon the carrying out of the Act which would be a wise provision. (Hear, hear.) Last week the Liberal candidate of the Leek division of Stafford- shire suggested that the Act might with great reason go further than it did, and make the employer liable to give compensation for accidents caused not only by the act of the master or agent but also by the workpeople he em- ployed, a suggest:m:l which he (Colonel Gamble) thought was worth consideration. (Applause.) At present if an em- ployer, or his agent, neglected anything that ceueed injury a workman would get compensation for the injury, but if the injury was caused through the neglect of a fellow workman he did not get compensation. He thought an employer should be responsible for the workmen he employed, and for the injuries that they might do. (Applause.) The next question was" Will you vote for the amendment of the Mines Regulation Act ?" The only amendment he had thought much about was the employment of the miners' check-weighman, for at preeent they were justly suspicious that it was possible for him to be unduly influenced by their employers, and he consequently thought the request of the miners that they should appoint their own check-weighman was a most reasonable one. The miners wished the right to appear at inquests, and the question arose from most coroners being unwilling to admit any evidence unless it was presentee in the ordinary way through a solicitor. Mr. Percy held that the mimes ought to be able to appear with- out a solicitor—(applauss)—bat he (Colonel Gamble) woald rather not express an opinion en the matter. tie believed ' coroners required the ordinary practice of the courts of law, so that they must ILive evidence laid before them by some- one who thoroughly knew what the law was and the pro- cedure of the court. If anyone and everybody was allowed to address the court it would occasion great confusion, and oocupy an enormous amount of time, and probably prevent jnetice being done in many instances. If, however, any- thing could be arranged which, without incon- venience, would allow the miners to be better represented it should hive his support. The next question WAS " Will you vote for a change of the land acts ?" He was in favour of such amendments as would make land more available for the benefit of the community,

Burrow v. Wanatricyrow—The return match between these clubs was played in Sefton Park on Saturday, a slow- scoring game ending in a victory for the home club by eight wickets and 20 runs. A start was made shortly after three o'clock, Warrington going in to the IA veiling of F. Jones and T. Evans. Thre- wickets were down for 9, and then G. Clarke and C. G. Lawton put on 38 runs, and the former and T. Armstrong looked like making another stand. At 65 W. S. Fay bowled vice Evans, and the change took immediate effect, and the Innings was over at 81, the new bowler getting four wickets for 14 runs, Clarke carrying out his bat fer a 43, which contained eight 3's, but was not alto- gether spotless. Sefton began batting with E. Roper and C. Jones and the bowling being well on the spot and the field- ing close, runs came tardily, and the two were together close on an hour for 45. Six runs added and C. Overton left; but on Harold Ratcliffe joining his captain the pace increased, and the match was won and time played out. NOTES BY THE WAY. Lancashire appeared at Kennington Oval on Monday against Surrey. They had the worst of the first day's cricket and were placed in the position of following on. Tbe second attempt was a great improvement on the first, and when the last wicket fell Surrey required 116 runs to win. It was generally felt that this would be easily done, but a most exciting finish took place, five runs being wanted when the last Surrey batsman went in. They were obtained, and Surrey won by one wicket.

Middler:ex and Yorkshire -Met at Sheffield on Monday. Yorkshire had an advantage on the first innings of 32 runs, chiefly owing to the batting of Lee and Peel. The s-cond Middlesex innings closed for 226 runs, which left Yorkshire a large total to make up before they ....mild score a win. The match ended in a win for Middlesex by 49 run?. The Cheltenham week commenced on Monday, the match being the return between Gloucestershire and Sussex. The latter county gained a single innings victory on the first meeting at Brighton, mainly due to the 215 not-out innings of Mr. F. M. LUCAS. In this match Sussex scored 300 and the home county 159, as, of course, a follow•on took place. The second innings assumed a different complexion from the first, and closed for 376 runs. Sussex began their se- cond attempt well, and eventually won the match by four wickets.

In the Kent v. Surrey match, which was played at the Oval, the first innings was taken by the home county, and as the team was an exceptionally strong ene, Kent were thought lucky in sending them all back, for 147. When the visitors came to bat, however, they failed to reach this score by 44 runs. In the second Surrey innings some more remarkable scoring was shown, and not until 441 runs had been registered was the final score hoisted, Lohmann (not out, 92) being at the head of the list, On Saturday Kent, having such a large majority against them, had little chance of winning, and of coulee had no alternative but to try and make a draw of it, and in this they were successful. In the match at Horeforth Park, near Leeds, promoted by the Hon M. B. Hawke the Yorkshire team won the toss and began with Ulvett and Hall, both of whom scored brilliantly, but the rest of the team were not particularly successful, 215 representing their total. Against this Mr. Hawke's team only scored 150, the captain himself having 42 (not out) to his name. In the second innings of the county' team Sir. Rock bowled with great effect, and had it not been for the efforts of Lee and Peel the total would be deemed ridiculous. The termination of the match was a win for Mr. Hawke's side by three wickets.

COLONEL GEORGE MoCOntitrontaa, J.P.—The pro- spectus of a proposed International Exhibition of Naviga- tion, Travelling, Commerce, and Manufacture, to be held in Liverpool next year, has just been issued by the general committee. Besides giving details as to the regulations which have been adopted for the exhibition, the prospectus gives a complete list of the various committees. vice-presi• dents, dm. The patron of the exhibition is her Majesty the Queen, and his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales is the president. Among the list of vice-presidents appears the names of Colonel George McCorquodlle, J.P. (Newton-le- Willows), Lord Gerard (Aehton-in-Makerfield), and John Pearson, Esq., J.P. (Golborne Dale, Newton-le-Wallows), chairman of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Com- pany. Colonel George McCorquodale is also a member of the Executive Council, and a member of the Exhibits Com- mittee, the Advertising, Printing, and Stationery Commit- tee, the Traffic Committee, and Sectional Committee. • Effective dog-shows—Their teeth. The dentist always goes armed to the teeth. A cricketing paradox—Any eleven can make a score. Queaion by a naturalist-1s the mantle of earth its lands- cape? What word is that composed of five letters from which if you take two one remains 2—Stone. "Do you enjoy good health 2" asked Cross. "Why, yes, of course. Who doesn't 2" replied Ross, tersely. FACT LEFT OCT OF SIGICT.—Some ore says, "Man is born to rule the world." "Yes; but he sometimes get married." When a Patagonian husband kills his wife, he is fined, says a Transatlantic paper, two goats. Goat-raising is carried on in Patagonia to a large extent. About the worst case of indecision on record is that of a man who sat up all night because he could not determine which to pull off first, his coat or his boots. A boy in one of the public schools, while engaged in de- fining words a few days since, made a mistake that was not a mistake, he said: "A demagogue is a vessel that holds beer, wine, gin, whisky, or any other kind of intoxicating liquor." A prelate was once asked if he did not think that such a one followed his conscience. "Yes," said his Grace ;"I think he does follow it, as a man does a horse in a gig—he drives it first." HALVING AND QUARTERING.—When Doctor Wendell Holmes's brother John was advised to take a wife and live In a better house, he said he presumed, if he should get a better half, he would be sure of better quarters. Junior partner: Our traveller ought to be punished. He told one of our customers.in.Croydon that I am an ignorant
fool.—Senior partner: I shall speak to him without fail, and insist that no more office secrets be divulged. • _ _ .

"What is your calling?" asked the magistrate of a pri- soner who had been locked up for being drunk and disor- derly. Prisoner, in a hoarse voice: "Inventor." Magis- trate: " What have you invented?" Prisoner: "Nothing; but I am trying to." Jerusha told Ezekiel that she would not marry him unless he signed the total-abstinence pledge, so he signed two of them. Jerusha asked him why he duplicated the pledge, and Ezekiel replied innocently that he signed two pledge& 80 that if he broke one, he might still keep the other. SOMETHING NEW IN OGOKERY.—A gentleman seated be- hind a plate of beef and beans in one of the coffee and cake saloons in New York said to the waiter, "Bring me a nap- kin." "A what?" "Napkin! " The waiter shook his head dubiously. "I don't believe we've not any," he said ; "but I'll ask the boss. P'rhaps he'll send out for it. How do you want it cooked?" Sundarschool teacher: "Can you tell me, Jessie, what Is meant by the mantle of the prophet?" Jessie: "His dolman, miss." Agnes, sitting next to her : " Her mither'a a dressmaker, miss, an' kens a' aboot mantles." Teacher, facetiously: "I dare say she knows more about the profit of a mantle than the mantle of a prophet, though!" OF LIMITED SYMPATHlBB.—Scene—Vestry of village church; time—prior to morning service. Arrival of Mr. Cochrane, deacon, and owner of small farm in vicinity. Clergyman, in low whisper: " Ah, Mr. Cochrane, good morning, my dear friend! Charming weather, is it not? We ought indeed to be thankful for such blessings!" Mr. Cochrane, gleefully and in stentorian tones: "Oh, ay, gran' w'ather ! 'Od, man, we had twa cases o' sunstroke re- ported in the neeboorhood yesterday. Gran' w'ather I Beeutiful w'ather I "

A LONDON AUCTIONEEE.—The London auctioneers, as a class, are noted for their wit and humour. The following report of the auctioneer's dissertation at a picture sale will give readers an idea of the manner in which the audience were interested :—" HAMLET AND THE Gnosr."—" Here we have a picture now. I'm a cheap dealer, but it appears I'm dear to some of the ladies; they can't bid for admiring my fine figure. But I don't bid 'em to look at me. I want 'em to bid for me. This picture represents, I believe, Hamlet and the Ghost. Now, here you have spirits on a picture. If you hang this up your spirits will always be high. You don't need to go to the public-house while you have this private for yourself. Bless me! you don't appreciate art. I shall break my 'art soon. I wish I had the art of per- suading you to buy—such a tine painting as this. Half-a- crown—um ! I think the one that made that bid has only half-a-crown to his head. Half-a-crown! Pehaw ! Bid higher. Find at least a crown and you'll get a sovereign to wear it. This is an oil painting. I wish I had only an oily tongue wherewith to paint its beauties. Three shil- lings—go on. Three and six, a little better half, as the man that married a small woman said. Why, the paint's worth that; then just endeavour to calculate the amount of inspiration necessary to produce such a marvellous result. Can you find any fault in the picture? Is there anything badly drawn? Aye—the money I've drawn from you to-night, for I've drawn but little. Look how well that ghost is drawn. It was drawn in the artist's chief drawing-room, so that it would have the effect of drawing more spectators to see it. Bee how well Hamlet's tooth is drawn, but not by the dentist. Criticise the figure of the Prince of Denmark. He's worth half-a-crown himself, but he didn't even get his father's. Four shillings—right. Pay attention to the moon—yon might pay attention to a young lady if there were one on the canvas, but there ain't—and pay me, too, when you've bought this. Look at the expression of sorrow at his father's being sold to a base death, and also himself being near sold for four shillings. The picture's not a foul one, but it's BO (h) entirely well done you can almost hear the cock crow in the neighbouring farmyard. Four and six. ' six. We are ascending, but to drop again, as the convict said when he stepped on to the scaffold at his execution. Five shillings! Here you be ! Take it and preserve it, but not as jam; it's not a pair; there's only one; preserve it in spirits; now our spirits should revive a little !"

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of 'this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present— the Rev. Q. F. Roberts (chairman), and Messrs. Balharry, Blackhurst, Brown, Appleton, William Houghton, John Houghton, Ratcliffe, Derbyshire, Broadbent. Humphries, Greenell, Foster, Harrison, Owen, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk), MR. JEAN'S ACCOUNT. Amongst the accounts submitted was one of £2l is Id from Messrs. W. D. Jeans and Co. for legal expenses in the recent action between the Guardians and the Newton Corn- missioners.—The CLERK said he had communicated to Mr. Jeans that the Board was prepared to pay the full amount of his bill. As there had been no means of submitting the bill for taxation, Mr. Jeans said he would prefer to deal with it in such a way as that there could be no possible bad result to the Board in that respect, so that instead of asking the amount the Board was willing to pay him—the original bill amounting to £36 lfls lid—Mr. Jeans himself in a very liberal manner had taxed the bill and reduced it to the sum of £2l Is Id.—The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Jeans had dealt in a very liberal way with the Board.—The accounts were passed. THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.—THE ttosprrat. A meeting of this committee was held at the Padgate Schools on the 18th inst., when there were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), and Messrs. Jolly, _Blackhurst, Houghton, and W. Houghton.—The SUPERINTENDENT reported the children to be healthy and cheerful. The schoolrooms bad been cleaned and painted since the last meeting of the committee. It was recommended that Mr. Owen be instructed to draw up a specification of the alterations necessary at the hospital. An application was made by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, St. John the Baptist's Church, Earlestown, for use of band on the occasion of the Sunday school treat on the on the 22nd August, and the application was complied with. —The CHAIRMAN, in moving the confirmation of these minutes, said that since the last meeting of the committee they had had to deal with dry rot in the floor and joists at the schools, and about 15 square feet of wood had lead to be taken up and replaced. With respect to the hospital they proposed, in order to meet the requirements of the medical officer and the Local Government Board inspector, adding a yard to the present one and furnishing that yard with the requisite offices, and putting in the present yard, which is larger than the new one would be, a chamber for the pur- pose of disinfecting clothes and things of that kind. (Hear, bear.)—Mr. BROADBENT : And to put in a more direct foot- path—The CHAIRMAN said they had concluded to have a road made direct from the schools to the hospital, and to have it gravelled over.—Mr. JOIZAIII seconded the adoption of the minutes. The committee he thpught, were unanim- OnS that the little matters referred to were absolutely neces- sary for the proper working of the place.—Mr. DARBISHIRZ said that although lie had been at the committee meeting, he did not understand that the committee had come tq, a definite decision as to the making of the footpath across ;Tie field. He consulted several members of the committee, and from what he gathered he thought it was not their feeling that the footpath should be made direct across the field. They thought that the footpath already in existence was a sufficient road to the hospital, arid especially considering that very often there was no patient its the hospital. He did not suppose that the same complaints would be made about the footpath hereafter that had been made before, and be did not think so much good land should be wasted in making another footpath.—The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the subject of the new footpath was not mentioned in the minutes, and be merely made leis remarks in answer to a question from Mr. Broadbent. The majority of the com- mittee, though Mr. Derbyshire was not with them, had in- spected the hospital, and they were, with a single excel> tion, unanimous that they should proceed in due time to the.censtruction of that footpath.—Mr. BROADBENT thought it was important that there should be a more direct path between the schools and the hospital. It was more import- ant that they should have a direct path than that they should secure a yard or two for potatoes or oats.—The minutes were confirmed.
SCHOOL FEES. The School Fees Committee reported that school fees had been allowed in 77 old and 19 new cases.—.on the mo- tion of Mr. BLACBHURST, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY. the minutes were adopted.

The following letter, signed by C. V. Dalton, was read from the Local Government Board, viz. :—" lam directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 27th ult., enclosing a letter from Mr. Cooper, the vaccination officer of the Newton district of the Warring-ten Union, with reference to arrears of vaccination in his district. The Board have also received a detailed statement as to each of the cases not fully accounted for in , returns for the year 1893 and the first half of 1884. and I from Mr. Holford, the vaccination officer of the Warrington district, a statement relating to the default shown in his returns for the seine periods. As regards Mr. Holford's statements, lam to observe that it does not give ths infor- mation asked for in the Board's letter.to you on the 30th June last, and I am to request that he may be called noon to.furnish the information at once. With regard to Mr. Cooper's letter, I am to state that the Board recognise the difficulty with which he has to contend, bat they are not sure that he has in all cases acted with sufficient prompti- tude in dealing with cases of default. Is some instances of children born in 1883 there is no record of notice having been sent until after the commencement ef the April atten- dances in 1884, and in the case of children who are ill the evidence of the vaccination officer's efforts to obtain certifi- cate of postponement is not always satisfactory. lam to add that the Board will instruct the inspector at the next inspection of vaccination in the Warrington Union to spe- cially report on the way in which Messrs. Cooper and Idol- ford perform their duties."—The CLIMB said he would com- municate with the vaccination officers on the matters men- tioned in this letter.

div.head: ALTERATIONS AT PADGATE.
div.p: THE ALTERATIONS AT PADGATE.

Six tenders for the carrying out of the proposed altera- tions and improvements at Padgate Schools were considered, These were as follows :—Mr. W. Taylor, Warrington, £447 ; Mr. John Norbury, Warrington, .£438 lOs ; Mr. G. Wallington, junr., Warrington. £400; Messrs. John Collin and Son, Warrington, £375; Mr. J. Dolan, Warrington £422, 10s; Mr. R. Beckett, Hartford, £392. It was stated that the architect's (Mr. Owen) estimate was £350.-Mr. BLACICHURST moved, and Mr. JOLLEY seconded, that Messrs Collin and Son's tender, which was the lowest, be accepted. —Mr. DARBYSITIRE said he should like to throw out the hint that a few pounds extra given to the builder at the first was not often thrown away. It was not always best to take the lowest estimate, and they need only scrutinise the state of things at Padgate Schools to verify this. He hoped whoever got the work would be able to do it so as to be a credit to himself, and be trusted that no one had put in BO small a tender that they could not do the work well. —Mr. BLACKIIIIRST said the tender he proposed should be accepted was above the architect's estimate, and it would be left to the architect to see that the work was properly done.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he understood Messrs. Collie's to be a good firm, and besides it would be left to the archi- tect to look after the work. If he did not do his duty the members of that Board ought to bring the matter up.—Mr. JOLLEY said all the builders who had contracted were of a height, and capable of doing the work satisfactorily.—Mr. BROADBENT did not quite agree with Mr. Jolley as to the contractors being all of a height, and as for the architect looking after the work, he thought if Mr. Owen had been there he would have told them that the best architect in the world could not prevent a jerry builder from scamping his work. They were not in a position to suppose that any of the builders who had tendered would do his work in a jerryl manner' and he tirought that Messrs. Collin's, who happened to be the lowest, could be trusted under Mr. Owen's super- vision to do the work thoroughly well. At the same time he would be sorry if they should think that they were bound to accept the lowest tender because it was the lowest without reference to the character of the builder. (Hear, hear.)—The motion of Mr. BLACKHURST was then unani- mously adopted. This was all the business of interest..

P. R. ; tnothoetennor fifteen farms which he says my family con- James saw him long ago, solitary and meditative. ,xins and myself occupy. The ex act number is six, die- But the park is deserted, and at its best, too, for the playing agains wonderful accuracy of statement. trees are still luxuriantly green and the flower beds I think, Mr. Editor, I have now taken length enough, and ablaze with colour. I hope I have succeeded in showing that his own letter is The political world is for the moment as quiet as ! sufficient confirmation of my evidence given to the Assess- the aspect of a town. But this, to use a not tm- ment Committee. Should, however, that experienced and familiar quotation, is but "the torrent's stillness ere discriminating body require additional information I con it dash below," and presently we shall be in the full ; 830" ten'old what I gave them can be procured with the uproar of a general election. Already here and, greatest of ease. I tender my apology for the length of this ' there across the stillness of town come the sounds letter, and beg to remain, of impending battle. Members of the House of ! Faithfully yours, Commons who intend to offer themselves for re- - - WM. HOUGHTON. election have for the most part gone away for a holiday. But, they have not gone far, and are anxiously keeping their eyes upon the constituency of their choice. It would be a very, sensible thing if it were possible that a truce should be arranged for at least two months. The general election will not take place till the third week in November. Why should energies be wasted, scattered over a desultary warfare extending over three months? If everyone would consent not to take up arms till the first day of November it would be an exceed- ingly sensible proceeding, and would save much , time and worry not only to candidates but to the ! general public. That, however, is impossible. Here ' and there two candidates, secure in the monopoly ; of a contest, have agreed not to take active pro-' ceedings till October is far advanced. But these cases are rare, and we shall have for the next three' months a dropping fire culminating in a grand can- nonade carried on all through November. It is an old saying that history repeats itself. Anyone familiar with the history of political affairs this time seventeen years ago will acknowledge the -accuracy of the axiom. Then, as now, a great Re- form Bill had been passed. Then, as now, Parlia- ment was dissolved with the Conservatives in power. Then, as now, Mr. Gladstone was at the head of an enthusiastic Liberal majority; and it isl not rash to predict that now, as then, the result of ; the General Election will be to displace the Censer-1 vatives and bring back Mr. Gladstone. One curt- ' ously precise parallel that makes this assumption not seem rash is the identity of the course assumed I by the leaders of the Conservative party and that of I their predecessors in 1868 in view of the probabilities of the succeeding year. Within the first week of as- suming the leadership of the House of Commons, Sir M. H. Beach spoke with well assumed confidence of what the Government would do "next year." The House of Commons laughed at this. But it will be noted since then the Conservative Ministers have assumed a regular habit of talking about what they will do next year, disdaining even the use of the saving clause "should we then be in office." It was exactly the same in 1868. On the 9th November in that year Mr. Disraeli, replying at the Lord Mayor's banquet to the toast of her Majesty's Minis- ters, suggested the friendly interposition of the Great Powers in the quarrel, even then manifesting itself, between Prince and Prussia. "I hope," said Mr. Disraeli with chrracteristic audacity, "that when this day next 3,ear I have the honour to res- pond to the toast of her Majesty's Government, I may be permitted to remind you of these observa- tions." Two days later Parliament was dissolved, and within three weeks Mr. Disraeli was on his way to Windsor to place his resignation in the hands of the Queen. • The course of events in 1868 were, in point of time, it little in advance of those we are now living through. Parliament was prorogued on the 31st July, the dissolution was decreed on the 11th No- vember, and the elections were practically over by , the 30th, giving Mr. Gladstone a majority of 121. But as the course then followed will be a precedent for to-day, it will not be without interest to recall what happened. Mr. Disraeli, introducing a prece- dent much questioned at the time but since gener- ally adopted, did not await the meeting of Parlia- ment in order to tender his resignation. This, as I have mentioned, was placed in the hands of the - Queen on the 2nd of December. On the 4th Mr. Gladstone, who was peacefully resting at Hawarden Castle, was summoned to Windsor, and promptly accepted the office tendered to him. On the 10th December the new Parliament met, and Mr. Denison was elec,ted Speaker. The swearing-1n of members commenced on the following day, and continued through the week. On the 15th the new writs were issued for members who had accepted office, and the House adjourned till the 29th. On that day the new members took their oaths and their seats, and there was a further adjournment to February 16th, 1869, when this ever-memorable Parliament began its work. It is curious, looking down the lists of Mr. Glad- stone's ministry of 1868, to note how fate has fared with the men who formed it. • A remarkable pro- portion have been made peers, Mr. Gladstone him- self being a distinguished and desirable exception to the rule. Sir W. Page Wood immediately became Lord Hatherley on elevation to the wciolsack, and has since gone to another place. Earl de Grey, Lord President of the Council in this historical Ad- ministration, is now the Marquis of Ripon. Robert Lowe, Chancellor of the Exchequer, is now Lord Sherbrooke, and has published a book of poetry. Mr, Bruce, Home Secretary, is now Lord Aberdare.

. WHAT DID COLONEL GAMBLE SAY?
• LYIII3I. LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Barton, C. Lester, and H. Stanton. _ I

REFUSING TO QUlT.—Stephen Gibbon, who lives at Man- I chaster, a yeunk man, was charged with having refused to quit the premises of the spread Eagle Inn Lvmrn, on the let August, when requested to leave 1-.:y Mr. Kane, the landlord.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed.

A CARELESS DnaYsta.—Herbert Lewis, a youth, was charged with having left a horse and cart an unreasonable time on the highway, at Partington, on the 15th July.—lt was stated by P.C. Buchanan that the defendant had been catching birds in a field for about an hour.—He was ordered to pay the costs. DAMAGING PEAS AND POTATOES.—GIorge Rowell, John Rowell, Thomas Lea, and Frederick Butterworth, four lads, living at Newfield, Lymm, were charged with having,on the 16th instant, destroyed peas and potatoes, the property of Edwin Massey, doing damage to the extent of ss.—lt was stated that the two Rowells had been in the field before, and were in fact never out of mischief—George and John Rowell were each fined 2s 6d, and 2s 6d damages, and costs; the other two being simply ordered to pay costs. DEFAMATORY LArrovanz.—Samuel Pollard was charged with having used defamatory language concerning Annie Rose, on the 30th Jelly, at Partington. He was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognisances of .£lo.—Mary Astbury was charged with using defamatory language concerning Ann Elizabeth Wood, at Lynam, on the 18th inst.—The case was dismissed.

Assaurr ow A WOMAN.—John Southern, a labourer, liv- ing at Higher-lane, Lynem, MO charged with having as- saulted Ann Bradbury on the 25th July. The defendant was represented by Mr. Fletcher, Northwich.—lt was stated by Ann Nicholson that on the day in question she saw the defendant, who lives with Bradbury, between seven and eight o'clock In the evening. He struck Bradbury both with his closed and open fist, and he took her by the legs and threw her over his shoulders, but as she pinched his back he had to let her down again. He afterwards kicked her and knocked her into a hedge. There were several people who saw the assault and they cried " shame" at the defendant.—Corroborative evidence was given by a lad named James Mayers and a girl named Ann Cowsell.—Ser- geant Harrington stated that on the 28th telt, he attended an inquest as to the death of a child of Bradbury, and the de- fendant there admitted that he struck Bradbury, but denied kicking or knocking her down.—ln defence; it was conten- ded that the defendant had only been doing his beet to get Bradbury into the house as she was quarrelling with another woman outside. !Nit% Fletcher also mentioned that the defendant had told him that he and Bradbury in- tended to marry each other„—Ann Bradbury was celled for the defence and eaid those proceedings were taken entirely against her wish, and she and the defendant had been living comfortably together since the time of the alleged assault. One of the marks OA her face which were apparent at the time of the inquest was caused by the witness Ann Nichol- son, and she could not say how the other marks were caused' —Mr. Ditchfield said that the mark on the side of Brad- bury's face was canned by her falling against a clothes post. —A fine of 20a and costs was imposed, and defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months on his own ' recognisance of £lO. CLAIM FOR DAMAGSS.—AIfred Leather, a fastian cutter, Lymm, was sued by John Daniels for 4s 10-1, damages caused by leis having wrongfully neglected to finish his work.—Defendant was ordered to pay the amount and costs a 2s ad per month. DRIJNKENNESS.—Thomas Lee was charged with haying been drunk and disorderly at Lymm on the 26th July —A fine of ss, Including costs, was imputed,

Sir,—l am a Radical—a Radical who has a firm belief I and trust in Mr. Gladstone and the other popular leaders of our party—and what is more, I hope to seal Colonel Gam- ble secure a glorious victory over the "stranger" who has dared to presume that the people of St. Helens will desert the man who has done so much for us, and accord their sup- port to him, who has no more claims on our sympathy than , the man in the moon. I only wish to point out how unfair ,to Colonel Gamble and misleading to the working classes have been the so-called "full reports " et the candidate's i excellent speech. I and many others of my fellow-workmen , were extremely anxious to hear Col. Gamble's exposition of : his opinions, and we trusted that as that was his first public I apparance since the enfranchisement at the borough it I would be fully and accurately reported. But we have been grieviously disappointed. More especiaLy has this been the I core with regard to the journal which publicly announced ! a "full report" of the meeting. I have scanned and compared the various reports in the Liverpool and local i papers, bat I must say, sir, that the report in the Examiner seemed to me to be the most accurate and reliable. This I I will show in one or two striking examples. In the early ' part of his speech Col. Gamble spoke of his support of Liberal Governments, and his remarks were reported in one 'of your contemporaries as follows :—" I told them that I was a consiQtent supporter of all the Liberal Gevernments during my time, and that I had supported the Liberal cause in South-West Lancashire on all occasions." But on turning to your paper I found that an important passage bad been °mitred. The Examiner's report pave:—' I told them that I bad been a consistent supporter of all the Libtral Govern. . ments during my time, and that I had supported the Liberal cause in South-West Lancashire on all occasions with al/ ' the infuenpe I could, and was always willing to bear my share of the expense of the work." It Colonel Gamble really , said he had supported the Liberal cause "with all the in- fluence he could and was willing to bear his share of the ex- -1 pulse of the work," I would ask, sir' why was that omitted I from the so-c died " full reports." Was it by "accident" or design? I have italicised the words in your report, for they are mest important as showing that Colonel Gamble is always ready with his moral and material support to bear , his share of the expense which would otherwise fall on other people.

Coming to another point,sir, I find anotherglaring omission. Colonel Gamble's words are given as follows :—" I told them—what I believe le exactly correct—that I did not ! know there was any difference between the political prin. ciplP9 of our leader and my own. (Cheers.)" But, again, sir, the Examiner says :--" I told them—what I believe is exactly correct —that I did not know that there was any difference between my political principles and those of our leader. Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) I presume you want to send to Parliament a man who will support the great Liberal cayse—(hear, hear)—and though there might be dif- ferences of opinion they were all trying to make to one great poMl, the greatest good to the greatest number—(applause)— where men are not bound by the trammels, as we consider the Tories are, there will be different ideas as to the exact means to be adopted. There is no avoiding these dif- ferences in the Liberal party, but the one great point is whether the candidate you send to Parliament will support the party tchichyou intendhim to support. (Applause.)" Here Is the omission of another most important observation affect- ing the Liberals. Your contemporary again save :—" I said that I was in favour of a considerable modification of the constitution of the House of Lords, and was in favour of the repeal of the law of primogeniture;" but the Examiner report credits the gallant Colonel with the additional ob. servation—"as well as great modifications in the Land Acts, such as the transfer of land." This I consider to have been one of the most important remarks of our candidate, and yet We find it omitted from the 't fall report." Either Celonel Gamble said he was in favour of mo- difications of the Land Acts or he did not, and your paper says be did, while the other is silent. Which is the " correct card," as the fre- quenters of tracts say ? There was an extraordinary differ- ence in the reports of Colonel Gamble's speech effecting the taxation question, hat I find that yours is the only paper which gives Colonel Gamble's forcible and expressive words: " Two-thirde of the taxes of the country—£44,ooo.ooo out of about £65 o£o,ooo—comes from indirect taxation on the ,eve..ities of life ; that is to say, on tea, sugar, cocoa, spirits, and beer, towards which everyone contributes in pro- portion to the amount he consumes, not in proportion to his wealth or hie income. I do not mean to say I should give a boon to the working classes. I hate the expression, but what the workinj- men should have is equality of taxation. It is no wonder, sir, that there were" loud cheers" follow- ing these words. We working-men dislike so-called "boons," and Colonel Gamble was just 'expressing our opinions on the subject when he said : "I hate the expres- -non. hut what the working-men should have is equality of taxation." Why did the "full report " fail to give this characteristic observation of our "Colonel 2" Echo answers " Why ?" My only object in writing this to von, sir, is to Point out the. various reports do or candidate's speech, in one or two important particulars, and I trost you will ex- cuse me troubling you upon the matter.—Yours, August IS, 1885. A ST. HELENS RADICAL.

THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST 22, 1885. VISIT . OF MR. CHAMBERLAIN TO WARRINGTON. We are glad to be in a position to definitely announce that the Rt. Hon. Joseph Chamberlain will shortly pay a visit to Warrington for the pur- pose of giving an address on political topics to the Liberals of the district. Mr. Chamberlain, as the " bright particular star" of the advanced and ad- vancing section of Liberals, will be warmly wel- comed when he reaches this part of Lancashire. The right hon. gentleman is wanted everywhere, but, as he cannot accede to more than a few of the calls upon him, the Liberals of Warrington may regard themselves as especially favoured in being promised a visit within the next few weeks.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. A MAN KILLED. Yesterday afternoon an accident occurred st Runcorn which has caused a widespread feeling of grief in the town. The Runcorn Market Hall is undergoing renovation and repairs, and engaged upon the work was Mr. Geo. Littler, grocer, of Surrey-street, who followed the occupation of slater and plasterer. About four o'clock yesterday after- noon he wished to plaster a portion of the ceiling, and in order to reach the spot he placed the bottom of the ladder upon a table in the centre of the building, the top resting upon a beam. The angle of the ladder was very considerable, and a by- stander suggested to Mr. Littler that it would be very dangerous ascending it in that position. '' Oh," replied Mr. Littler. "it's all right," and at once mounted the ladder. He had no sooner commenced his work than the bottom of the ladder Blipped and he was precipitated to the fleor, a distance of 30 feet. Alighting upon his back and bead upon the Rags, he sustained a fearful fracture of the skull, and a pool of blood quickly collected. He was plac,d anon the table by several persons present and a medical gentleman sent for. Dr. Mangan was promptly upon the scene of the catastrophe, and after an examination stated that not the slightest hopes of recovery could be entertained, so serious were the injuries, and ordered his removal borne. Inspector Roche, who had been rendering every assistance in his power, sent for a stretcher from the Old Quay, and upon this the dying man was conveyed home, where he ex- pired an hour and a half later. The deceased, who was a strong young fellow, 26 years of age, and six feet one inch in height, belonged to a very respectable family in the town, and the greatest sympathy is expressed for his rela- tives. He leaves a wife and two young children to mourn his loss, but they are not left altogether unprovided for. His family have been most unlucky. A few months ago his uncle, who resides in Greenway-road, sustained serious in- juries by falling off the roof of Camden Wesleyan Chapel, his brother was lamed for life by a fall from a building in the Runcorn Soap and and Alkali Company's works, and several years ago his cousin, who was a frequent correspond• ent to the Examiner, was downed in the Mersey when sailing in a Canoe.
TERRIBLE FALL FROM A TELEPHONE POLE AT WIDNES.-ANOTHER DRINK VICTIM.

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquiry at the Widnes Accident Hospital as to the death of Robert Kerr, 36 years of age, a labourer, in the employ of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company, who was killed on the previous day by falling off a telephone pole. Mr. C. H. Winshurst (from the office of Mr. Bateson and Co.) appeared on behalf of the company.—Mr. Thomas Rowe' superintendent to the cOmPanY, Paid the pole from which chcearied fell was 65 feet bib, and fired with "dogs," or iren stanchione. T Wag le May rte to —The Coroner : Tkat depends upon whether a man is drunk or sober—Witness : Exactly gm—Thomas Alfred Morgan, 17 years of age, said the deceased, Jonathan Birch, and himself went to Widnes to work for the company. After leaving their tools at Mrs. unsworth's cookshop, they all went ietto Walker's vaelte. Here the two men had a pint of beer each, and witness a glass. They then went to the yard of the Mersey Ibtel, which they reached about a quar- ter to eleven. Witnees went up the telephone pole, which was near the Mersey Hotel, for the purpose of painting it. At five minutes to twelve the three went into the Mersey Hotel for dinner. The twe men had a pint of beer each, and witness a glass to dinner. Deceased had DO more beer until he went up the pole and met his death. About one o'clock witness commenced to go up the pole, bet before he did so he told deceased not to go up it, as he would try to manage himself. Deceased said "What another man will do I will, or I will break my neck."—fhe Coroner : Why dida't you want him to go up ? Because he looked as If he had had too much drink—But he was 30 and you 17 ; he had only had twice as much as you.—Witness proceeded to say deceased went up the pole until be got to the first arm of it. He then put his right leg across the second arm, and was getting hold of it, when he slipped and fell to the bottom, and dashed his brains out ueon the flags. Dr. MDonnell was cent for, and pronounced life extinct. Deceased lived at Marlberough-street, Vauxhall-road, Liverpool.—Jonathan Birch was then called. He admitted that at Lime-street station, Liverpool, the deceased bor- rowed Is from him, another Is in the train, and a third at Widnes. At Lime-street deceased left him several times under various pretences—he believed to get drink. At Widnes he told deceased not to go up the pole, because he did not consider he was steady enough to do so. Kerr was a little intoxicated. Witness did not see him have any drink in Widnes.—Morgan was recalled, and repeded his evi- dence.—Birch admitted it was true deceased had a drink as soon as he got off the station.—The Coroner severely cen- sured Birch fer having sworn the contrary, and said he would not have recollected this at all if the youth bad not said it, thus obliging him to make the admission. Mr. Brighouse also asked him why he had let the deceased go en, as he (witness) was managing the work—Witness: I didn't —Mr. Dutton (auctioneer) : This is a very serious position for this witness to be in, for he is in a measure responsible for this man's life. Seeing that deceased could not do his duty he ought not to have allowed the man to go ap the pole.—Witness said a child could go up the pole.— I The Coroner: But not when deceased had had several pints of beer. He would not have lost his life if.he had not been intoxicated.—Witnes : Well, hold him not to go up, and it was his own fault, for he went up when my bank was turned. —The Coroner said the witness ought to have discharged the man when he found he was not sober. When, however, a foreman of workmen took pints of beer with those under him he placed himself in their power, and could not be ex- pected to discharge them if they were not capable of doing their work. The witness might have discharged his legal dote' to the man, but certainly not his moral one to see that he came to no harm—Tile jury returned a verdict of "Ac- cidental death."

CHEATING THE RAILWAY COMPANY.—At War- rington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a man named Morris, a labourer at Vulcan Foundry, Earlestown, was summoned for riding on the Lon- don and North-Western Railway from Warrington to Earlestown, without having paid his fare. When asked for his ticket at Earlestown Station, he denied having come by train. Her then became abusive, and P.C. Hunt was sent for. Defendant was under the influence of drink at the time. Next morning he went to the station master and, tendered the fare, which was then refused. Defendant, who told the magistrates that he was so drunk that be did not know what he was doing, was fined 5s and costs.— At the same Court a rather ingenious attempt to cheat the Railway Company was disclosed. Thomas and Rebecca Gre,gson, husband and wife, were charged with travelling from Wigan to Earlestown without tickets. At noon on the 25th July the two were seen at Earlestown Station, whence they went to Wigan. In the evening the male defendant ar- rived at Earlestown by the 7-32' train from Wigan. On being asked for his ticket, he denied haying come by train, and said that he was waiting for his daughter. By the nine o'clock train the woman arrived, and was seen to leave the train and go into the waitinguroom. She also•denied coming by train, and said that she was waiting for her husband. The Bench fined them .10s and costs. each. THE SHIP CANAL.—Mr. Daniel Adamson, as will be seen from an advertisement in another column, will address a meeting in the Drill Hall, Warrington, on Wednesday next. The Mayor will occupy the chair, and the meeting will be addressed by various gentlemen. Judging from, the demonstration the other week, Mr. Adamson, as chairman of the pro- moters of the Ship Canal, may count on a most en- thusiastic reception. The weekly meeting of the Provisional Committee was held in the Board- room, 70A, Market-street, Manchester, yesterday afternoon, Mr. Daniel Adamson, the chairman of the Board of Directors of the Company, presiding. It was stated that inquiries had been made at the office as to what would be the liability of share- holders in the company, and instructions were given by the committee to reply to all such inquiries 1 that the liability of shareholders will be absolutely limited to the amount unpaid of the shares I held by them. The London correspondent of 1 the "Manchester Evening Mail" says :—Every step taken in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal is watched with the keenest interest in Lon- don commercial circles, and the proceedings of Wednesday's meeting in the Town Hall have naturally attracted a good deal of attention. The earnestness which has all along been shown Py the promotors has undoubtedly had a marvellous effect, and you meet very few people now who entertain any doubt in respect to the raising of the capital, though nearly everybody thinks Parliament will have next year to be asked to sanction the payment of interest out of capital during the construction of the works. It is amusing to notice some of the support which the scheme has attracted since it be- I came a stem reality. Members of Parliament, who in the first instance pooh-poohed it, and refused to give a penny towards the parliamentary expenses. are now found among its champions, ready to do anything rather than incur the of the elec- tors; but the promoters can well afford to look over this sort of thing. s They have much to do be- fore they get the canal, and their object will, I. am sure, be to make Mende 'wherever they can.

div.head: LOCAL BANKRUPTCY CASES.
div.p: LOCAL BANKRUPTCY CASES.

A sitting of Warrington Coanty Court was held before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes on Thursday, when the follow- ing bankruptcy cases were taken. RELtaaw PORTER.—The public examination of Wil- liam Porter, builder. contractor, and timber merchant, was proceeded with. The debtor stated that he had carried on business since 1877, whet, he commenced with a capital of £250, his own money. Having mentioned the various places at which be had carried on business, the debtor said that when he gave no business in Church-street he was worth £3,000 or £l,OOO, chiefly in property. He disposed of his property in Church-street by public auction, and the sale realised £3OO or £4OO. When he left Church-street he went to Edgworth-street, where he had carried on business since, having purchased it for £l,OOO. The goodwill was put down at £2OO, as far as he could remember. A fire took place at the Edgworth-street place of business, but he was not responsible for the loss. Since he had been in business he had made out balance sheets, which were somewhere in the office. He had sold four houses in Crosfield-street, and received about £1,500, and he had had to pay a mortgage of £1,200 in round figures on it. He made out a balance sheet for 1884, and be considered, speaking from memory, that he was worth about £5,000 in property in December. In March last he had a statement of affairs prepared for the purpose of a private meeting of creditors. That showed a balance of £5OO to the creditors. He accounted for the difference between his yearly statements of accounts by saying that the equities were considerably reduced. A con- tract had been completed at Bootle, and a sale of plant had taken place, which realised about £lOO. In March the creditors agreed to receive payment of 20e in the pound in four instalments, but he could not make such an offer now that the mortgagees had taken the equities. The official receiver (Mr. Ridgway) questioned the bankrupt at length on this matter and on his management of affairs. The debtor repudiated the management, and said that he had simply acted under the direction of the trustees, who had paid him weekly wages since Hie 23rd March, and had checked the accounts almost daily. His average income since he commenced business would be about £5OO a year. He had drawn about £2OO a year out of his business. His personal expenses would not be more than £soa year. He denied having spent a lot of money in pleasure. In answer to a creditor' the debtor said some few of the creditors were paid 20s by the trustees. It might have been preferable for the balk of the creditors had he remained in charge, but he thought the trustees had done what they censidered to be the best for the es- tate. In answer to Mr. Ridgway the bankrupt said that he had told several creditors of the way in which the trustees were acting, and they asked him to make the best he could of the job.—A Creditor : How much did you lose on the Conservative Club? Mr. Potter: Nothing.—The Creditor: How much did you gain? Mr. Porter : I did not pin anything ; it was like giving change out of a shilling.l— examination was adjourned.

Broaann SPANN.—This bankrupt was again brought up in custody. Having read through the shorthand writer's transcript of the evidence given by him at the previous sit- ting of the court, he made one or two amendments, and sigaed the depositions. On the application of the Official Re- ceiver, the examination of the hanknapt was then closed.— Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of the bankrupt, made applica- tion for certain tools to be delivered to the bankrupt's wife, which was granted.

kw JAMBS TOWNEND 111001111.—Thes debtor, a solicitor, attended to undergo his publie examination, and was questioned by the Official Receiver and Mr. P. Davies, who represented three creditors. He said that when be first commenced business he had no capital of his own, and simply went into the office after his talker's death. His father died in 1884, and he had been carrying on business since on his account. He was admitted in 1880 and joined his father, but had no specific share in the profits of the business. As far as he could make out the total indebted- ness would be about £4OO or £5OO. He attributed his failure to the amount of debts that he had to pay off out of his own earnings. There had been a vast amount of money owing by the office. He did not know of any other Cause to which to attribute his position. Thought his profits last year would be about £4OO, out of which he had to pay £2OO for his mother's maintenance, also some of brie father's private debts, and office liabilities. He did not keen an account of his personal expenses, but they would be D. or £1 108 a week, including travelling expenses. He was married in September last year, when he thought that he was in a good position.—after a long questioning, the examination of the bankrupt was adjourned until next court day. He made a settlement on his marriage of the furniture bought from Mr. Marsh, and the other furniture, as far as be could remember. Some of the goods were paid for by his father- in-law, and those were by deed muds out to his wife, but at the time he did not know such a deed was being prepared. He had executions in his house, and, on the advice of the solicitor who drew up the deed of assignment, he produced that document to the bailiffs, knowing that he had a mar. riage settlement —Mr. Ridgway: What moneys do yow owe to your father's or your mother's trust, or to the trust of Mr. and Mrs. Moore's marriage settlement? There was a sum of £5O received from the trust. I think. He believed it was received by cheque, but be could not recollect that the elteque was endorsed by his brother in blank and handed to him. He made use of the money for paying away, one use being to pay an account for his father's funeral. That had nothing to do with tbe trust matter. He could not swear through whom he cashed the cheque. This was the only trust fund he had had anything to do with. The£so went towards paying private debts and so on. His mother was entitled to the life interest of the amount, it came to about £25 a year, and his idea was that , the £25, for two years, would ply the principal buck. He could give no reason for his failure beyond what he had stated. He had not spent money recklessly. In tha face. of a letter banded in he distinctly said that he attended to business, but there was a modicum of truth in the letter. He had pawned a ring since the receiving order was made, 13:.cause he bad no money. He knew the ring belonged to the trustee of the eetate. He got a man to take the ring, but was not on that day drinking ; he wag in a public. house. He had asked for money for maintenance and was bound to get it to carry on his home. He got 12i for the ring and would swear that lOs went towards the kou.e. He had not pawned any other property. After a further searching examination regarding money transactions the Cane was adjourned. (
