GA.3fE TRESPASS AT CATLCHETII.-At the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, a man named James Tay- lor,. alias "Paddle," residing at Cadishead, was charged with trespassing in search of game, and Joseph and Benjamin Warburton were summoned for aiding and abetting. Taylor was fined 40s and costs, and the other men 20s and costs.—Another man named Luke Taylor, alias "Tar," also of Cadis- head, was summoned forusing a gun for the pur- pose of killing a rabbit. The defendant called Peter Mann and John Taylor, both of whom swore he was in the house of the latter at Cadishead at the time of the alleged offence. The charge was dismissed.

• BOWLING.—On Saturday the second open handi- cap main at bowls took place on the green attached to the Bull's Head Inn, Church-street, when the landlord added a copper kettle to an entrance fee of is each. There were 64 players, who contested the various games in a friendly manner, and the green was in its usual good order. The result of the main was as follows :-1, J. Bridge, Si and kettle; 2, J. Shaw, 12s and a small trunk; 3;.5. Price, 6s and hat box; 4, P. Wells, 6s; and 12 other prizes to com- petitors who won their second rotuid.—The Bank Quay Bowling Green was well attended on Thnrs- day afternoon, when a handicap main of bowls took place, Nit there were only 24 subscribers, who paid an entrance fee of 2s each. The green was in ex- cellent condition, and the bowling throughout the main was of a good character, which resulted in the President (Mr. W. Lawless) gaining first prize, J. T. Massey second, and George Cheshire third. DEATH ON THR RAILWA Y.-011 Thursday morn- ing an inquest was held in the Patten Arms Hotel, touching the death of Richard Edwards, aged 23, a i shunter n the employ of the London and North- Western Railway. Company, who was killed on Monday whilst following his occupation at Bank :Quay low level station. The coroner was Mr. Brig- house. Gie deceased, it appeared, was the son of a, ;Welsh farmer, livink near Llandudno, but had, as stated, been engaged as a shunter at Bank Quay. On Monday afternoon he was engaged coupling and 'uncoupling wagons near Crosfield's Crossing on the .low level line. The train having been made up he gave the engine driver, Joseph Pennington, the sig- nal to go on, and, after the train was in motion, he was seen to be riding on one of the waggons by Frederick Massey, a signal-man. In passing he said to MassOthat he had heard he (Massey) had just got mariied, and that he would have to stand' his wedding glass. The train stopped for a short time in Bank Quay station, and after it moved out the attention of a porter named Arthur Smith was Called to the dead body of the, deceased which was lying on the rail. No one had seen how deceased got under the wheels, but Mr. Ashurst, the station- master, gave it as his opinion that he had been creeping across the line beneath the wagon when the train started to leave the station, andhad been caught by the wheels. The father of the deceased, who, it was stated, could not speak English, was in attendance at the inquest, but was not called upon to give evidence as to identity, because deceased's head and face had been so mutilated as to be un- recognisable. M. verdict of " Acciddital death" was returned. •

A • Crcurars' Rug.—On Thursday evening nearly thirty members of the St. Helens Cyclists Club had I a pleasant run from St. Helens to Warrington. Leaving St. Helens at about /45, the party reached Warrington about eight o'clock, just when the streets were at their busiest. The machines in- cluded bicycles, tricycles, and a tandem—driven by a lady—and the procession, in the dusk of the even- ing, was unusually imposing. Mr. Wolfenden was captain. At the Norton Arms, Warrington, a supper had been provided for the cyclists, and, it having received full justice at their hands, the tables were cleared and the usual toasts honoured. The toast of the L. Helens Cyclists' Club was received with enthugium. Ip was ,proposed by Mr. Ashton (pre- sident), and seconded by Mr. Broadhead. Afterwards Mr. Broadhead sang "Sailing, sailing," Mr. Ashton . sang "Our Jack's come home from sea," Mr. Broad- head sang "He's got 'em on," Mr. C. Brown (sub- captain) sang "Our Nellie," and Mr. J. B. Warren sang "They dursent do it now." The party under- took the return journey at eleven o'clock, arriving home at about midnight. THE ROBBERY FRODI A LADY IN THE MARKET.— At the Borough Court, on Monday, John Rakin, a young man, described as a bookmaker's clerk, of Liverpool, was charged on remand with stealing .£4B lOs in a purse, from a satchel, carried by Mrs. Martha Oates, wife of the landlord of the Fleetwood Arms Inn, Runcorn, while in the Market Shed, on the 12th inst. Chief Constable Hunt now reported that he had made inquiries regarding the house in Gerard-street, Liverpool, where the prisoner said he lodged, and found that it was one frequented by thieves and persons of bad character. That fact was made known to prisoner, who then gave a second account of himself, and said that he came from a district in Birmingham. Inquiries made at Bir- mingham resulted in that story being found un- true. Under the circumstances it was thought beat ' to have the prisoner photographed, which he strongly resisted.—Prisoner: Why should I be sub- jected to have my photograph sent about. I have got respectable parents, and I don't want them to know. It is gambling that has brought me to it. I am sure it will never occur again.—The Bench said that the charge was a serious one, and sent prisoner to gaol for two months, with hard labour.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Lord Tollemache Is progressing favourably, The death is announced of Pei tjor-General Sir Harry Ord, C.B.
Mr. Ruskin continues to rest well and to take his food moderately. . ... _ ._
A telegram from Madrid states that a popular movement is b.ing organised in favour of granting certain tariff con- cessions to England.

A distress to recover extraordinary tithes took place at Lower H.lston, Kent, on Friday. The farmers passed reso- lutions condemning tithes. Official inquiry at St. Petersburg has elicited the fact that the recent robbery of 220,000 roubles from the State Bank was committed by employes of the bank. An exploeion took place on Friday morning between ten and eleven o'clock at the Dartford Gunpowder Works. A German who was experimenting wee seriously injured, and others were injured slightly. The distress amongst Oldham operatives on strike but not In the union becomes daily more severe, and the nunber of persons applying te the Guardians for relief is enormous, but in very few MOS It it 6rantql. The strike hap reac'led the firth Ilek, Ten Puma or WALES.—The Prince of Wales arrived in Perth on Friday morning. en route for Aberdeen. His Royal Highness was accompanied by Sir Allan Young and Mr. Mackenzie, of Kintail. The Prince was loudly cheered. The Prince arrived at Aberdeen at noon. UNLAWFUL DNIENTION OF A o.llll.—Our Winchester cor- respondent telegraphs that by direction of the Secretary of State inquiries are being made, at the inst ince of Mrs. Jose- phine Butler, Into the alleged abduction and detention of Eliza Armstrong, a girl un.ter fourteen years of age. The girl's case has bass before the London police courts, and has attracted considetable attention.

SERIOUS CARTAGE ACCIDENT.—WhiIst driving in the neighbourhood of Trefnant, on Friday, the Dean of St. Asaph and Mr. Bonnor were thrown from their carriage owing to the hor,es taking fright at a passing tricycle. The Dean escaped comparatively unhurt, but Mr. Bonnor was somewhat seriously injured. The coachman was kicked bY both horses, in addition to being thrown, and sustained severe injuries. Tun SHOEBURYNE99 CAMP.—Tha volunteer camp at Shoeburyness broke up on Friday morning. A considerable number of the volunteers marched out of camp soon after nine o'clock, and left by train for their destination. They were headed by the baud of the Ist Sussex (Brighton) Corps. The remainder of the men left by train at ten o'clock. The meeting is regarded as having bean a success- ful one so far as shooting is concerned. WRECK AND Loss OF EIGHTEEN LIVES.—A. Central News telegram, dated New York, Friday, states :—A telegram has reached here from San Francisco recording the loss of the British barque liaddingtonshire of Glasgow, the vessel hav- ing been totally wrecked off that port. The captain and seventeen men were drowned. _ The Haddingtonshire was almost a new ship of 1,175 gross tannage. She was built of iron and launched only last year.

AN ELOPER SENT TO PRISON.,--00 Friday morning, at Rochdale, Edmund Hartley, a painter, residing off Spot- land-road, and a prominent member of a political club in Rochdale, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment with hard labour for deserting his wife and family and elop- ing with a young woman named Mary Jane Turner, a neigh- bour. He was captured in Halifax living with the young woman in furnished apartments. Tun Pnorncrion OF GIRLS,—At a national conference on the protection of girls, in St. James's Hall, Loudon, on Friday morning, with Mr. George &melt, M.P., in the chair, on the motion of Mr. Stanteld, M.P., a resolution was carried, with but one dissentient, recommending the forma- tion of national vigilance association of man and women for the enforcement and improvement of the laws for the repression of criminal vice and public immorality. Lord Lyrnington moved a resolution calling upon the Local Vigilance Committees to affiliate themselves to the national association.

TRAGIC AFFAIR IN LONDON.—At twenty minutes to eight o'clock on Friday morning, Mr. S. Henderson Williams, of Nor 3, Temple Gardens, Temple, Lendon, committed suicide by leaping from a higk window overlooking the Embank- ment.. He fell into the gardens beneath, and so injured himself that he died a qaarter of an hour afterwards. A man belonging to au Aberdeen steamer lying at Temple Pier, who helped to remove the body, fall down, dead soon after returning to his vessel. It appears that Mr.. Williams had been eufaering from a severe attack of rheumatic fever,which may have affected his mind. RIOT err A POLITICAL Mmensro.--Au extraordinary riot took place on Thursday night at a meeting; at Solihull, near Birmingham, in support of Mr. Phipson Beale, the Liberal candidate for North Warwickshire. The platform was stormed, by a mob of young Conservatives. Several ladies, including Mrs. Beale, the wife of the candidate, rushed from the platform in great alarm. Sticks were freely used, and free fights occurred in various parts of the hall. A rush was made at Mr. Jesse Coinage while helves speaking, and it VMS only by the formation of a body guard that he was protected from personal violence. The tables and chairs were smashed, and the meeting in the end was broken up amidst a scene of indescribable disorder. The Liberals say asveral well-known gentlemen in the locality were instru- mental in instigating the proceedings. Tim CHORLRY MURDER CASES.—OD Friday morning, Alfred Holbrooks and Andrew Goldsberry were charged at the Chorley Police Court with the wilful. murder of Jas. Fallon, On Saturday last. The evidence adduced showed that the affair was of the most brutal character. John Hed• shavr, etated that when he handed his hat to Goldsberry, Holbrooks came up, and they kicked deceased on the body while he was on the ground. Holbrooks kicked him about the head, Goldeberry calling out, " lick him in the neck." Holbreoke did so, and Gobliberry said, " You've done enough," and Holbrooks again kicked.him, and then said, " Let'elnish .hint," and again kickedlim violently. At Chorlev,Yeatotekll• Holbrpoks and Geldsborry were com- mitted for trial on the charge of murdering. James Fallon by brutally kicking and beating him.

• NE' '. VORIS, FRID,L4 —A despatch from Lima announces that the insurgent leader Caceres arrived at Cants co the 18th inst., the day after the defeat at that place ofi the Government troops. It is added that he ordered the execu- tion of. several of the prisoners. THE CHOLERA IN FRANCE.

A Central Now tele4ram from Mirseilles says that on Thursday night 40 deaths occurred in the city, of which 25 are doe to cholera. Nearly all of those who succumbed bad only been recently attacked, death in some asses re• suiting in a few hours after tho attsck. The Phan Hospi- tal is now crowded with persons suffering from cholera, and more accommodation Is required. THE AFGHAN FIiONTIE.R.—ALARMING INCIDENT.

A.Meshed telegram in the second edition of the Tinaes save that a collision nea-iv occurred on the 13th inst., be- tween the Afghan. and Russian outposts at Kara Tepe, 18 miles from Chemin Raid. A few Russian troopers ap- proacined the former place, and the Afghans stood to their arms. The Ruasian cami.r ordered his teen to unsling their carbines, and was accidi.ntally shot by one of his own men in obeying the order. The Af4hans detained the Russians pending orders from Herat, treating the wounded man kind- ly, and finally gent him back to Cb.aman Bald. The Af- ghans have been exonerated from all blame, and have been thanked for their humanity by the Russian commander, who has promised that his men will not again advance beyond the Chamaia Bald. Sir West Ridgway and his escort are still in the vicinity of Herat, where four officers of the Royal Engineers are superintending the repair of the fortifica- tion,.

GUY'S HOSPITAL. The MEDICAL SESSION COMMENCES on Thursday. October lit. The Hospital contains, besides the beds for medical and sur- gical cases, wards for obstetric, ophthalmic. and other special departments. Special classes are held in the Hospital for students preparing for the Examinations of the University of London and of other examining boards. Appointments.—The house surgeons and house physicians, the obstetric residents, clinical asastants, and dressers are se- lected from the students according to merit and withmt pay- ment. There are also a large number of junior appointments, every part of the Hospital practice being systematically em- ployed for instruction. Entrance ficholarshlpc—Opan scholarship of 125 guineas In classics, mathematics, and modern languages. Open cholar- ship of 123 guineas in chemistry, physics', botany, and zoology. Prises, toc.—Six scholarships, varying in value from £lO to ego each, for general prone ency in medical study; the Trea- surer's gold medal in medicine ; the Treasurer's geld medal in surgery; the Gurney Hoare prize of £35 for clinical study; the Beaney prize of 30 guinea.‘ for nathology ; the Sands Cox schol- arship of £l5 per annum for three years for physiology ; the Joseph Hoare prizes of .225 and £10; the Michael Hsrros prize of £lO for anatomy ; the Mackenzie Bacon priza of £lO for ophthalmoseopy. For prospectus and further information apply to the Dean. Dr. B. Taylor. Guy's Hospital. Landon, B.E , July, 1885.
